units.title: I. Of the difference between Pure and Empirical Knowledge

items.text: Human knowledge begins in experience because sensory objects awaken the cognitive faculties.
Experience supplies the occasion and raw material of cognition, but does not thereby account for everything contained in knowledge.
Empirical knowledge is potentially composite, consisting of sensory impressions and contributions supplied by the cognitive faculty itself.
The decisive question is whether any knowledge exists that is independent of all experience rather than merely independent of a particular experience.
A priori knowledge is defined as absolute independence from experience, whereas empirical knowledge is possible only through experience.
A priori knowledge divides into pure and impure according to whether empirical elements remain mixed within it.
Knowledge begins with experience in temporal order.
Sensory objects awaken the faculty of cognition into activity.
Cognition converts sensuous impressions into knowledge of objects through comparison, connection, and separation.
Experience provides sensuous impressions that function as the raw material of empirical knowledge.
The cognitive faculty can supply elements that are not received through sensory impressions.
Empirical knowledge can therefore be a compound of sensory reception and cognitive contribution.
The cognitive contribution may initially be indistinguishable from the sensory element.
Temporal priority of experience does not establish that every element of knowledge originates from experience.
Knowledge is a priori only when it is independent of all experience, not merely independent of a particular experience.
Empirical knowledge is possible only through experience.
A priori knowledge may contain empirical elements and thereby become impure.
Pure a priori knowledge contains no empirical element.
The concept of change is derived from experience.
Knowledge does not arise exclusively from sensory impressions.
The fact that knowledge begins with experience does not entail that all knowledge arises out of experience.
A priori knowledge is not knowledge merely acquired without waiting for a particular event.
A general rule borrowed from experience is not genuinely independent of experience.
A priori knowledge is not necessarily pure.
Pure a priori knowledge is not knowledge containing an empirical conception.
Empirical knowledge is not reducible to the passive reception of impressions.
The origin of cognition in experience and the source of every component of knowledge must be analytically distinguished.
Sensory impressions are necessary conditions for the awakening of cognition without being sufficient conditions for the resulting knowledge.
The possibility of a priori knowledge follows from the presence of cognitive elements not supplied by experience.
Immediate non-derivation from experience is insufficient to establish a priori status when the governing rule itself originates in experience.
The distinction between pure and impure a priori knowledge depends on whether the content under examination contains an empirical concept.
Identifying a priori knowledge requires separating cognitive contribution from the empirical material with which it is initially fused.
The text separates the temporal condition of cognition from the epistemic dependence of knowledge, preventing the beginning of knowledge from determining the origin of all its content.
Experience functions simultaneously as the initiating condition of cognition and as an insufficient explanation of the cognitive structure produced from it.
The distinction between empirical and a priori knowledge is established by dependence, not by psychological sequence or the absence of a particular observation.
The classification of knowledge requires a layered analysis of source, content, and mixture rather than a single opposition between experience and non-experience.
The system depends on the falsity of the assumption that temporal priority and epistemic derivation are identical.
The system excludes the assumption that sensory receptivity is the whole of cognition.
The system excludes the assumption that whatever is not immediately inferred from experience is therefore independent of experience.
The system excludes a binary in which knowledge is either wholly empirical or wholly detached from the conditions of experience.
The system excludes the assumption that the empirical and non-empirical components of knowledge are transparently distinguishable at first encounter.
The system excludes the assumption that independence from experience guarantees absence of all empirical content.
The argument is organized around the impossibility of inferring the complete structure of cognition from the conditions under which cognition is awakened.
The text forecloses a purely receptive model of knowledge without yet fully specifying the internal principles supplied by cognition.
The possibility of a priori knowledge remains dependent on a separation that ordinary consciousness initially cannot perform.
The text presupposes that the boundary between received material and cognitive contribution is real even though its criteria of demarcation remain undeveloped here.
Sensory affection → cognitive activation → comparison, connection, and separation → object-directed knowledge.
Experience as temporal beginning + cognitive contribution → composite empirical knowledge.
Composite knowledge → analytical separation of received and supplied elements → possibility of identifying a priori content.
Absolute independence from all experience → a priori knowledge; dependence on experience → empirical knowledge.
A priori knowledge + retained empirical element → impure a priori knowledge; a priori knowledge + absence of empirical element → pure a priori knowledge.
Apparent immediate independence → test of the origin of the governing rule → rejection or confirmation of a priori status.
Sensory initiation → cognitive processing → composite knowledge → distinction between temporal beginning and epistemic origin.
Ambiguous meaning of “a priori” → restriction to absolute independence from experience → division into pure and impure a priori knowledge.
Experience is reclassified from the total source of knowledge to the initiating condition and material occasion of cognition.
The opposition between empirical and a priori knowledge is shifted from chronology to dependence.
The apparent unity of experience is divided into sensory reception and cognitive contribution.
The category of a priori knowledge is internally differentiated rather than treated as homogeneous.
The question of knowledge becomes a problem of component analysis and origin-tracing rather than mere observation of acquisition.
Surface — The text distinguishes knowledge beginning with experience from knowledge arising wholly out of experience.
Structural — Cognition is modeled as an operation that organizes sensory material through comparison, connection, and separation.
Metastrategic — The argument establishes definitional controls against loose uses of “a priori” and redirects inquiry toward absolute rather than local independence.
Ontological/Temporal — Time governs the awakening of cognition, while epistemic dependence governs the classification of knowledge.
Epistemic — Knowledge is treated as potentially heterogeneous in constitution, with sensory and cognitive elements requiring retrospective separation.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the central distinction between knowledge beginning with experience and knowledge wholly derived from experience.
The axioms are sufficient to derive the definitions of empirical, a priori, pure, and impure knowledge.
The reconstruction preserves the argument’s decisive movement from temporal sequence to epistemic dependence.
The system remains underdetermined concerning the specific faculties or principles that supply non-empirical elements.
The system is internally coherent at the level of distinction and classification, but its promised investigation of a priori knowledge is not completed within the passage.
The argument depends on the unresolved methodological possibility of separating cognitive contribution from sensory material after their initial fusion.

units.title: II. The Human Intellect, even in an Unphilosophical State, is in Possession of Certain Cognitions “à priori”.

items.text: The argument seeks a secure criterion for distinguishing pure cognition from empirical cognition.
Experience establishes how objects are constituted in observed cases but cannot establish that they could not be otherwise.
Necessity and strict, exceptionless universality identify cognition as independent of experience and therefore a priori.
Mathematical judgments and causal judgments exhibit the required necessity and universality.
The certainty of experience itself presupposes non-empirical rules, preventing empirical cognition from serving as its own ultimate ground.
The same a priori origin appears in concepts when empirical predicates are removed but space and substance remain unavoidable in thought.
Experience teaches the actual constitution of an object but not the impossibility of its being otherwise.
A proposition that contains necessity in its conception is a priori.
A proposition is absolutely a priori when it is not derived from any proposition lacking necessity.
Empirical universality is only assumed and comparative universality established through induction.
Strict universality admits no possible exception and therefore cannot be derived from experience.
Necessity and strict universality are inseparably connected and each can serve as an infallible test of a priori cognition.
Human cognition contains judgments exhibiting necessity and strict universality.
The concept of a cause entails a necessary connection with an effect and a universally valid rule.
The certainty and possibility of experience presuppose rules that are not themselves empirical.
Removing all sensible predicates from the concept of a body leaves the occupied space unremovable in thought.
Removing empirical properties from the concept of an object leaves the relations through which it is thought as substance or as adhering to substance.
Pure cognition is not cognition whose validity is established only by observed regularity.
Strict universality is not an enlarged form of inductive universality.
Necessity is not generated by the repeated conjunction of representations.
Causality is not reducible to a subjective habit formed by frequent association.
A causal judgment is not merely a report of successive occurrences.
The concept of a body is not exhausted by color, hardness, softness, weight, or impenetrability.
The concept of an object is not exhausted by properties supplied through experience.
Modal necessity distinguishes a priori cognition from cognition that merely records actual regularities.
A proposition possesses absolute a priori status only when its necessity is not inherited from a contingent source.
Induction cannot convert comparative universality into strict universality.
Either necessity or strict universality can operationally identify a priori cognition, even though the two criteria belong together.
Mathematical propositions and the proposition that every change must have a cause function as instances of a priori judgment.
If causality were derived from frequent association, the necessity of causal connection would become merely subjective and the concept of cause would disappear.
Empirical rules cannot serve as first principles of experience when the certainty of experience depends upon those rules.
Space has an a priori origin because it remains thinkable after empirical bodily predicates have been removed.
Substance has an a priori origin because its determining relations cannot be removed from the thought of an object.
Human cognition must possess and exercise a faculty of pure a priori cognition.
The distinction between empirical and pure cognition becomes a distinction between contingent acquisition and necessary conditions of intelligibility.
The modal structure of a judgment, rather than its subject matter alone, determines its epistemic source.
Experience is rendered epistemically dependent upon a priori rules rather than being treated as the ultimate origin of those rules.
The a priori extends beyond judgments into the conceptual conditions under which objects can be thought.
The critique of associationism preserves objective causality by locating necessity in cognition rather than in repeated succession.
The removal of empirical predicates operates as a negative method for exposing non-empirical cognitive structures.
Experience cannot be the complete ground of the certainty that experience possesses.
Finite observation cannot supply the transition from repeated occurrence to impossibility of exception.
Objective necessity cannot be reduced to a psychological state produced by habit.
The conditions governing experience cannot themselves be treated as contingent contents of experience.
The intelligibility of an object cannot be exhausted by predicates that vary with sensory encounter.
No purely empirical account can explain why certain structures remain unavoidable when empirical content is removed.
The system excludes an epistemology in which experience supplies both its contents and the ultimate validity of the rules organizing those contents.
The system excludes a continuous passage from frequent regularity to strict necessity by accumulation alone.
The system excludes a causal order whose necessity exists only as a subjective effect of representation.
The system excludes a conception of objects in which all intelligible structure disappears with sensible predicates.
The system establishes the existence of a priori cognition without fully specifying the internal constitution of the faculty that supplies it.
Actual observation is separated from modal impossibility.
Necessity in conception is used to classify a proposition as a priori.
Inductive regularity is separated from strict universality.
Necessity and strict universality converge as reciprocal diagnostics of a priori cognition.
Mathematical and causal judgments instantiate the diagnostic criteria.
The Humean derivation of causality is rejected because association yields only subjective necessity.
The dependence of experience upon rules produces a transcendental reversal: experience presupposes a priori cognition.
Empirical predicates are progressively removed from concepts, revealing residual structures that cannot be thought away.
Judgmental and conceptual residues converge in the conclusion that human cognition possesses a pure a priori faculty.
Empirical contingency → demand for a criterion → necessity and strict universality.
Comparative induction → failure to establish exceptionlessness → a priori source.
Mathematical and causal judgments → rejection of subjective associationism → objective necessity.
Conditions of experience → conceptual subtraction → establishment of a priori cognition in judgments and concepts.
Pure and empirical cognition are reclassified by modal force rather than by subject matter or degree of observational support.
The distinction between “true in most cases” and “valid without exception” becomes structurally decisive.
Experience is repositioned from foundational source to conditioned field of cognition.
Causality is removed from the domain of psychological association and placed within necessary cognition.
The a priori is extended from propositions to the residual structures of concepts.
Abstraction becomes a diagnostic operation: what survives removal of empirical content marks the non-empirical architecture of cognition.
Surface: Judgments are classified according to necessity, strict universality, and empirical derivation.
Structural: Experience is shown to depend upon non-empirical rules that organize its certainty and intelligibility.
Metastrategic: The argument shifts the burden of proof from empirical accumulation to the conditions that make experience and judgment possible.
Ontological/Temporal: Reality is divided between contingent occurrence and necessary connection, while space and substance persist as unavoidable forms of objectual thought.
The extracted axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the movement from the empirical–pure distinction to the existence of a priori cognition.
The reconstruction preserves the sequence from criterion, through examples and transcendental grounding, to conceptual analysis.
The system is internally coherent if necessity and strict universality are accepted as marks of non-empirical validity.
The relation between necessity and strict universality remains asserted as inseparable while their separate diagnostic use introduces an unresolved operational tension.
The argument does not fully specify how conceptual necessity, judgmental necessity, and the structure of the a priori faculty are related.
The subtraction argument establishes the persistence of space and substance in thought but leaves open whether this persistence alone establishes their full objective validity.

The reconstruction depends on the text’s compressed transition from the certainty of experience to the existence of its a priori conditions, but it preserves the argument’s essential generative logic.

identity.title: II. The Human Intellect, even in an Unphilosophical State, is in Possession of Certain Cognitions “à priori”.

units.title: III. Philosophy stands in need of a Science which shall Determine the Possibility, Principles, and Extent of Human Knowledge “à priori”

items.text: Human reason forms cognitions that claim validity beyond the bounds of possible experience.
The importance of supersensible problems makes reason pursue them even without experiential guidance.
Metaphysics becomes dogmatic when it attempts to solve these problems before determining whether reason is capable of doing so.
The argument is diagnostic and transcendental: it shifts attention from metaphysical conclusions to the origin, possibility, extent, validity, and worth of a priori cognition.
Mathematical success and analytic concept-resolution generate a false impression that reason can extend knowledge without limit.
The argument culminates in distinguishing genuine a priori knowledge from the unrecognized addition of foreign concepts to given concepts.
Cognition can claim validity beyond possible experience through concepts for which no corresponding object is given in experience.
Pure reason is unavoidably directed toward the problems of God, freedom, and immortality.
Metaphysics traditionally attempts to solve supersensible problems without first investigating reason’s capacity for the task.
A legitimate science of cognition must determine the source, possibility, extent, validity, and worth of a priori knowledge before constructing conclusions from it.
Experience provides the secure field of cognitive constraint but cannot directly guide inquiry into the supersensible.
Mathematics demonstrates that some cognition can be a priori, certain, and productive.
Mathematical a priori cognition depends upon intuition, including intuition that can itself be given a priori, rather than upon mere conceptual analysis.
The success of mathematics can be misinterpreted as evidence that reason has no limit beyond experience.
The absence of experiential opposition permits speculative reason to extend its claims without an external check.
Analysis of already possessed concepts can yield a priori clarification without adding new conceptual content.
The formal novelty and practical usefulness of analytic results can make clarification appear to be substantive cognitive expansion.
Reason can introduce a priori concepts foreign to given concepts without recognizing how those additions arise.
Analytic and synthetic modes of a priori cognition must be distinguished.
Metaphysics is not initially grounded in a prior critique of reason’s ability or inability.
Supersensible inquiry is not secured by instruction or guidance from experience.
Mathematical a priori cognition is not equivalent to cognition derived from pure concepts alone.
The analysis of a concept is not an addition of new content to that concept.
The absence of contradiction is not proof of speculative validity.
The expansion of judgment beyond experience is not automatically an expansion of knowledge.
A speculative construction does not cease to be fictional merely because it is carefully constructed.
A completed conceptual edifice is not evidence that its foundation is sound.
The possibility of metaphysics must be investigated before metaphysical problems can be legitimately solved.
The primary question concerning supersensible cognition is epistemic rather than doctrinal: how such cognition arises and what validity it possesses.
Mathematical success cannot by itself authorize speculative metaphysics because mathematical a priori cognition is mediated by intuition.
The lack of experiential resistance removes the principal check against extending concepts beyond their legitimate domain.
Analytic clarification can generate the appearance of cognitive progress without increasing conceptual content.
Analytic success can conceal the unauthorized insertion of synthetic content.
The absence of an account of origin makes a priori additions epistemically suspect even when they appear formally coherent.
Critical inquiry must distinguish the clarification of what is already thought from the production of genuinely new a priori cognition.
The critical project does not abolish supersensible questions; it reverses the order of inquiry by requiring the examination of reason before the construction of answers.
The same general form of a priori cognition can support genuine science in one domain and speculative illusion in another.
The limits of reason are not external restrictions added after cognition; they are conditions for determining whether cognition has validity at all.
Speculative overreach is produced by transferring a legitimate local method of cognition into a domain where its enabling conditions are absent.
The text establishes the necessity of critical investigation without yet supplying the positive criterion by which every valid synthetic a priori claim will be identified.
The existence of a priori cognition does not entail unrestricted metaphysical cognition.
The certainty of mathematics does not function as a universal warrant for every claim made independently of experience.
Formal clarification does not constitute material enlargement of knowledge.
The absence of empirical refutation does not establish validity in a domain beyond experience.
Escape from experiential limits does not amount to access to supersensible truth.
The successful completion of a system does not retroactively establish its foundations.
Reason cannot treat the origin of its own additions as irrelevant to their validity.
No unrestricted bridge connects conceptual possibility with the existence or knowability of a corresponding supersensible object.
No self-authenticating form of pure reason guarantees that its extensions beyond experience are knowledge rather than fiction.
No transfer principle permits mathematical a priori validity to pass automatically into metaphysical a priori validity.
No experiential tribunal is available to settle supersensible claims directly.
No completed edifice can supply the missing investigation of the conditions under which its cognitions are possible.
Supersensible problems arise as unavoidable and elevated aims of pure reason.
The absence of corresponding objects in experience drives reason beyond the secure ground of experience.
The importance of these problems produces dogmatic metaphysics before reason’s capacity has been examined.
The demonstrated productivity of mathematical a priori cognition supplies a misleading model for unrestricted reason.
The obscured role of intuition and the absence of experiential resistance permit conceptual extension beyond its legitimate conditions.
Analytic clarification produces apparent novelty without added content, thereby concealing the insertion of foreign synthetic concepts.
The distinction between analytic and synthetic a priori cognition initiates the required critical science.

Unavoidable supersensible problems → dogmatic metaphysical construction → foundation problem → mathematical analogy → overextension beyond experience → analytic illusion → unrecognized synthetic addition → distinction of a priori modes.
The governing question shifts from what reason can construct to how a priori cognition arises and what extent, validity, and worth it possesses.
Metaphysics is reclassified from a doctrine-producing enterprise into an object of prior epistemic investigation.
A priori cognition is divided into different operative types rather than treated as a single undifferentiated capacity.
Mathematical success is reclassified as condition-dependent evidence rather than proof of unrestricted rational reach.
The lack of contradiction loses its status as an adequate test of supersensible cognition.
Apparent conceptual expansion becomes diagnostically separable into clarification, genuine addition, and unauthorized importation.
The temporal order of inquiry is reversed: foundation must precede the construction of the system.
The boundary of possible experience becomes a methodological criterion for evaluating claims rather than merely a limit to be overcome.
Surface — The text concerns reason’s pursuit of God, freedom, immortality, and other supersensible objects.
Structural — The text analyzes how experience, intuition, concepts, and resistance condition the validity of a priori cognition.
Metastrategic — The text replaces premature doctrinal construction with a prior investigation of reason’s powers, limits, and procedures.

Ontological/Temporal — Possible experience functions as the boundary of object-directed cognition, while the order of foundation before edifice becomes the governing temporal model of legitimate inquiry.
The extracted axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the movement from supersensible ambition through dogmatic metaphysics to the demand for critical investigation.
The system remains underdetermined concerning the positive conditions that would validate synthetic a priori cognition.
The structure is internally coherent because mathematical success, analytic clarification, and speculative overreach are treated as distinct but causally connected phenomena.
The strongest component is the diagnosis of how legitimate a priori cognition can become the model for illegitimate extension.
Reconstruction depends on retaining the distinction between intuition and concept, and between formal clarification and material addition.
The central unresolved tension is that supersensible problems are presented as unavoidable while experience cannot adjudicate them directly.
The reconstruction preserves the argument’s real movement from the demand for metaphysical knowledge to the prior demand for a science of the conditions and limits of knowledge.

identity.title: III. Philosophy stands in need of a Science which shall Determine the Possibility, Principles, and Extent of Human Knowledge “à priori”

units.title: IV. Of the Difference Between Analytical and Synthetical Judgements.

items.text: The argument distinguishes judgments according to whether the predicate is contained in the subject-conception or stands outside it while remaining connected to it.
Analytical judgments explicate what is already contained in a conception through identity, whereas synthetical judgments augment the conception through a non-identical predicate.
Analytical judgments require no appeal to experience because their predicates can be extracted from concepts through analysis and the principle of contradiction.
Judgments of experience are synthetical because experience connects separately conceived representations within a larger whole.
Experience can ground the possibility of empirical synthesis but cannot ground the universality and necessity claimed by synthetic a priori judgments.
The decisive problem is therefore the unknown ground that makes a non-contained predicate necessarily connectable with a conception.
The argument subordinates analysis to synthesis by treating conceptual clarification as preparation for the genuine acquisition of knowledge.
A judgment cogitates a relation between a subject-conception and a predicate.
A predicate relates to a subject either by being contained in its conception or by standing outside it while remaining connected to it.
An analytical judgment is governed by identity between the predicate and the subject-conception.
An analytical judgment explicates constituent content already thought in the subject-conception.
Analysis can disclose an analytical predicate through conceptual clarification and the principle of contradiction.
A synthetical judgment connects a predicate with a subject without the predicate being contained in the subject-conception.
A synthetical judgment augments knowledge by adding content unavailable through analysis of the subject-conception alone.
Judgments of experience are synthetical because their predicates are connected with their subjects through experience rather than conceptual identity.
Empirical synthesis establishes contingent connection but cannot establish universal and necessary connection.
A synthetic a priori judgment connects a non-contained predicate with a conception universally and necessarily without relying on experience.
The ground of synthetic a priori connection is an unknown condition upon which the understanding relies when it joins a foreign predicate to a conception.
Analytical judgments are preparatory to the clearer and more extended synthesis on which speculative a priori knowledge depends.
Analytical judgment is not founded on empirical testimony.
Analytical judgment does not extend the subject-conception by adding new content.
A synthetical predicate is not recoverable through analysis of the subject-conception alone.
The connection in a synthetical judgment is not identity between predicate and subject.
Experience does not provide the universality or necessity required by synthetic a priori judgment.
The empirical connection of two concepts does not by itself establish their necessary connection.
The concept of a cause is not contained in the mere concept of something that happens.
Synthetic a priori knowledge cannot appeal to experience as its sufficient foundation.
Analytical judgments can be established without consulting experience.
Analytical judgments possess a priori necessity because their truth is disclosed within the subject-conception rather than learned from contingent occurrences.
Empirical knowledge necessarily involves an addition to concepts that analysis alone cannot supply.
Experience can join independently conceived representations as parts of one experiential totality.
The distinction between analytical and synthetical judgment is independent of the distinction between a priori and empirical cognition.
The possibility of synthetic a priori judgment cannot be explained by either conceptual containment or empirical association alone.
The proposition that everything that happens has a cause functions as a test case for a predicate that is non-contained yet claimed to be necessarily connected.
The clarification of concepts is a necessary condition for reliable synthesis but is not itself the principal acquisition of knowledge.
The argument transforms a classificatory distinction between judgments into a foundational problem concerning the possibility of necessary knowledge that extends concepts.
The system assigns different epistemic functions to analysis and synthesis: analysis secures intelligibility, while synthesis produces augmentation.
Experience occupies an intermediate epistemic position: it is sufficient for contingent synthesis but structurally insufficient for necessary synthesis.
Synthetic a priori judgment requires a mode of connection that is neither conceptual identity nor empirical conjunction.
The entire project of speculative a priori knowledge depends on explaining how augmentation can acquire necessity without becoming reducible to analysis.
The passage establishes the problem of synthetic a priori cognition without yet determining the nature of its unknown ground.
Necessary knowledge cannot be reduced to repeated empirical conjunction.
Augmentative knowledge cannot be reduced to the explication of concepts already possessed.
The relation between subject and predicate cannot be exhaustively modeled either as containment or as contingent association.
The source of universal necessity cannot be located in the testimony of experience.
The possibility of speculative knowledge cannot be secured by conceptual analysis alone.
A non-contained predicate cannot become necessary merely by being repeatedly found alongside the subject in experience.
The distinction between analysis and synthesis cannot be collapsed into the distinction between verbal clarification and factual observation.
The ground that makes synthetic a priori connection possible remains unexhibited within the passage.
Neither the subject-conception nor experience, taken alone, contains the principle of necessary augmentation.
The system excludes any account in which all genuine knowledge is either conceptual repetition or empirical accumulation.
The possibility of necessary synthesis is treated as indispensable but not yet positively formalized.
The argument’s force depends on the absence of an available foundation for connecting foreign predicates with concepts universally and necessarily.
Subject–predicate relation → classification by containment versus external connection.
Containment → identity → analysis → explication → a priori necessity.
External connection → non-identity → synthesis → augmentation.
Synthesis grounded in experience → contingent connection within an experiential whole → empirical judgment.
Non-contained predicate claimed with universality and necessity → exclusion of experience as sufficient ground → synthetic a priori problem.
Synthetic a priori problem → search for an unknown condition of necessary augmentation.
Conceptual analysis → clarification of conditions for judgment → preparation for extended synthesis.
A subject–predicate relation is divided into conceptual containment and non-identical connection.
Containment yields analytical, explicative, and a priori judgment.
Non-identical connection yields synthetical and augmentative judgment.
When non-identical connection is supplied by experience, it yields contingent empirical synthesis.
When non-identical connection is asserted universally and necessarily without experience, it produces the synthetic a priori problem.
The synthetic a priori problem redirects the argument from classification toward the unknown ground of speculative knowledge.
The argument closes by assigning analysis a preparatory function within the larger task of synthesis.
Judgment is reclassified according to the mode of connection between subject and predicate rather than according to subject matter alone.
The opposition between a priori and empirical cognition is separated from the opposition between analytical and synthetical judgment.
Experience is reclassified as a source of contingent synthesis rather than a source of necessity.
The distinction between analysis and synthesis becomes a theory of epistemic functions: clarification versus augmentation.
Synthetic a priori propositions become the central problem of speculative knowledge rather than a marginal hybrid category.
The apparent opposition between conceptual reasoning and experience is displaced by a threefold structure of analysis, empirical synthesis, and synthetic a priori synthesis.
Surface — Judgments differ according to whether the predicate is contained in or external to the subject-conception.
Structural — Analysis operates through conceptual identity and contradiction, while synthesis operates through the connection of distinct representations.
Metastrategic — The argument shifts inquiry from determining judgment-types to locating the ground that authorizes necessary expansion of knowledge.

Ontological/Temporal — Experience organizes representations as parts of a whole, while synthetic a priori cognition claims necessity concerning relations such as cause and effect beyond mere temporal succession.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the distinction between analytical and synthetical judgments.
The structure is sufficient to reconstruct the movement from conceptual taxonomy to the problem of synthetic a priori knowledge.
The system remains underdetermined because the unknown ground of synthetic a priori connection is identified but not explained.
The central tension is that analysis supplies necessity without augmentation, while experience supplies augmentation without necessity.
The passage is internally coherent as a problem-setting argument but incomplete as an account of the solution.
Reconstruction preserves the real movement of the text because the final priority of synthesis is generated from the limits of both analysis and experience.

identity.title: IV. Of the Difference Between Analytical and Synthetical Judgements.

units.title: V. In all Theoretical Sciences of Reason, Synthetical Judgements “à priori” are contained as Principles.

items.text: The text contests the inference from mathematics’ conformity to contradiction to the analyticity of its principles.
It distinguishes logical discernibility of a conclusion from the synthetic ground required to generate that conclusion.
It establishes mathematics as a priori yet synthetic by showing that conceptual analysis must be supplemented by intuition.
It extends the model from mathematics to physics, whose necessary principles add predicates not contained in their concepts.
It defines metaphysics by its necessary attempt to enlarge a priori knowledge beyond analytic clarification and empirical limits.
The argument moves from a diagnostic correction of analytic misclassification to a general architecture of theoretical science grounded in synthetic a priori principles.
Necessity cannot be supplied by experience and therefore marks a priori cognition.
An analytical judgement contains its predicate in the concept of its subject and is governed by the principle of contradiction.
A synthetical judgement adds to a concept a predicate not thought within that concept itself.
Conformity with the principle of contradiction does not prove that a judgement is analytical.
Mathematical cognition requires intuition to determine what conceptual combination alone does not contain.
Proper mathematical propositions are necessary, non-empirical, and synthetical.
Principles of pure physics necessarily add determinations not contained in the concepts to which they apply.
Metaphysics necessarily seeks an enlargement of a priori cognition beyond the analytic exposition of concepts.
A science whose proper aim is a priori enlargement consists, as such, in synthetical judgements a priori.
Mathematical propositions are not analytical deductions from definitions.
The principle of contradiction is not a productive source of synthetic mathematical knowledge.
Necessity is not an empirical acquisition.
The numerical result of a sum is not contained in the mere concept of combining its addends.
The quantitative determination of a geometrical relation is not contained in the merely qualitative concept of straightness.
Metaphysics is not exhausted by analytical dissection of a priori concepts.
Analytically valid mathematical propositions are not the generative principles of mathematics.
Apodeictic certainty can depend on a synthetic ground even when its conclusions are tested or ordered by contradiction.
Arithmetic requires an intuitive construction to determine the sum that is not recoverable by analysing the concepts of the addends.
Geometry requires intuition because its necessary quantitative predicates exceed the qualitative content of its elementary concepts.
Conservation and reciprocal-action principles in physics are synthetic because they determine matter and motion beyond their given concepts.
Metaphysics can count as a distinctive science only insofar as it supplies principles that extend rather than merely clarify a priori concepts.
The division between analytic and synthetic judgement reorganizes theoretical science by separating logical legitimacy from cognitive production.
Theoretical science is constituted not by deduction from concepts alone but by necessary additions to concepts under non-empirical conditions.
Metaphysics is structurally compelled by reason’s demand for a priori extension, even before its particular claims are validated.
The same formal category, synthetic a priori judgement, is made to underwrite mathematical construction, physical law, and metaphysical ambition despite their differing objects.
The system excludes the model in which logical non-contradiction alone can generate substantive knowledge.
The system excludes the model in which all cognition extending a concept must derive from experience.
The system excludes a strict equivalence between a priori cognition and analytic cognition.
The system excludes the reduction of science to either empirical generalization or conceptual tautology.
The system excludes the confinement of metaphysics to conceptual clarification if metaphysics is to retain its proper aim.
The argument is organized around the denial that reason can be both necessarily truth-bearing and merely formal.
The argument forecloses the empiricist restriction under which necessity is unavailable before experience.
The argument presupposes that a non-empirical source of synthetic determination is available, while leaving its unified account outside the present demonstration.
The argument cannot admit that every claim beyond experience is thereby cognitively void, because metaphysics is defined through such extension.
Necessary cognition → exclusion of empirical origin → classification as a priori.
Predicate not contained in subject-concept → classification as synthetic → insufficiency of conceptual analysis.
Mathematical insufficiency of concepts → recourse to intuition → construction of necessary synthetic judgement.
Physical law exceeds object-concept → necessary synthetic principle → pure natural science.
Reason seeks a priori enlargement beyond analysis and experience → metaphysical principles must be synthetic a priori.
Synthetic a priori principle across distinct sciences → theoretical science is reclassified by its mode of grounding rather than by its object-domain.
Mathematical apodeicticity → mistaken identification with analyticity → distinction between logical test and cognitive ground.
Conceptual insufficiency in arithmetic and geometry → intuition → mathematical synthesis a priori.
Necessary physical laws → predicates exceeding empirical object-concepts → physical synthesis a priori.
Metaphysical demand for a priori enlargement → rejection of merely analytic metaphysics → metaphysics as synthetic a priori cognition.
Mathematics, physics, and metaphysics → shared synthetic a priori principle-form → unified account of theoretical sciences of reason.
Logical contradiction is relocated from the role of knowledge-generator to the role of criterion operative upon already grounded cognition.
Mathematics is reclassified from conceptual analysis to intuitive construction under conditions of a priori necessity.
Physics is reclassified from empirical description to a discipline containing necessary principles irreducible to empirical observation.
Metaphysics is reclassified from analysis of inherited concepts to the attempted extension of a priori cognition beyond experience.
The analytic/synthetic distinction cuts across disciplinary objects and becomes the principal map of theoretical legitimacy.
Surface — Arithmetic, geometry, physical laws, and metaphysical propositions are classified according to whether their predicates are conceptually contained or added.
Structural — The possibility of theoretical science depends on distinguishing conceptual containment, intuitive supplementation, empirical origin, and a priori necessity.
Metastrategic — The text displaces the question from whether a proposition is logically consistent to what ground permits necessary cognitive extension.
Ontological/Epistemic — Objects of mathematics, nature, and metaphysics become knowable in science only insofar as they can be determined through synthetic a priori principles.
Temporal — Metaphysical claims concerning the world’s beginning exemplify reason’s movement beyond experiential conditions toward a priori determination of totality.
The axioms suffice to reconstruct the central claim that theoretical sciences contain synthetic a priori principles.
The reconstruction preserves the argument’s decisive distinction between contradiction as a test of judgement and synthesis as a source of cognitive extension.
The mathematical demonstration is structurally stronger than the physical and metaphysical extensions because it explicitly exhibits the need for intuition.
The account of physics asserts but does not derive the conditions under which its synthetic a priori principles are possible.
The account of metaphysics establishes its required form from its aim but does not establish the validity of particular metaphysical syntheses.
The system remains underdetermined concerning whether one account of intuition and synthesis can ground mathematics, physics, and metaphysics alike.
The principal structural tension is that metaphysics must exceed experience to fulfill its aim while the demonstrated model of synthesis is supplied through mathematical intuition.

identity.title: V. In all Theoretical Sciences of Reason, Synthetical Judgements “à priori” are contained as Principles.

units.title: VI. The Universal Problem of Pure Reason.

items.text: The decisive problem of pure reason is whether synthetic judgments a priori are possible.
The scientific standing of metaphysics depends on resolving this problem or proving its impossibility.
Hume’s causal scepticism is diagnostically important but fails because it treats one synthetic a priori claim as the whole problem.
Mathematics and pure natural science are existing instances whose possibility requires an account of synthetic a priori cognition.
Metaphysics exists naturally as an inextinguishable rational disposition but remains unestablished as a science.
Recurrent contradiction requires reason to examine its own competence before extending itself beyond experience.
Critique converts metaphysics from dogmatic construction into a decision concerning the legitimate scope and limits of pure reason.
Metaphysics can be a science only if synthetic judgments a priori are possible.
Analytic judgment explicates what is already contained in concepts and does not extend a priori knowledge.
Mathematics necessarily contains synthetic judgments a priori.
Pure natural science necessarily contains synthetic judgments a priori.
The actual existence of mathematics and pure natural science establishes that their possibility must be explainable.
Human reason naturally generates questions that empirical reasoning cannot answer.
The natural generation of metaphysical questions produces some metaphysical system in every exercise of speculative reason.
Previous attempts to answer metaphysical questions have generated unavoidable contradictions within reason.
A science of metaphysics requires a determinate judgment concerning reason’s ability or inability to know its objects.
Determining reason’s competence requires determining both the extent and the limits of its a priori use.
Critique concerns Reason and its self-generated problems rather than an inexhaustible plurality of external objects.
Uncritical dogmatic use of reason generates groundless assertions and culminates in scepticism.
The natural root of metaphysics in human reason persists even when particular metaphysical systems fail.
Metaphysics is not established as a science merely because metaphysical systems have historically been produced.
The universal problem of pure reason is not reducible to the causal principle.
A priori necessity is not adequately explained as experiential habit.
The natural disposition toward metaphysics is not proof that metaphysical knowledge is valid.
Metaphysical questions are not answerable by empirical applications of reason alone.
Analysis of concepts is not metaphysics proper because it cannot explain the a priori origin or valid extension of knowledge.
Dogmatic construction without critique is not a route to metaphysical science.
Contradiction among metaphysical claims is not a basis for confident doctrinal extension.
The critique of reason is not primarily an investigation of a manifold of objects beyond experience.
Limiting pure reason is not equivalent to abandoning the rational demand for metaphysics.
The possibility of mathematics and pure natural science becomes evidentially prior to the possibility of metaphysics as a science.
Hume’s denial of synthetic a priori causality cannot be universalized without also undermining pure mathematics.
Metaphysics has a double status: it is unavoidable as a rational disposition and unverified as a science.
The persistence of metaphysical questioning does not license any answer to those questions.
Contradiction changes the philosophical task from constructing metaphysical doctrines to adjudicating the powers of reason.
The legitimate extension of a priori cognition is conditional upon a prior determination of its validity.
Earlier dogmatic metaphysical systems count as failures of metaphysics proper, even where they contain useful conceptual analysis.
The argument differentiates three modes of metaphysical existence: actual science, natural rational disposition, and dogmatic historical system.
Critical limitation is the enabling condition of valid a priori extension rather than a merely negative restriction.
Reason must become both the investigator and the object of investigation because the source of metaphysical problems lies within reason itself.
Historical metaphysical failure functions as methodological evidence against dogmatism without functioning as evidence against the irreducible rational need for metaphysics.
The critique must account simultaneously for the reality of successful a priori sciences and the failure of metaphysics to attain comparable scientific status.
No domain of alleged objects beyond experience can independently authorize pure metaphysical knowledge.
No question is answerable merely because reason necessarily poses it.
No conceptual decomposition can establish the a priori genesis or objective validity of synthetic cognition.
No unrestricted use of pure reason can claim legitimacy before reason determines its own competence.
No historical accumulation of metaphysical systems can substitute for a transcendental account of their possibility.
No escape from metaphysics is available through scepticism because the source of metaphysical questioning is internal to reason.
The system forecloses an uncriticized transition from the natural fact of rational questioning to the scientific validity of metaphysical knowledge.
The system excludes both final dogmatic possession of metaphysical objects and sceptical cancellation of reason’s metaphysical demand.
The absent object organizing the argument is a metaphysics that could be scientific without first becoming a critique of its own source.
The system denies that reason can secure its transcendence of experience by spontaneous assertion while preserving rational necessity.
Existing synthetic a priori sciences plus unavoidable metaphysical questioning generate the universal problem of pure reason.
The universal problem separates actual scientific existence from mere natural rational disposition.
The distinction between analytic explication and synthetic extension excludes conceptual analysis as a sufficient foundation for metaphysics.
Recurrent contradiction converts doctrinal production into a problem of rational jurisdiction.
Rational jurisdiction requires critique of reason’s powers in relation to experience and beyond experience.
Critique yields the alternative of warranted extension or strictly delimited restraint, thereby making metaphysics as science conditionally thinkable.

Vacillating metaphysics → universalization of the synthetic a priori problem → mathematics and pure natural science as proof cases → metaphysics as natural disposition → contradiction in dogmatic metaphysics → critique of rational competence → determination of legitimate extension and limit.
Hume’s partial sceptical diagnosis → failure of its universal implications → necessity of a more comprehensive critique of pure reason.
Metaphysics is reclassified from a body of disputed doctrines into a problem concerning the conditions of valid a priori cognition.
Mathematics and pure natural science are reclassified from unquestioned bodies of knowledge into evidence requiring transcendental explanation.
The opposition between extension and limitation collapses because valid extension depends on prior limitation.
Scepticism is reclassified from a final philosophical position into the terminal effect of failed dogmatism.
Reason is reclassified from a faculty that merely applies principles to objects into a self-problematizing source of its own questions and standards.
Surface — The explicit inquiry asks how synthetic judgments a priori, mathematics, pure natural science, and metaphysics are possible.
Structural — The argument distinguishes analytic containment from synthetic extension and distinguishes actual science from natural rational propensity.
Metastrategic — The argument replaces dogmatic construction of metaphysical claims with critique of the authority entitled to make them.
Ontological/Temporal — Reason is presented as an enduring self-generative power whose metaphysical demand persists across the historical collapse of particular systems.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the transition from the universal problem of synthetic a priori judgment to the necessity of critique.
The system remains underdetermined concerning the positive conditions that make synthetic judgments a priori possible.
The structure is coherent insofar as it distinguishes the inevitability of metaphysical questioning from the legitimacy of metaphysical knowing.
The structure is strongest where the actual existence of mathematics and pure natural science blocks a universal sceptical denial of a priori synthesis.
The system depends on the compressed inference that actual scientific existence guarantees the availability of a satisfactory account of its possibility.
The system leaves a reflexive tension because reason must determine the limits of reason through an inquiry conducted by reason itself.
The reconstruction preserves the argument’s movement from doctrinal failure through self-critique toward conditional scientific legitimacy.

identity.title: VI. The Universal Problem of Pure Reason.

units.title: VII. Idea and Division of a Particular Science, under the Name of a Critique of Pure Reason.

items.text: The problem is to determine whether and how knowledge claimed as absolutely a priori can be validly extended.
Pure reason is reframed as a faculty whose a priori principles require critical examination before they can ground a system.
A Critique of Pure Reason is constituted as a preliminary investigation of reason’s sources, scope, and limits rather than as a completed doctrine.
The argument moves from the uncertain possibility of an organon to the necessary establishment of a negative touchstone for judging a priori cognition.
Transcendental inquiry shifts attention from objects to the a priori conditions under which objects are given and thought.
The projected science is divided according to the faculties that give objects and think them, because conditions of givenness precede conditions of thought.
Reason supplies principles of knowledge a priori.
Pure reason contains principles for cognizing objects absolutely a priori.
An organon of pure reason would contain the principles sufficient for producing all pure a priori cognitions.
The possibility and legitimate scope of an organon cannot be assumed before reason’s capacity for a priori cognition is critically assessed.
A critique of pure reason investigates the sources and limits of a priori cognition.
Transcendental knowledge concerns the a priori mode of cognition of objects rather than objects themselves.
The critical task is to assess synthetic a priori cognition, while analysis is pursued only as required for that assessment.
Transcendental philosophy is the architectonic system of all principles of pure reason.
A complete transcendental philosophy requires a complete analysis of human a priori knowledge.
Transcendental philosophy admits only completely pure a priori concepts.
Practical cognition involving motives depends on feeling and therefore on empirical sources of cognition.
Human knowledge arises from sensibility, through which objects are given, and understanding, through which objects are thought.
A priori conditions of sensibility are conditions under which objects can be given.
Conditions under which objects are given must precede conditions under which they are thought.
The a priori cognitive capacities of the mind form a bounded investigable field even if the nature of external objects is indefinitely extensive.
Critique is not a doctrine that directly enlarges knowledge.
Critique is not an organon that already supplies procedures for generating all pure a priori cognition.
Transcendental inquiry is not inquiry into the empirical nature of objects.
The Critique of Pure Reason is not identical with completed transcendental philosophy.
The critical examination of reason is not a critique of philosophical books, systems, or their historical authors.
Transcendental philosophy is not a mixed field containing empirical concepts.
Pure morality is not included within transcendental philosophy insofar as its construction necessarily incorporates empirical motives and feelings.
The critique does not require a complete analysis and deduction of every derived a priori concept.
Sensibility is not reducible to understanding, because giving an object differs from thinking one.
Critical inquiry must precede any legitimate claim to possess a system capable of extending pure a priori knowledge.
The immediate use of critique is negative because it purifies reason from error before it authorizes doctrinal expansion.
Critique functions as a universal touchstone for the worth or worthlessness of claims to a priori knowledge.
A future canon remains possible even if an organon proves unavailable.
The Critique can claim completeness only at the level of the radical concepts required to judge synthesis a priori.
Moral principles may be a priori without belonging to transcendental philosophy.
The Doctrine of Elements must begin with transcendental sensibility.
The argument converts uncertainty about metaphysical knowledge into a bounded jurisdictional inquiry over the faculties that make such knowledge possible.
The possibility of a positive system is made conditional upon a prior negative delimitation of illegitimate cognitive claims.
The field of philosophy is redrawn by separating the purity of a principle from the empirical conditions required for its practical operation.
The architectonic order of the science follows the dependency order of cognition rather than the order in which objects appear to consciousness.
The finitude of the subject’s a priori cognitive field makes systematic completion conceivable without requiring exhaustive knowledge of external reality.
Validity cannot be secured by inherited metaphysical systems, historical authority, or the mutual correction of unsupported assertions.
The form of cognition cannot be treated as transparent merely because cognition is exercised.
No claim to universality belongs to cognition whose constitutive concepts require empirical material.
The systematic unity of reason cannot be presupposed as accomplished before its elementary sources and limits are discriminated.
Objectivity cannot be analyzed solely through objects, because object-givenness itself depends on subjective a priori conditions.
The text excludes immediate access to an unrestricted absolute knowledge generated by pure reason.
The common root of sensibility and understanding is treated as unavailable to the inquiry, although their coordinated operation is required.
The completed system of pure reason is held open as a regulative possibility while denied as a present possession.
The ultimate ground of the faculties is not supplied, so the science begins from functional division rather than from a demonstrated first origin.
Claim to pure a priori cognition → uncertainty concerning its legitimate extension → necessity of critique.
Critique of sources and limits → negative purification from error → touchstone for the validity of a priori claims.
Transcendental redirection from objects to cognitive conditions → isolation of pure a priori elements → determination of the field of transcendental philosophy.
Requirement of systematic completeness → restriction of present analysis to conditions necessary for judging synthetic a priori cognition → critique as incomplete idea of transcendental philosophy.
Purity requirement → exclusion of empirical practical motives → restriction to speculative pure reason.
Sensibility gives objects and understanding thinks them → givenness precedes thought → transcendental doctrine of sensibility becomes the first element.

Uncertain a priori extension → critique of reason’s sources and limits → negative touchstone of validity → transcendental relocation to conditions of cognition → restriction to pure speculative principles → architectonic division into elements and method → priority of sensibility over understanding.
Philosophical evaluation is relocated from comparison among doctrines to examination of the faculty that makes doctrinal claims possible.
The distinction between critique and doctrine separates the validation of cognitive authority from the production of new cognition.
The distinction between an organon and a canon separates unrestricted constructive power from rule-governed legitimate use.
The distinction between pure a priori principle and empirically conditioned practical application removes morality from the transcendental field without denying its a priori status.
The distinction between givenness and thought establishes a non-interchangeable division of cognitive labor between sensibility and understanding.
The mind’s a priori constitution becomes a finite field of inquiry, while the empirical infinity of external nature ceases to determine the scope of the critique.
Surface — The text defines the Critique of Pure Reason as an investigation into the validity, sources, and limits of a priori cognition.
Structural — The text orders cognition through the distinct functions of sensibility, which gives objects, and understanding, which thinks them.
Metastrategic — The text requires philosophy to establish a criterion of judgment before it authorizes systems, histories, or doctrinal constructions.
Ontological/Temporal — The argument locates systematic possibility in the bounded structure of the cognizing mind while deferring completed transcendental philosophy to a future achievement.
The axioms reconstruct the central transition from the doubtful organon to the necessary critique because they preserve the distinction between productive doctrine and limiting examination.
The reconstruction remains underdetermined concerning the positive inventory of radical concepts, because the text asserts their required completeness without supplying them here.
The system is coherent insofar as the priority of critique follows from uncertainty about the scope of pure reason.
The system depends on a tension between calling the critique complete as an idea and withholding the complete analysis required for transcendental philosophy as a science.
The exclusion of morality depends on a further tension between its a priori principles and its necessary relation to empirical motives in practical construction.
The architecture relies on an unproved coordination of sensibility and understanding, whose common root is admitted but declared unknown.
Reconstruction preserves the argument’s movement only if negative delimitation is retained as the condition for every later positive system of pure reason.

identity.title: VII. Idea and Division of a Particular Science, under the Name of a Critique of Pure Reason.

units.title: § I. Introductory.

items.text: Human knowledge immediately relates to objects through intuition, not through thought alone.
Intuition requires an object to be given through the mind’s receptivity to affection.
Sensibility supplies intuitions, while understanding supplies concepts through which intuitions are thought.
Empirical cognition is divided into sensation as matter and form as the a priori ordering of phenomenal content.
A transcendental reduction removes conceptual determinations and sensation in order to isolate the pure form of sensibility.
The investigation thereby establishes transcendental æsthetic as the science of a priori sensibility and prepares the identification of space and time as its pure forms.
Knowledge immediately relates to objects through intuition.
Human intuition occurs only when an object is given to the mind through affection.
Sensibility is the receptive capacity through which objects are given and intuitions arise.
Understanding thinks what sensibility gives and produces conceptions.
Sensation is the effect of an object upon the faculty of representation insofar as the mind is affected.
An intuition related to an object through sensation is an empirical intuition.
The matter of a phenomenon is what corresponds to sensation.
The form of a phenomenon is what enables its content to be arranged under relations.
Phenomenal matter is given a posteriori, while phenomenal form lies a priori in the mind.
Pure intuition is the a priori form of sensibility in which phenomenal multiplicity is arranged, independently of sensation.
Transcendental æsthetic is the science of the a priori principles of sensibility.
Empirical criteria of taste cannot function as determinate a priori laws.
Knowledge does not immediately relate to objects through understanding or conception alone.
Intuition is not possible without the givenness of an object.
Sensibility is not understanding, and receptivity is not conceptual thought.
The form of a phenomenon is not itself sensation.
Pure intuition is not empirical content, sensory quality, or conceptual determination.
Phenomenal form is not received a posteriori in the same manner as phenomenal matter.
Transcendental æsthetic is not a science of taste or the beautiful.
Transcendental æsthetic is not transcendental logic.
Human cognition cannot obtain an object through conceptual thought without an ultimate relation to intuition.
An empirical phenomenon is constituted by sensory matter organized under form.
The relational organization of phenomenal content cannot itself be identified with sensory content.
The a priori form of sensibility is isolated by subtracting conceptual determinations and then sensory content.
Pure intuition is the residual structure through which phenomenal multiplicity can be arranged and viewed.
Sensibility is epistemically prior to understanding because understanding requires what sensibility gives.
Extension and shape remain after conceptual and sensory predicates are removed from the representation of a body.
The reduction of sensibility yields space and time as the two pure forms of sensuous intuition.
The term æsthetic is redirected from the critique of taste to the science of a priori laws of sensibility.

Human object-cognition is generated through a layered sequence in which affection produces sensation, sensation supplies empirical intuition, pure form orders the intuition, and understanding conceptualizes it.
Sensibility is not merely receptive material but a priori structured receptivity.
The object is cognitively available only through conditions that belong partly to the object’s affection and partly to the mind’s form of reception.
The distinction between sensibility and understanding becomes a division between two distinct sources of cognition rather than a distinction between passive and active versions of one faculty.
Transcendental inquiry changes the apparent given into a problem of the conditions under which givenness is possible.
Phenomenal objectivity is neither raw sensation nor pure conceptual construction but sensory content ordered through a priori form.
The system excludes an unmediated relation between the knowing subject and the object.
The system excludes the reduction of phenomenal form to an accumulation of sensations.
The system excludes the derivation of object-directed cognition from concepts without intuition.
The system excludes a homogeneous faculty in which receiving, intuiting, thinking, and conceiving are indistinguishable operations.
The system excludes the treatment of pure intuition as a contingent sensory product.
The system excludes the use of “æsthetic” as a designation for empirically grounded rules of taste.
No single source of cognition can independently supply both the object and the conditions under which it is thought.
There is no cognitively sufficient “raw phenomenon” prior to the distinction between sensory matter and organizing form.
Unconditioned object-relation is unavailable within human cognition.
A unified doctrine of cognition is impossible without separating the principles of sensibility from the principles of pure thought.
An account of the object apart from the conditions of its givenness remains outside the operative scope of this introductory analysis.
Object affects mind → sensation arises → empirical intuition relates sensation to an object → phenomenon is constituted.
Sensory matter + a priori relational form → phenomenal content arranged under relations.
Sensibility gives intuitions → understanding thinks them through concepts → thought ultimately returns to intuition.
Remove conceptual determinations → isolate empirical intuition; remove sensation → isolate pure intuition.
Pure intuition → space and time; a priori sensibility → transcendental æsthetic; pure thought → transcendental logic.
Object-relation → intuition → givenness → affection → sensibility → empirical intuition.
Empirical content → distinction of matter and form → a posteriori matter / a priori form → pure intuition.
Isolation of sensibility → removal of conceptual additions → removal of sensation → identification of space and time → constitution of transcendental æsthetic.
Object-cognition is reclassified from direct apprehension to intuition-mediated givenness.
Sensibility is reclassified from mere receptivity to a faculty with a priori organizing form.
The phenomenon is reclassified from undifferentiated appearance into a composite of matter and form.
The boundary between empirical and a priori cognition is relocated within sensibility itself.
Æsthetic inquiry is reclassified from taste criticism to transcendental analysis of sensibility.
The architecture of cognition is divided into the conditions of intuition and the principles of thought.
Surface: The passage asks how knowledge immediately relates to objects and answers through intuition, sensation, and conception.
Structural: Cognition is organized as a division between receptivity, sensation, empirical intuition, pure form, and conceptual thought.
Metastrategic: The argument replaces description of experienced objects with a reductive inquiry into the conditions that make experience possible.
Ontological/Temporal: Human objectivity is conditioned by affection, while the formal ordering of phenomenal multiplicity is a priori and culminates in space and time.
The extracted axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the passage’s central movement from object-affection to intuition, from intuition to phenomenon, and from phenomenon to pure form.
The reconstruction preserves the distinction between what sensibility receives and what the mind contributes a priori.
The exact argument establishing why the pure forms are specifically space and time is announced rather than demonstrated in this introductory passage.
The relation between external affection and the mind’s a priori form is asserted functionally but not further explained.

The tension between object-dependent empirical intuition and pure intuition without sensation is contained by distinguishing empirical content from the form of sensibility, but the reconciliation is not fully developed here.
The system is internally coherent at the level of division and method, but its conclusions depend on the legitimacy of the two-stage subtraction that isolates pure form.
Reconstruction preserves the real argument provided that space and time are treated as the announced result of the reduction rather than as conclusions fully proven within the section.

identity.title: § I. Introductory.

units.title: § 2. Metaphysical Exposition of this Conception.

items.text: The exposition determines whether space is an empirical acquisition, a relation belonging to things independently of intuition, or an a priori form of intuition.
External objects can be represented as outside, separate, and spatially related only if spatial representation already precedes external experience.
Space is therefore a necessary a priori condition of the possibility of external phenomena rather than a determination derived from them.
The inability to represent the nonexistence of space distinguishes its necessity from the contingent absence of objects within it.
The unity, non-discursive character, and infinite givenness of space identify it as a pure intuition rather than a general conception.
The apodeictic certainty of geometry is grounded in this a priori intuition.
A metaphysical exposition represents what belongs to a conception insofar as that content is given a priori.
External sense represents objects as outside the mind.
The shape, dimensions, and mutual relations of external objects are determined or determinable only in space.
Representing sensations as external, separate, and differently located requires an antecedent representation of space.
External experience is possible only through an antecedent representation of space.
Space is a necessary a priori representation that grounds all external intuitions.
The nonexistence of space cannot be represented, although the absence of objects within space can be thought.
Space is a pure intuition rather than a discursive or general conception.
Only one space can be represented, while apparent plurality consists of parts of that one space.
Particular spaces can be represented only as limitations within the one all-embracing space.
Space is represented as an infinite given quantity whose parts can be extended without limit.
Geometrical principles derive their apodeictic certainty from a priori intuition rather than from general concepts alone.
Space is not derived from outward experience.
Space is not produced by abstracting relations from external phenomena.
Space is not a determination dependent on phenomena.
Space is not a discursive or general conception.
Space is not an aggregate constructed from independently prior spaces.
Space is not a finite concept containing an infinite multitude of subordinate representations.
Space is not abolished by the absence of objects within it.
Space is not presented as an object through internal sense.
External experience functions as an effect of spatial representation rather than as its source.
The distinction between outside, near, separate, and differently located sensations already presupposes spatial form.
The necessity of space is modal rather than merely regular: space makes external intuition possible instead of merely accompanying it.
The possibility of an empty spatial field confirms that spatial form is independent of the contingent presence of objects.
Spatial plurality is derivative because particular spaces are bounded portions of one prior space.
The infinite character of space belongs to the original intuition rather than to a concept that progressively accumulates infinite contents.
Geometry obtains apodeictic force because its principles are grounded in the intuition of space rather than inferred from abstract definitions alone.
External phenomena are spatially ordered only under the condition supplied by a priori intuition.
The explanatory direction is reversed from objects producing space to spatial form making objects available as external phenomena.
Empirical derivation is blocked at the origin of external experience, while conceptual derivation is blocked at the origin of geometrical certainty.
All local spatial determinations become derivative limitations within a single prior field.
The distinction between empty space and nonexistent space makes spatial form independent of occupancy.
Infinity is treated as a structural property of the given spatial field rather than as the result of summing indefinitely many finite regions.
No intelligible externality exists prior to the spatial form that organizes sensations as outside and apart.
No empirical sequence can explain the prior availability of spatial relations without presupposing what it seeks to explain.
No spatial framework can be constructed from relations among objects that are already spatially individuated.
No total space can be generated by assembling independently given parts.
No apodeictic geometry can be grounded in discursive generality alone.
No representation of external phenomena is possible from a standpoint that first removes the spatial form of intuition.
The system forecloses a knowable pre-spatial domain of external objects.
The system forecloses the use of spatiality as an explanatory property established independently of possible intuition.
The system forecloses the possibility that geometrical necessity originates in observation of external regularities.
The relation between spatial form and things considered independently of intuition remains outside the completed exposition.
The announced analogy between space and time remains programmatic because the present exposition develops only the metaphysical account of space.
External sense presents objects as outside the mind and thereby requires distinctions of location, separation, and relation.
The required distinctions presuppose a representation of space that cannot itself be obtained from those distinctions.
The presupposed representation is therefore necessary, a priori, and constitutive of external experience.
The inability to represent the absence of space, together with the ability to represent empty space, separates spatial necessity from object occupancy.
The unity and infinite givenness of space distinguish a pure intuition from a general concept.
Geometrical certainty follows from the a priori intuition that grounds spatial determination.

Ontological question concerning space → definition of a priori exposition → regress from external experience to antecedent spatial representation → necessity of space → pure intuition → unity and infinite givenness → geometrical apodeicticity.
