External location requires space → space cannot be empirically derived → space conditions external phenomena → spatial multiplicity depends on one intuition → geometry depends on that intuition.
Externality is reclassified from an immediate feature of objects into a relation made possible by a priori spatial form.
Space is relocated from the status of an empirical object-property to the status of a condition of phenomenal objectivity.
The opposition between empirical acquisition and conceptual abstraction is replaced by the category of pure intuition.
Separate spaces are reclassified as limitations within one space rather than as independently fundamental spatial units.
Geometry is detached from derivation through general concepts and attached to the certainty of a priori intuition.
The absence of objects is separated from the absence of spatial form.
Surface: Space determines the shape, dimensions, separation, and relations of externally represented objects.
Structural: Spatial representation is the antecedent condition under which external experience and phenomenal ordering become possible.
Metastrategic: The argument reverses ordinary explanation by deriving the possibility of object-experience from the form of intuition rather than deriving space from experienced objects.

Ontological/Temporal: Spatial predicates are assigned within the conditions of intuition, while the status of space as a reality independent of intuition remains an unresolved boundary of the exposition.
The extracted axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the exposition’s principal movement from the presupposition of space to its status as pure a priori intuition.
The reconstruction preserves the decisive regress from external experience to the antecedent representation that makes external experience possible.
The system is internally coherent if the distinction between empirical content and a priori form is accepted as its governing condition.
The status of space as a real existence or as a predicate of things independently of intuition is posed but not fully resolved by this subsection alone.
The transition from necessary a priori representation to the full doctrine of subjective constitution is suggested by the framing but not separately demonstrated in the numbered exposition.
The relation between infinite given space and the finite act of representing particular spatial regions remains compressed into the distinction between intuition and concept.

Reconstruction preserves the argument’s real movement: empirical externality is made dependent on a priori spatial intuition, spatial plurality is subordinated to unity, and geometrical certainty is derived from that structure.

identity.title: § 2. Metaphysical Exposition of this Conception.

units.title: § 3. Transcendental Exposition of the Conception of Space.

items.text: The problem is to determine what conception of space makes synthetic a priori geometrical cognition possible.
A transcendental exposition explains a conception as a principle from which the possibility of other synthetic a priori cognitions can be discerned.
Geometry exceeds conceptual analysis while retaining apodeictic necessity.
Because geometry exceeds a mere conception, its ground must be intuition rather than conception alone.
Because geometrical cognition is necessary and a priori, its intuition must be pure and prior to empirical perception.
Pure spatial intuition is possible only as the subject’s form of receptivity to external objects.
The subjective form of external sense explains the possibility of geometry and discriminates the adequate explanation from merely similar alternatives.
A transcendental exposition must explain a conception as a principle of possible synthetic a priori cognition.
The cognitions derived from the conception must actually flow from it.
The cognitions must be possible only under the proposed mode of explaining the conception.
Geometry determines properties of space synthetically and a priori.
A mere conception cannot yield propositions that extend beyond the content of that conception.
Cognition that extends beyond a conception requires intuition.
Geometrical principles possess apodeictic necessity and therefore cannot be empirical judgments or conclusions from empirical judgments.
The intuition grounding geometry must be available prior to perception of objects.
An intuition prior to objects must be pure rather than empirical.
Space is an intuition belonging to the subject’s mode of receptivity to objects.
The subject’s receptivity to objects provides the form of external sense in general.
The possibility of geometry becomes comprehensible only when space is explained as the pure form of external sense.
Space is not merely a conception from which geometrical propositions are analytically extracted.
Geometrical cognition is not generated by conceptual decomposition alone.
The ground of geometry is not empirical perception.
Geometrical necessity is not inferred from empirical judgments.
The intuition of space is not an empirical representation acquired after encountering objects.
Space is not posited here as an independently existing external object.
An explanation that fails to establish the possibility of synthetic a priori geometry is not an adequate transcendental explanation.
Geometry requires a non-conceptual ground because it produces synthetic propositions that exceed the content of a mere conception.
The ground of geometrical cognition must be intuitive rather than merely conceptual.
The geometrical ground must be a priori because geometrical principles are apodeictically necessary.
The geometrical ground must be pure because it precedes perception of objects.
The required pure intuition cannot be explained as an object-independent external entity if it is to account for the subject’s cognition of objects.
Space functions as the condition under which external objects can be immediately represented.
Geometry is possible because it articulates the formal structure of external intuition rather than extracting properties from empirical objects.
The proposed explanation is transcendental because it connects the conception of space to the possibility of a specific synthetic a priori science.
The necessity of geometrical cognition is relocated from the independently given world to the subject’s a priori mode of receiving external objects.
Space becomes both objectively applicable to external appearances and subjectively grounded as the form through which those appearances are received.
The possibility of synthetic a priori knowledge depends on a distinction between the content supplied by objects and the formal conditions supplied by the subject.
The validity of geometry is secured by explanatory necessity rather than by empirical confirmation.
Transcendental explanation functions as a discriminating test: an account of space is admissible only if it generates the possibility of geometry.
The subject is constituted as receptive rather than productive in relation to external objects, while nevertheless supplying the form of their intuition.
The possibility of necessary geometrical knowledge cannot depend on the contingent occurrence of particular objects or perceptions.
The formal condition of external experience cannot be derived from the empirical contents whose appearance it makes possible.
The universality of geometry cannot be secured by treating spatial relations as inductive generalizations.
The subject cannot be reduced to a passive container receiving already spatially constituted representations.
Space cannot be treated as a purely subjective fiction lacking objective applicability to appearances.
The explanation cannot separate the possibility of space from the possibility of external object-representation.
The argument excludes a reality in which geometrical necessity is wholly independent of the subject’s cognitive constitution.
The argument excludes a subject that encounters external objects without any prior formal condition of externality.
The argument excludes the possibility of grounding synthetic a priori cognition without a constitutive relation between subject and object.
The argument leaves no admissible explanatory space between empirical realism and the subject’s pure form of external intuition.
The argument presupposes that the conditions of object-experience can be identified independently of the objects empirically encountered.
Synthetic a priori geometry → propositions exceeding conceptual content → requirement of intuition.
Apodeictic necessity → exclusion of empirical derivation → requirement of a priori grounding.
A priori intuition → exclusion of empirical intuition → requirement of purity.
Pure intuition of externality → location in the subject’s receptivity → identification with the form of external sense.
Form of external sense → possibility of immediate spatial representation → possibility of geometry.
Possibility of geometry → validation of the conception of space → rejection of rival explanations that cannot generate that possibility.
Transcendental exposition = conception → conditions of synthetic a priori cognition → necessity of the proposed explanatory mode.
Synthetic a priori geometry → demand for a ground beyond conceptual analysis → intuition.
Intuition → demand for a priori necessity → purity.
Pure a priori intuition of externality → demand for a subject-relative locus → form of external sense.
Form of external sense → immediate representation of objects → possibility of geometry.
Possibility of geometry → transcendental validation → exclusion of competing explanations.
Space is reclassified from an apparently given object or concept into a formal condition of external representation.
Geometry is reclassified from an empirical description of spatial objects into a science grounded in a priori intuition.
The opposition between subjective form and objective validity is reorganized: space is subject-grounded while remaining valid for external appearances.
Necessity is relocated from observed regularity to the formal conditions of possible experience.
Rival theories of space are judged by whether they can generate the possibility of synthetic a priori geometry.
The subject-object relation is rendered structurally prior to empirical cognition because external objects are representable only within the subject’s spatial form.
Surface — Geometry contains synthetic, necessary, a priori propositions concerning space.
Structural — The possibility of geometry depends on pure intuition as the form of external sense.
Metastrategic — An explanation is validated by the possibility it makes intelligible, not by resemblance to the phenomenon explained.
Ontological/Temporal — Space is not established as a thing independently of cognition; it is prior to empirical objects as the subject’s a priori condition for their external appearance.
Epistemic — Synthetic expansion beyond concepts requires intuition, while necessity requires that intuition to be a priori and pure.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the movement from geometry’s synthetic a priori character to the conception of space as pure external intuition.
The reconstruction preserves the distinction between conceptual analysis, intuition, empirical perception, and a priori necessity.
The central explanatory mechanism is internally coherent: geometry requires pure intuition, and pure intuition is identified with the form of external sense.
The system remains underdetermined concerning how the subject’s form of receptivity relates to objects beyond their status as appearances.
The argument compresses the transition from the necessity of geometry to the subjectivity of space into the claim that only the proposed explanation makes geometry possible.
The principal tension is that space is treated as prior to objects for cognition while being described through the subject’s receptivity to objects.
The reconstruction preserves the argument’s decisive operation: the possibility of geometry serves as the criterion for the adequate conception of space.

identity.title: § 3. Transcendental Exposition of the Conception of Space.

units.title: § 4. Conclusions from the foregoing Conceptions.

items.text: The text asks whether space belongs to objects independently of the subject or arises from the conditions of external intuition.
It reframes space as the form of external sensibility rather than as a property or relation of things in themselves.
It grounds this form in the subject’s receptivity, which precedes actual perception and makes space a pure a priori intuition.
It derives the possibility of spatial principles and objective validity for all objects of possible external experience.
It restricts that validity to phenomena and denies its extension to things in themselves or to the unknown intuitions of other thinking beings.
It concludes that space is empirically real for experience but transcendentally ideal with respect to things considered in themselves.
The argument is transcendental, classificatory, and boundary-setting: it secures spatial cognition by limiting its ontological reach.
Space does not represent a property of objects considered as things in themselves.
Space does not represent relations belonging to objects independently of the subject’s mode of intuition.
Space is the form of all phenomena of external sense.
External intuition is possible only under the subjective condition of sensibility.
The subject’s receptivity precedes actual intuitions of objects.
Space is a pure intuition given a priori in the mind.
All objects of possible external experience are determined in space.
Spatial judgments possess universal validity only when their objects are limited to external phenomena of sensuous intuition.
Space has empirical reality with respect to all possible external experience.
Space has transcendental ideality with respect to objects considered as things in themselves.
The conditions of sensibility determine only the possibility of phenomenal existence, not the possibility of things in themselves.
Things in themselves cannot be cognized through spatial representations.
Sensations such as colour, sound, and heat are subjective changes rather than intuitions that independently yield object cognition or synthetic a priori cognition.
Space is not a property attached to objects in themselves.
Space is not an independently existing relation among objects in themselves.
Absolute or relative spatial determinations are not intuitable a priori as determinations of things existing independently of intuition.
The special conditions of human sensibility are not conditions of the possibility of things in themselves.
Space does not apply without qualification to all things whatsoever.
The spatial conditions binding human intuition cannot be projected without judgment onto the intuitions of other thinking beings.
Colour, taste, sound, and heat are not adequate illustrations of the ideality of space.
Sensations are not themselves intuitions that disclose objects or generate a priori object cognition.
Nothing intuited in space is thereby established as a thing in itself.
The representation of space has no meaning once the condition of possible external experience is withdrawn.
Because receptivity precedes actual intuition, space can be present a priori before particular perceptions occur.
Because all externally experienced objects are determined in space, spatial relations can provide principles governing objects prior to particular experience.
Spatial judgments become universally valid when their objects are explicitly conceived as external phenomena rather than as things in themselves.
When the subjective condition of external intuition is removed, the concept of space loses its applicability rather than becoming a property of things in themselves.
The proposition that all objects are beside one another in space requires restriction to objects of human sensuous intuition.
The universal validity of space is restricted to the conditions of human sensibility and cannot be extended to other thinking beings without evidence about their modes of intuition.
Space alone among subjective representations referring to the external has the status of an a priori intuition capable of grounding synthetic a priori propositions.
Treating the spatially presented object as a thing in itself converts a phenomenon into an illegitimate metaphysical object.
The spatial representation gives access to the structure of appearance without giving access to the intrinsic constitution of what appears.
The empirical understanding can mistake phenomenal presentation for a thing in itself when it treats the form of sensibility as an objective property of the object.
Space acquires a dual status: it is objectively valid for every possible external experience while remaining non-constitutive of things in themselves.
The argument preserves the necessity of spatial cognition by relocating its ground from the ontology of objects to the constitution of the experiencing subject.
Universal spatial claims are valid only through an indexed universality whose domain is human external phenomenal experience.
The distinction between empirical reality and transcendental ideality prevents the choice between unrestricted spatial realism and the claim that spatial experience is meaningless.
The framework treats space as subjective in origin but objective in phenomenal validity, thereby assigning two distinct senses to objectivity.
The thing in itself functions as the inaccessible boundary of representation: it is asserted as the real correlate of appearance while being excluded from cognition through appearance.
The universality of space is humanly universal but not established as universal for thinking beings as such.
The system remains coherent only by preventing a priori priority from being reinterpreted as an ontological property of reality independent of sensibility.
No standpoint outside sensibility is available from which objects could be spatially compared as they are in themselves.
No condition governing appearance can be converted into a condition governing things independently of appearance.
No unqualified spatial universality is available beyond the domain of human external intuition.
No representation of an object can establish that the represented object is identical with the object in itself.
No symmetry exists between space and sensations such as colour, sound, or heat with respect to a priori object cognition.
No inference from the conditions of human sensibility to the conditions of other possible subjects is licensed.
No phenomenal description can disclose the intrinsic constitution of the represented object.
The possibility that spatial structure belongs to things in themselves is foreclosed.
A non-sensuous access to objects that would bypass the conditions of intuition is unavailable.
An unconditioned standpoint from which space could be judged as a property of reality as such is excluded.
The identity of appearance and thing in itself is inadmissible.
The possibility that all thinking beings share the human form of external intuition remains structurally undecidable.
Complete objectivity, understood as validity independent of every mode of sensibility, is unavailable to cognition.
The positive constitution of the thing in itself remains absent; only its function as the limit of phenomenal cognition is retained.
The argument begins by separating objects as things in themselves from objects as given in external intuition.
Subjective receptivity → form of sensibility → possibility of external intuition.
Form of external sensibility → pure intuition → a priori determination of spatial relations.
A priori spatial form + objects of external experience → universal principles valid for phenomenal objects.
Phenomenal restriction → empirical reality of space + transcendental ideality of space.
Withdrawal of the subjective condition → withdrawal of the meaning and applicability of space.
Comparison with sensations → exclusion of colour, sound, heat, and taste from the role of a priori object-producing intuition.
Phenomenal cognition secured → noumenal cognition excluded → space retained as a condition of appearance rather than a property of things.
Question of space as an object-property → distinction between things in themselves and appearances → receptivity as the ground of external intuition → space as a pure a priori form.
Pure a priori form → spatial principles for possible experience → restricted objective validity → empirical reality plus transcendental ideality.
Phenomenal restriction → rejection of noumenal spatiality → exclusion of sensory analogies → boundary of cognition at the thing in itself.
Space is reclassified from an independently existing feature of objects to the form under which external objects can appear.
The opposition between spatial realism and subjective unreality is replaced by the distinction between empirical reality and transcendental ideality.
Universal judgments are reclassified as domain-dependent judgments whose validity changes with the conception of their objects.
Sensory qualities are separated from space because subjectivity alone does not constitute an a priori intuition or object cognition.
The boundary between appearance and thing in itself becomes the governing boundary of spatial knowledge.
Human sensibility becomes the reference frame for universal spatial validity without being established as the form of intuition for all possible subjects.
Surface: The immediate issue is whether space belongs to objects independently of the subject or belongs to the mode in which objects are intuited.
Structural: The operative mechanism is the dependence of external intuition on receptivity and the form of sensibility.
Metastrategic: The argument preserves objective spatial cognition by restricting the domain in which spatial judgments may claim validity.
Ontological/Temporal: Space is treated as a priori with respect to actual perception, while the being of objects independently of sensibility remains inaccessible.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the central movement from the question of spatial objectivity to the distinction between empirical reality and transcendental ideality.
Reconstruction requires preserving the difference between space as a form of sensibility and space as a property of things in themselves.
The system is internally coherent if “objective validity” is restricted to possible external experience rather than extended to things in themselves.
Its strongest operation is the qualification of universal spatial judgments by the conception of their objects.
The system remains underdetermined concerning the positive status of the thing in itself and the precise relation between the inaccessible correlate and phenomenal representation.

Its principal tensions are the coexistence of subjective form with objective validity, the assertion of a real correlate with the denial of its cognition, and human universality with uncertainty about other subjects.
Reconstruction preserves the real movement of the text if it retains the sequence: subjective condition → a priori spatial form → phenomenal validity → transcendental limitation.

identity.title: § 4. Conclusions from the foregoing Conceptions.

units.title: § 5. Metaphysical Exposition of this Conception.

items.text: The account seeks the ground of temporal coexistence, succession, and temporal relations.
It relocates that ground from empirical perception to an a priori representation.
The necessity of temporal representation establishes time as the universal condition of possible phenomena.
The apodeictic principles of time are treated as conditions governing experience rather than conclusions extracted from experience.
The distinction between intuition and conception establishes time as a pure form of sensuous intuition rather than a general concept.
The structure of temporal infinity is reconstructed through one unlimited time and the limitation that yields determinate temporal quantities.
Temporal coexistence and succession presuppose an a priori representation of time.
Time is a necessary representation underlying all human intuitions of phenomena.
Phenomena cannot be represented apart from time, whereas time can be represented without phenomena.
Time is the universal condition under which the reality of phenomena is possible.
The fundamental principles of temporal relation possess apodeictic validity because they ground the possibility of experience.
Time is a pure form of sensuous intuition, not a discursive or general conception.
All determinate times are parts or limitations within one time.
Temporal succession is immediately contained in the intuition of time and cannot be derived from concepts alone.
The representation of time is originally unlimited, while determinate temporal quantities arise through limitation.
Concepts require immediate intuition as their basis in order to represent determinate temporal quantities.
Time is not an empirical conception derived from perceived coexistence or succession.
Temporal principles are not generalizations from accumulated experience.
Time is not a discursive or general conception.
Phenomena cannot be represented as outside or disconnected from time.
Time itself cannot be annulled as phenomena can be annihilated in thought.
Determinate temporal representation cannot be furnished by concepts alone.
Different times are not coexistent in the manner of different spaces.
Coexistence and succession are intelligible only after temporal representation has been presupposed.
The temporal order of phenomena cannot be established with strict universality or apodeictic certainty by experience alone.
Temporal axioms function as rules for the possibility of experience rather than as findings produced within experience.
The annihilation of all phenomena in thought does not entail the annihilation of the condition under which phenomena can be represented.
The proposition that different times are successive is synthetic because it is supplied by temporal intuition rather than conceptual analysis.
Every determinate temporal interval presupposes a prior unity of time from which it is delimited.
Concepts can represent temporal determinations only by depending on an immediately given temporal intuition.
Time functions simultaneously as the enabling condition of every temporal phenomenon and as a representation that is not itself constituted by those phenomena.
The universality and necessity of temporal order are secured by relocating their source from empirical regularity to the form of intuition.
Temporal multiplicity is generated as internal differentiation of one time rather than as a plurality of independently given times.
The possibility of determinate temporal knowledge depends on a prior non-conceptual synthesis that concepts cannot produce by themselves.
Temporal infinity is not an independently completed totality but the structural availability of indefinite determination through successive limitation.
The possibility of experience cannot be grounded in the temporal objects that experience already presupposes.
Temporal order cannot be reduced to a habit, regularity, or inductive expectation formed from prior observations.
The unity of time cannot be reconstructed by aggregating discrete temporal parts.
Temporal determination cannot originate exclusively in logical division or conceptual classification.
Phenomenal reality cannot be conceived as temporally unconditioned while remaining phenomenal reality.
The system excludes a temporal order whose validity would depend on contingent empirical confirmation.
The system excludes a plurality of times existing as independent coexistent wholes.
The system excludes a completed representation of time assembled from finite conceptual representations.
The system leaves no admissible account of phenomena that would be genuinely outside temporal form.
The system excludes any account in which temporal necessity is derived from the contents of experience rather than presupposed as their condition.
A priori temporal representation grounds the possibility of representing coexistence and succession.
Grounded temporal representation establishes time as the necessary condition of phenomenal intuition.
The necessary condition of phenomenal intuition yields apodeictic principles governing temporal relations.
The non-empirical and non-discursive status of those principles identifies time as a pure form of intuition.
Pure temporal intuition generates one-dimensional succession and the unity of all temporal parts.
The unlimited unity of time generates determinate intervals through limitation.
The dependence of determination on intuition subordinates conceptual representation to immediate temporal givenness.

Empirical insufficiency → a priori temporal ground → necessary condition of phenomena → apodeictic temporal principles → pure intuition rather than concept → unified unlimited time → determinate quantities through limitation.
Temporal order is reclassified from an observed feature of phenomena into a condition of their possible observation.
The opposition between experience and necessity is reorganized: experience supplies the field governed by temporal principles, but not the ground of their necessity.
The distinction between concept and intuition becomes a distinction between secondary determination and original temporal givenness.
Temporal plurality is mapped as limitation within a single form rather than coexistence among separate temporal substances.
Infinity is reclassified from an indefinitely large quantity into the unlimited ground from which finite temporal quantities are delimited.
Surface: Temporal coexistence and succession require a prior representation of time.
Structural: Time supplies the universal form within which phenomenal reality and temporal experience become possible.
Metastrategic: The validity of temporal principles is secured by reversing the direction of explanation from experience-to-rule into condition-to-experience.
Ontological/Temporal: Time is treated as one unlimited form whose internal limitations generate determinate temporal parts without reducing the form to those parts.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the movement from the failure of empiricism to the a priori status of time.
The distinction between pure intuition and general conception is indispensable for reconstructing the argument’s middle transition.
The account of unlimited time and limitation is necessary to reconstruct the final treatment of temporal infinity.
The system is internally coherent if time is treated as the form of phenomenal intuition rather than as an empirical object among phenomena.
The principal unresolved tension is that time is represented independently of phenomena while its operative significance is defined as the condition of phenomenal representation.

A second tension remains between the claim that time is one unlimited whole and the production of determinate times through limitation; the text provides the relation but not a further account of the limiting act.
Reconstruction preserves the real argumentative movement, but depends on accepting the distinction between transcendental condition and empirical content as its governing premise.

identity.title: § 5. Metaphysical Exposition of this Conception.

units.title: § 6. Transcendental Exposition of the Conception of Time.

items.text: The possibility of change and motion requires a prior representation of time.
Time is reframed as an internal a priori intuition rather than an abstract concept.
Temporal succession makes it possible for one object to bear contradictorily opposed determinations without simultaneous contradiction.
The temporal condition of change grounds the possibility of synthetic a priori knowledge concerning motion.
The argument moves from the transcendental status of time to its explanatory function in the general doctrine of motion.
Change is possible only through and in the representation of time.
Motion is change of place.
Time is an internal a priori intuition.
Without time as an intuition, the possibility of change cannot be rendered comprehensible.
Change involves the succession of contradictorily opposed determinations in one and the same object.
Temporal succession permits opposed determinations to belong to one thing at different times.
The conception of time explains the possibility of synthetic a priori knowledge displayed in the general doctrine of motion.
Time is not merely a concept through which change becomes intelligible.
Change is not comprehensible independently of an a priori intuition of time.
Opposed determinations in one object are not simultaneous contradictory predicates.
Motion is not conceptually primary over time.
Synthetic a priori knowledge of motion is not explained without reference to the temporal form of intuition.
Because motion is change of place and change requires time, motion presupposes temporal intuition.
Because opposed determinations can belong to one object successively, temporal succession makes change intelligible without treating contradiction as simultaneous.
The intelligibility of change depends on a form of representation that precedes the changing empirical determinations.
The general doctrine of motion contains synthetic a priori knowledge because its object is constituted through the temporal form of intuition.
Time functions as the condition that unifies successive states under the identity of one object.
Temporal succession converts an otherwise unintelligible conjunction of opposed determinations into the intelligible structure of change.
The transcendental analysis of time establishes a condition for objective alteration rather than merely describing the order in which perceptions occur.
The possibility of a priori knowledge of motion is transferred from the objects of motion to the temporal form through which alteration can be represented.
Identity through change is possible only as identity maintained across temporally successive determinations.
The system excludes the possibility that change could be explained by empirical observation alone.
The system excludes the possibility that time is derived from relations among changing objects.
The system excludes a model in which contradictory determinations can belong to one object without temporal differentiation.
The system excludes the possibility that the principles of motion are merely analytic consequences of concepts.
The system excludes a conception of objects whose identity is independent of their temporal ordering.
The argument forecloses a reality of change that is intelligible prior to the temporal form of intuition.
It denies that contradiction alone can explain alteration; contradiction becomes intelligible only through succession.
It leaves no explanatory route from motion to time, since time must already condition the possibility of motion.
It treats a non-temporal structure of changing identity as unavailable to cognition.
Internal a priori intuition of time → condition for succession.
Succession → possibility of opposed determinations belonging to one object at different times.
Temporally ordered opposed determinations → intelligibility of change.
Change of place → motion.
Temporal condition of motion → possibility of synthetic a priori knowledge concerning motion.
The explanatory order runs from transcendental condition to experienced alteration, not from alteration to the derivation of time.

Incomprehensibility of change without time → time identified as internal a priori intuition → succession distinguished from simultaneous contradiction → change and motion rendered possible → synthetic a priori knowledge of motion grounded.
Change is reclassified from an unexplained feature of objects into an event structured by temporal intuition.
Contradiction is divided into simultaneous incompatibility and successive opposed determination.
Motion is relocated from an independent empirical occurrence to a phenomenon conditioned by time.
The source of synthetic a priori knowledge is mapped to the subject’s temporal form of intuition.
Objectual identity is redescribed as persistence across successive determinations.
Surface — Change and motion require representation of time.
Structural — Time organizes opposed determinations as successive states of one object.
Metastrategic — The explanatory direction is reversed from empirical change to its transcendental condition.
Ontological/Temporal — Time functions as an internal a priori form through which alteration, persistence, and synthetic a priori knowledge become possible.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the argument from the a priori status of time to the possibility of motion.
The reconstruction preserves the distinction between temporal succession and simultaneous contradiction.
The central dependency is internally coherent: change requires time, while time is not derived from change.
The argument remains underdetermined regarding the further justification of time’s a priori and internal character.
Its strongest point is the conversion of succession into the condition of intelligible alteration.
Its compressed step is the passage from the temporal condition of motion to synthetic a priori knowledge in the general doctrine of motion.
The extracted structure preserves the original movement from transcendental condition to the possibility of change and motion.

identity.title: § 6. Transcendental Exposition of the Conception of Time.

units.title: § 7. Conclusions from the above Conceptions.

items.text: The argument asks how time can possess universal a priori necessity without subsisting independently of intuition.
The argument is transcendental and reconstructive: it determines the status of time by analyzing the conditions under which objects can be experienced.
Time is reframed from an intrinsic property of things into the form of internal, human, sensuous intuition.
Because every representation belongs to internal state, the temporal condition extends from inner phenomena to all phenomena, including outward phenomena.
The argument distinguishes empirical reality, which time possesses with respect to phenomena, from absolute reality, which time lacks independently of sensibility.
The conclusion preserves the necessity of temporal experience while denying that time belongs intrinsically to things in themselves.
Time does not subsist independently as a real entity.
Time does not inhere in things as an objective determination belonging to them independently of intuition.
Time is the a priori form of internal sense.
Time determines relations among representations in internal state rather than the shape or position of outward objects.
Every representation, including representation of an external object, belongs as a determination of the mind to internal state.
Time is the a priori formal condition of all phenomena, immediately for internal phenomena and mediately for external phenomena.
Space is the pure form of external intuition and is therefore limited to external phenomena.
Human intuition is always sensuous and therefore receptive to objects only under the conditions of sensibility.
Time has objective validity for every object that can be presented to the senses.
Time has no absolute reality independently of the form of sensuous intuition.
When sensuous intuition is abstracted, time is nothing.
Properties belonging to things in themselves cannot be presented through the senses.
Time is not a self-subsisting reality.
Time is not an objective determination inhering in things independently of intuition.
Time is not a determination of outward phenomena in the manner of shape or position.
Time is not an external spatial form.
Time is not absolutely real apart from the conditions of sensuous intuition.
The proposition that all things are in time is not valid when “things” means things in general independently of intuition.
Time is not a predicate that can be transferred from phenomena to things in themselves.
The transcendental ideality of time cannot be established through analogies that already presuppose the objective reality at issue.
Time can be represented prior to particular objects because it is a subjective form of intuition rather than a feature received from those objects.
The a priori status of time makes synthetic a priori propositions about temporal relations possible.
Temporal succession belongs directly to the ordering of representations in internal state rather than to the external geometry of objects.
The temporal representation can be analogically depicted as a one-dimensional line, although the line’s parts coexist while temporal parts succeed one another.
Every possible object of experience must stand in temporal relations because every representation of an object belongs to internal state.
External phenomena are temporally conditioned through the internal intuition in which they are represented.
The universally valid proposition is that all things as phenomena are in time, not that all things without qualification are in time.
Empirical reality and transcendental ideality describe different relations of time rather than mutually exclusive properties.
The universality of time is generated by the universality of the subject’s mode of intuition, not by an inference from the intrinsic structure of objects.
The account converts temporal objectivity from an absolute ontology into a necessary condition of experience.
Externality does not produce a temporal regime separate from internality because external objects are accessible only through representations belonging to internal state.
The distinction between phenomena and things in themselves limits the reach of temporal necessity to objects as they can be experienced.
Time is simultaneously subject-dependent and objectively valid, with the tension stabilized by assigning objectivity to phenomena rather than to things in themselves.
The structure permits necessary knowledge of the temporal conditions of experience without permitting knowledge of time as an intrinsic feature of reality beyond experience.
The system excludes a subject-independent temporal standpoint available within human sensibility.
The system excludes the conversion of conditions of appearing into properties of objects as they are in themselves.
The system excludes any external temporality that would bypass the internal intuition through which external objects are represented.
The system excludes the inference from empirical objectivity to absolute reality.
The system excludes a conception of “things in general” that silently retains the conditions of sensuous intuition while claiming to have abstracted from them.
The argument forecloses a time that remains meaningful after every relation to a mode of intuition has been removed.
The argument forecloses a subject-free temporal order that could be asserted without reference to possible experience.
The argument leaves no available cognitive route from sensuous phenomena to the temporal constitution of things in themselves.
The argument forecloses a representation that would make internal succession fully identical with an external spatial line.
The argument excludes the synthesis of empirical temporal objectivity with absolute temporal realism.
Independent subsistence and intrinsic inherence are rejected as inadequate accounts of time.
Time is assigned to the form of internal intuition, thereby acquiring priority over particular objects of experience.
Internal intuition supplies the ordering relation of representations as succession, with the line serving only as an imperfect external analogy.
Because every representation belongs to internal state, the temporal condition extends from inner representations to all phenomena.
The extension produces empirical objective validity for phenomena while denying absolute reality beyond sensibility.
The universal proposition is restricted from things without qualification to things as phenomena.
The restriction blocks the illicit passage from the conditions of experience to the properties of things in themselves.
The argument moves from the failure of self-subsistence and intrinsic inherence to the identification of time with the form of internal intuition.
The argument moves from internal intuition to temporal succession and the possibility of a priori temporal representation.
The argument moves from the internal belonging of every representation to the temporal conditioning of all phenomena.
The argument moves from universal phenomenal applicability to the distinction between empirical reality and transcendental ideality.
The argument ends by qualifying temporal universality and excluding any claim about time as an intrinsic property of things in themselves.
Time is reclassified from an object or objective property into a condition of object-presentation.
The opposition between inner and outer phenomena is reorganized as a distinction between immediate and mediate temporal conditioning.
Objectivity is divided into empirical validity within experience and absolute reality beyond the conditions of experience.
The qualifier “as phenomena” becomes necessary for universal claims about temporal order.
The boundary of temporal knowledge is relocated from the limits of experience to the distinction between appearance and thing in itself.
Surface level: the status, structure, and universality of time are determined.
Structural level: internal sense mediates the temporal ordering of every representation, including representations of external objects.
Metastrategic level: the argument resolves the apparent opposition between subjective form and objective validity by assigning each to a distinct domain.
Ontological and temporal level: time is necessary for phenomenal experience but has no status as an independently subsisting feature of things in themselves.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the movement from the rejection of realist accounts of time to the distinction between empirical reality and transcendental ideality.
The reconstruction depends on preserving the distinction between objective validity for phenomena and absolute reality independently of sensibility.
The system is internally coherent only if “subjective” denotes the necessary form of human sensuous intuition rather than an arbitrary private construction.
The strongest inferential link is the passage from the internal belonging of every representation to the mediate temporal conditioning of external phenomena.

The principal structural tension is that time is subject-conditioned while remaining universally and objectively valid for experience; the text resolves this tension through domain qualification rather than elimination.
The line analogy remains underdetermined as a representation of succession because it spatializes temporal order while failing to reproduce non-coexistence.
The reconstruction preserves the argument’s real movement only if temporal necessity, phenomenal objectivity, and noumenal non-applicability remain distinct.

identity.title: § 7. Conclusions from the above Conceptions.

units.title: § 8. Elucidation.

items.text: The objection infers the absolute reality of time from the empirical reality of change.
The reply concedes that change and time are real within experience while denying that this establishes time as a reality independent of sensibility.
Time is reclassified from an object or property of things into the form through which inner states are represented.
The apparent force of inner consciousness is limited by distinguishing phenomenal reality from knowledge of things in themselves.
Space and time ground synthetic a priori cognition only because they are pure forms of sensible intuition.
Competing theories fail because they must sacrifice either experiential coherence or the apodeictic validity of mathematics.
The argument closes by excluding motion and change from the a priori inventory of transcendental aesthetic because both require empirical perception.
Change is empirically real only as a determination represented in time.
Time is the real form of inner intuition and therefore has subjective empirical reality.
Time is neither a thing in itself nor an objective determination inhering in things.
The concepts of time and change vanish when the sensible condition of inner intuition is removed.
A phenomenon includes both an unknowable thing considered in itself and the subjective form through which it appears.
The forms of intuition belong necessarily and really to phenomenal objects without belonging to things in themselves.
Space and time are the two pure forms of all sensible intuition.
Space and time make synthetic a priori cognition possible, including pure mathematics.
Pure forms of sensibility have objective validity only within the sphere of phenomena.
Empirical knowledge remains valid whether space and time are treated as forms of intuition rather than as features of things in themselves.
Motion and change require empirical perception of an existing movable object and its successive determinations.
No pure datum of sensibility beyond space and time can be admitted into transcendental aesthetic.
Time is not an independently existing object.
Time is not a property or relation objectively inhering in things as they are in themselves.
The reality of experienced change does not prove the absolute reality of time.
Inner consciousness is not knowledge of the self as a thing in itself.
Space and time are not objectively applicable beyond sensible phenomena.
Space and time are not substances existing infinitely and eternally apart from things.
Space and time are not empirical abstractions whose apparent necessity is produced by imagination.
Motion and change are not pure a priori forms or concepts of sensibility.
The empirical reality of change entails the empirical reality of time as a condition of experience, not the absolute reality of time.
Consciousness certifies the actuality of inner representations without certifying that temporal succession belongs to the self as it is in itself.
Mathematical cognition has necessity and objective validity only for objects insofar as they are given under the forms of space and time.
The ideality of space and time does not undermine empirical knowledge because empirical objects are constituted within those forms.
A substantival theory of space and time preserves mathematical scope only by positing empty self-subsisting entities.
A relational-empiricist theory of space and time cannot ground apodeictic mathematical cognition because empirical abstraction cannot yield a priori necessity.
Motion and change can be cognized only as empirical determinations within spatial and temporal forms rather than as additional pure forms.
Transcendental ideality and empirical realism are mutually required: the forms must be subjective enough to avoid reifying them and objective enough to govern every possible phenomenon.
The conditions that make objects knowable also delimit knowledge to appearances, so epistemic constitution functions as a boundary on ontology.
The validity of mathematics is relocated from correspondence with things in themselves to necessity within the universally binding form of possible experience.
The purported completeness of transcendental aesthetic depends on converting every sensible concept beyond space and time into an empirical determination.
Immediate awareness does not provide an exception to the restriction of knowledge to phenomenal appearance.
The self cannot be known independently of the temporal form under which its states are internally represented.
Mathematical necessity cannot arise from relations abstracted from experience.
Objective validity does not require that the form of cognition be a property of things in themselves.
No determinate claim about non-sensible intuition is available, even though its possibility is used to mark the contingency of temporal representation.
No cognition can legitimately convert the necessary conditions of human experience into determinations of being as such.
No absolute temporal order is available from which phenomenal succession could be measured or justified.
No third pure sensible source can mediate between the formal conditions of intuition and empirical contents such as motion or change.
The thing in itself is structurally required as the limit of appearance but is unavailable as an object of determinate temporal or spatial knowledge.
Real change → succession in inner sense → empirical reality of time.
Empirical reality of time → subjective form of intuition → denial of absolute temporal reality.
Phenomenon as appearance → subjective form plus indeterminate thing in itself → restriction of objective validity to phenomena.
Pure forms of intuition → synthetic a priori mathematics → validity for possible experience.
Substantival absolutism or empirical relationalism → loss of experiential coherence or mathematical necessity → transcendental ideality as the required position.
Requirement of empirical movable content → motion and change → exclusion from the pure inventory of sensibility.
The inference from real change to absolute time is confronted.
Time is reframed as the real but subjective form of inner intuition.
Inner consciousness is subordinated to the phenomenon–thing-in-itself distinction.
Space and time are established as the exclusive grounds of synthetic a priori sensible cognition.
Their validity is confined to appearances while empirical certainty is retained.
Rival ontologies are shown to divide mathematical necessity from experiential legitimacy.
Motion and change are assigned to empirical experience, completing the boundary of transcendental aesthetic.
The opposition between the ideality of time and the reality of change collapses because empirical reality is separated from absolute reality.
Inner experience is reclassified from privileged access to an independently real self into phenomenal representation governed by inner sense.
Mathematics is no longer mapped onto things in themselves but onto the universal conditions under which objects can appear.
The dispute over space and time is redrawn as a forced choice among ontological reification, empirical derivation, and transcendental formalism.
Motion and change are relocated from candidates for transcendental forms to empirical contents presupposing those forms.
Surface — The text answers the claim that actual change proves that time is absolutely real.
Structural — The text distinguishes subjective forms of intuition, phenomenal objects, and indeterminate things in themselves.
Metastrategic — The text resolves rival failures by retaining empirical realism and mathematical necessity while denying transcendent ontological claims.
Ontological/Temporal — Time is not a self-subsisting entity or a feature of being in itself, but the necessary condition under which temporal succession can appear to a sensible subject.
Taxonomic — The text closes the field of pure sensibility at space and time by treating motion and change as empirically conditioned derivatives.

The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the reply to the objection, the restriction of temporal validity, the defense of mathematics, and the exclusion of motion and change from transcendental aesthetic.
The system depends decisively on the distinction between phenomenal objectivity and thing-in-itself reality.
The system is internally coherent insofar as subjective forms are treated as objectively valid conditions of possible experience rather than as private psychological states.
The system leaves underdetermined how the thing in itself relates to appearance while prohibiting determinate knowledge of that relation.
The claim that non-sensible intuition would remove temporal representation functions as a limiting counterfactual rather than as positive knowledge of another mode of intuition.
The closure of transcendental aesthetic depends on the compressed classificatory claim that every sensible concept other than space and time presupposes empirical content.

identity.title: § 8. Elucidation.

units.title: § 9. General Remarks on Transcendental Æsthetic.

items.text: The text addresses how necessary and universally valid cognition of spatial objects is possible if sensibility does not disclose things as they are in themselves.
It asserts that human intuition presents phenomena under subjective forms rather than objects with their noumenal constitution.
It relocates the distinction between sensibility and understanding from degrees of clarity to different origins and contents of cognition.
It proceeds by a transcendental argument from the synthetic a priori necessity of geometry to the subjective ideality of space and time.
It confirms this ideality by showing that intuition supplies relations and that internal sense gives the subject only as temporally affected.
It protects phenomenal reality from illusion by making illusion arise from objectifying space and time rather than from treating them as subjective forms.
It closes by delimiting finite, derivative intuition against an original intellectual intuition, using natural theology as illustration rather than proof.
Human intuition represents objects only as phenomena and not as things in themselves.
Space and time are pure a priori forms of human sensibility, while sensation supplies its empirical matter.
The constitution of objects independently of human sensibility is unknown.
The difference between sensibility and understanding concerns the origin and content of cognition rather than its logical clarity.
Validity for every human sensibility remains an empirical universality and does not disclose a thing in itself.
Cognitive intuition presents only relations and therefore cannot reveal the intrinsic nature of objects.
Apodeictic synthetic cognition in geometry requires pure a priori intuition rather than empirical experience or concepts alone.
Necessary synthetic cognition of external objects is possible only because space, and correspondingly time, are subjective a priori conditions under which objects can appear to us.
Internal intuition is temporal self-affection through which the subject represents itself as it appears rather than as it is.
Phenomena are genuinely given objects in relation to sensibility and are not illusory appearances.
Treating space and time as objective conditions of things in themselves turns them into self-subsistent necessities and destabilizes the reality of all empirical objects.
Finite human intuition is derivative, depending on objects that affect the subject, rather than original intellectual intuition.
Sensibility is not a confused or less distinct cognition of things in themselves.
The sensuous and the intellectual are not separated by degrees of conceptual clearness.
No sensory representation becomes noumenal cognition through exhaustive empirical clarification.
No feature shared by all human observers establishes a property of an object independently of sensibility.
Synthetic a priori geometry cannot arise from empirical intuition or from concepts alone.
Space and time are not predicates belonging to objects considered independently of their relation to a subject.
Internal self-consciousness is not an intellectual intuition through which the subject immediately knows itself.
A phenomenon is not an illusory appearance merely because its predicates depend on sensibility.
The possibility of an original divine intuition is not offered as proof of the theory of sensibility.
Increasing empirical clarity can disclose only the structure of human intuition and cannot approach cognition of things in themselves.
Intersubjective agreement within humanity remains phenomenal because it is still conditioned by a shared sensibility.
Geometrical necessity determines how externally experienced objects must appear and does not determine objects as they are in themselves.
The ideality of space and time permits empirical objectivity without granting transcendental reality to spatial and temporal predicates.
External cognition and self-cognition have the same phenomenal status, although one is ordered spatially and the other temporally.
The subjective ideality of space and time prevents the reduction of empirical objects and human existence to mere illusory appearance.
Natural theology can withhold spatial and temporal conditions from divine cognition only if those conditions are forms of finite sensibility rather than forms of being as such.
Necessary cognition acquires objective validity precisely by remaining within the conditions of possible experience rather than by transcending them.
The subject is simultaneously the formal condition of appearances and inaccessible to itself as it is independently of temporal self-affection.
Objectivity divides into empirical validity for phenomena and unavailable knowledge of the transcendental object.
Phenomenal dependence on the subject does not abolish reality; it defines the condition under which reality can be distinguished from illusion.
Even if all finite thinking beings shared human spatiotemporal intuition, that universality would not convert derivative sensibility into original intuition.
No comparison between a sensuous representation and a thing in itself can escape the forms of sensibility through which the comparison is made.
No empirical invariant, including universal human agreement, can serve as evidence for noumenal structure.
No transparent self-presence can ground self-knowledge because the self appears only through temporal affection.
No spatially external object can be known as absolutely external to the subject, because spatial externality is itself a form of intuition.
The ground of appearances must remain without positive determination, because every determination available to cognition belongs to phenomenal relation.
A cognition that gives its object immediately and through its own spontaneity is unavailable to finite human knowers.
A nonrelational cognition of either object or self is foreclosed for a subject whose intuition is receptive.
An object-independent spatiotemporal order cannot be admitted without collapsing the distinction between phenomenal reality and illusory appearance.
Receptive sensibility + space and time as a priori forms → relational intuition → objects given only as phenomena.
Phenomenal object + empirical investigation → greater clarity of human intuition → no cognition of things in themselves.
Apodeictic synthetic geometry → exclusion of empirical and merely conceptual sources → required pure intuition → subjective conditions of external experience.
Internal perception + temporal self-affection → self-intuition → subject given as appearance.
Subjective ideality of forms + real givenness of phenomena → empirical objectivity without illusory appearance.
Objective space and time → self-subsistent conditions of all being → ontological absurdity and generalized illusion → rejection of their objective reality.
Finite derivative intuition → exclusion of intellectual intuition → theological contrast that illustrates but does not establish the theory.

Phenomenal intuition → rejection of the confused-noumenal model → synthetic a priori geometry → subjective forms of space and time → relational and temporal confirmation → empirical reality without illusion → boundary between finite and original intuition.
Spatial and temporal predicates are reclassified from properties of things in themselves to relational predicates valid for objects of sensibility.
The distinction between empirical reality and transcendental reality becomes visible, so that an empirically real object can remain transcendentally phenomenal.
Geometry is reclassified from knowledge of independently spatial objects into evidence for the a priori conditions under which objects can be externally given.
Self-consciousness is reclassified from immediate self-possession into temporally mediated self-appearance.
Illusion is relocated from the subjective ideality of forms to the attempt to treat those forms as independently objective conditions of being.
At the surface level, the text concerns space, time, sensation, geometry, external objects, and self-consciousness.
At the structural level, cognition is organized by receptive subjectivity, pure forms of intuition, relational presentation, and phenomenal objecthood.
At the metastrategic level, the transcendental question displaces inquiry from what objects are to the conditions under which they can be given and known.
At the ontological and temporal level, finite beings inhabit derivative spatiotemporal intuition, while things in themselves and original intuition remain outside that mode of cognition.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the movement from phenomenal limitation through geometrical necessity to the distinction between empirical reality and transcendental ideality.
The system remains internally coherent only if objective reality is restricted to objects as given under universal forms rather than extended to predicates independent of every subject.
The argument is structurally strongest where the necessity of synthetic geometry excludes both empirical experience and concepts alone as its source.

The inference from relational intuition to the unknowability of intrinsic nature depends on a distinction between relation and inner constitution that the section asserts rather than independently establishes.
The account of self-affection leaves underdetermined how the subject can actively apprehend itself while receiving itself passively in temporal intuition.
The scope of the forms remains unresolved beyond humanity, since possible agreement among all finite beings is admitted but not decidable.
The reductio of objective space and time relies on treating their self-subsistence and applicability to all being as unavoidable consequences, which concentrates the polemical force of the argument.
The theological contrast preserves the system’s boundary only as illustration, so reconstruction does not require it as an independent proof.

identity.title: § 9. General Remarks on Transcendental Æsthetic.

units.title: § 10. Conclusion of the Transcendental Æsthetic.

items.text: The transcendental-philosophical problem concerns the possibility of synthetic a priori propositions.
Pure a priori intuitions are identified as the conditions through which synthetic a priori cognition becomes possible.
Space and time supply a priori content that exceeds what is contained in a concept while remaining capable of synthetic unification with it.
The resulting judgments possess validity only with respect to objects of the senses and possible experience.
The argument therefore establishes the possibility of synthetic a priori cognition together with the experiential boundary of its validity.
The possibility of synthetic a priori propositions is the governing problem of transcendental philosophy.
Space and time are pure a priori intuitions.
An a priori judgment can pass beyond the content of a given conception.
Pure intuition contains a priori material not discoverable in the corresponding conception.
The content supplied by pure intuition can be synthetically united with a conception.
Judgments enabled by pure intuition apply only to objects of the senses.
The validity of these judgments extends only to objects of possible experience.
Synthetic a priori judgment is not exhausted by analysis of the given conception.
Pure intuition is not empirical content received from actual experience.
The validity of judgments grounded in space and time does not extend beyond sensible objects.
The judgments do not possess unrestricted validity independently of possible experience.
The pure intuitions do not authorize cognition of objects outside the conditions of sensibility.
Synthetic a priori judgment is possible because pure intuition contributes content beyond the concept while remaining connectable to it.
Space and time function as enabling conditions rather than merely as objects or contents within empirical cognition.
The existence of synthetic a priori cognition does not entail cognition of reality without reference to sensibility.
The solution to the possibility-question is simultaneously a delimitation of the domain in which the solution holds.
A priori validity is compatible with experiential restriction because the relevant a priori conditions structure possible experience rather than transcend it.

The transcendental account converts the opposition between a priori necessity and experiential limitation into a single structure: necessity belongs to the conditions of experience, not to objects considered independently of those conditions.
The argument produces a bounded conception of knowledge in which extension beyond concepts is possible only through the forms of sensibility.
The partial solution of transcendental philosophy is inseparable from the exposure of a limit on metaphysical cognition.
The same conditions that generate synthetic a priori knowledge also prevent that knowledge from claiming validity beyond possible experience.
The system cannot treat a priori validity as evidence that cognition reaches objects independently of the forms of sensibility.
The system cannot identify the source of synthetic content with concepts alone.
The system cannot preserve both the transcendental account and an unrestricted application of its judgments beyond possible experience.
The system excludes a conception of knowledge in which necessity and objectivity require access to objects apart from sensible conditions.
Cognition of objects wholly independent of possible experience is structurally unavailable within the framework.
The possibility of synthetic a priori cognition is denied as a route to absolute or unrestricted knowledge.
The system leaves no legitimate standpoint from which the conditions of sensibility can be bypassed while retaining the same form of cognition.
The uncompleted remainder of transcendental philosophy is the excluded possibility of knowledge beyond the sensible field.
Governing problem: determine how a judgment can be both synthetic and a priori.
Enabling condition: pure intuitions provide a priori content exceeding the given conception.
Synthetic operation: the additional intuitive content is united with the conception in an a priori judgment.
Domain restriction: the judgment is valid only for objects presented under sensible conditions.
Terminal consequence: the possibility of synthetic a priori cognition is established as a conditionally valid and experience-bound achievement.

Possibility of synthetic a priori propositions → identification of pure intuitions → supplementation of concepts by a priori intuitive content → synthetic unification → restriction to sensible objects → validity within possible experience.
The source of synthetic a priori cognition is relocated from conceptual analysis alone to the relation between concepts and pure intuition.
The distinction between a priori validity and unrestricted applicability becomes explicit.
The boundary between possible experience and cognition beyond sensibility becomes the decisive limit of transcendental validity.
The problem of synthetic a priori knowledge is transformed from a binary possibility-question into a possibility-plus-domain question.
**Surface:** Synthetic a priori judgments are possible through the pure intuitions of space and time.
**Structural:** Pure intuition supplies non-conceptual a priori content that can be synthetically integrated with concepts.
**Metastrategic:** The argument solves the possibility problem by simultaneously restricting the scope of the resulting cognition.
**Ontological/Temporal:** Space and time function as a priori conditions of sensible objectivity, while objects outside possible experience remain beyond the established field of validity.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the movement from the problem of synthetic a priori judgment to its restricted solution.
The reconstruction preserves the distinction between conceptual content and intuitive contribution.
The reconstruction preserves the dual result: synthetic a priori cognition is possible, but only within possible experience.
The argument is internally coherent if pure intuition is accepted as both a priori and sensible in function.
The remaining underdetermination concerns the further account of how space and time themselves ground particular judgments.
The compressed system preserves the argument’s central tension: the same a priori conditions that enable cognition also delimit its reach.

identity.title: § 10. Conclusion of the Transcendental Æsthetic.

units.title: I. Of Logic in General.

items.text: Cognition requires the joint operation of receptivity, through which objects are given, and spontaneity, through which they are thought.
The irreducible division between sensibility and understanding requires a corresponding division between æsthetic and logic.
Logic must be stratified by whether it governs all thought or thought concerning a determinate class of objects.
General logic becomes scientifically valid only when purified of empirical conditions governing the actual exercise of understanding.
Pure general logic is delimited as an a priori canon of the formal use of understanding and reason, not as a doctrine of objects or subjective mental life.
Applied logic is reclassified as an empirical discipline concerning the hindrances and conditions of human thinking rather than as logic proper.
Objects are given through receptivity and thought through spontaneity.
Intuition and conception are jointly necessary elements of cognition.
Human intuition is necessarily sensuous and expresses the manner in which subjects are affected by objects.
Understanding thinks objects of sensuous intuition through conceptions.
Sensibility cannot think, and understanding cannot intuite.
Knowledge arises only from the united operation of sensibility and understanding.
The science of sensibility is distinct from the science of understanding.
General logic concerns laws of thought necessary for every use of understanding, independently of differences among objects.
Particular logic concerns correct thought only in relation to a determinate class of objects.
Pure general logic abstracts from all cognitive content, objects, and empirical conditions of the exercise of understanding.
Pure general logic contains only completely a priori principles governing the formal use of understanding and reason.
Applied logic concerns understanding under empirically given subjective conditions that can hinder or promote its use.
Applied logic necessarily depends on empirical and psychological principles.
Cognition is not produced by conceptions without corresponding intuition.
Cognition is not produced by intuition without conceptions.
Understanding is not a faculty of intuition.
Sensibility is not a faculty of thought.
General logic is not concerned with the content of cognition or with the specific objects thought.
Pure general logic is not derived from psychology.
Pure general logic is not an organon for extending cognition of objects.
Applied logic is not a demonstrated science or a canon of understanding in general.
Particular logic is not primary in the order by which a science of its objects is acquired.
Thoughts lacking intuition are formally thinkable but cognitively empty.
Intuitions lacking conceptions provide sensible givenness without cognition of an object.
The distinction between æsthetic and logic follows from the non-interchangeability of sensibility and understanding.
Pure intuition and pure conception can be a priori because they contain form without sensation.
General logic has universal validity only by abstracting from every distinction among objects and every empirical source of cognition.
A particular organon can be articulated only after a substantial cognition of its determinate object-domain has been acquired.
Applied logic can diagnose attention, error, doubt, hesitation, and conviction only as empirical modifications of human understanding.
The possibility of objective cognition is located neither in receptivity alone nor in spontaneity alone, but in their ordered synthesis.
Formal universality is purchased by the exclusion of object-content, psychological causation, and concrete error from pure logic.
Logic bifurcates into a canon that legislates necessary formal conditions of thinking and an empirical cathartic that regulates defective human performance.
The alleged autonomy of a special science is retrospective, because its logical organon presupposes prior acquaintance with the object-domain it organizes.
The systematic separation of faculties is required precisely because cognition depends on their cooperation.
No purely intellectual access to objects is available to finite human cognition.
No sensible datum counts as knowledge independently of conceptual determination.
No account of the psychological origin of thinking can establish the validity of logical laws.
No formal logical canon can determine the material truth of cognition by itself.
No universal logic can retain its universality while incorporating the contingent conditions of individual human thinkers.
The system excludes a standpoint from which cognition could be grounded by a single self-sufficient faculty.
The system excludes the reduction of normatively valid thought to the empirical history, psychology, or pathology of thinkers.
The system excludes a logic that would simultaneously be universally formal, materially cognitive, and psychologically concrete.
The system forecloses any direct transition from formal conditions of thought to knowledge of determinate objects.
Receptivity gives an object in intuition; spontaneity thinks that object under conceptions; their synthesis yields cognition.
The non-interchangeability of the two faculties requires the separation of laws of sensibility from laws of understanding.
Laws of understanding divide according to scope: universal laws of every thought and special laws for determinate object-domains.
Universal logic divides according to purification: abstraction from empirical conditions yields pure logic, while retention of subjective conditions yields applied logic.
Pure abstraction yields an a priori formal canon; empirical retention yields a practical diagnosis of the human use and misuse of understanding.
The distinction between canon, organon, and cathartic prevents formal logic, special science, and empirical psychology from being conflated.
The problem of cognition → the dual-source constitution of cognition → the necessary cooperation and separation of intuition and conception.
The division of cognitive faculties → the division of sciences into æsthetic and logic → the delimitation of logic as the science of understanding.
Logic as science of understanding → general versus particular use → canon versus organon.
General logic → abstraction from empirical conditions or attention to them → pure logic or applied logic.
Pure logic as a priori formal canon → applied logic as empirical cathartic → the exclusion of psychology from logical validity.
The distinction between having an intuition and cognizing an object becomes visible as the distinction between sensible affection and conceptual determination.
Logic is reclassified from a general account of mental activity into a formal science whose purity depends on exclusion of empirical psychology.
Error, doubt, attention, habit, and inclination are displaced from the foundation of logic to the empirical conditions of its human application.
