Modal predicates → cognitive-relational reinterpretation → formal criterion of possibility → perceptual criterion of reality → causal criterion of necessity → empirical restriction of modality.

Reality criterion → idealist challenge → temporal analysis of self-consciousness → dependence on external permanence → general dependence of categories on external intuition → reduction of pure principles to conditions of possible experience.
Modality is reclassified from a set of intrinsic object-properties into a set of relations between conceptions and cognitive procedures.
The boundary between the thinkable and the possible is redrawn through formal compatibility with possible experience.
Reality is relocated from conceptual completeness to the perceptually connected field of experience.
The epistemic priority of inner over outer experience is reversed by making temporal self-determination depend on external permanence.
Necessity is narrowed from absolute or substantial being to law-governed dependence among phenomenal states.
Categories are reclassified from self-sufficient representations of being into formal operators requiring intuition for objective use.
Questions about absolute possibility, alternative experiential worlds, and modal totality are transferred from understanding to reason and transcendental dialectic.
At the surface level, the text establishes distinct criteria for possibility, reality, and necessity.
At the structural level, modal validity is generated by the cooperation of understanding, intuition, perception, judgment, and empirical law.
At the metastrategic level, the text converts idealist doubt and metaphysical assertion into tests of the conditions required for experience.
At the ontological and temporal level, phenomenal reality forms a lawfully unified field in which temporal self-consciousness depends on external permanence and necessity remains conditioned.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the three modal postulates, the refutation of idealism, and the final restriction of pure understanding to possible experience.
The reconstruction remains dependent on prior accounts of space and time, the analogies of experience, causality, apperception, and the distinction between phenomena and things in themselves.
The system is most coherent where one experiential domain supplies parallel criteria for modal validity and category use.
The refutation of idealism compresses the transition from the need for permanence in temporal determination to the claim that only external matter can supply it.
The designation of external experience as immediate remains structurally tense because its necessity is established through a transcendental argument.
The claim that modality is merely subjectively synthetic coexists with claims of objective validity; coherence depends on treating objectivity as validity under experiential conditions.
The exclusion of leaps and hiatuses extends the requirement of unified experience into continuity claims whose complete deduction is not supplied here.

Reconstruction preserves the argument’s movement only if the idealism proof and the dependence on external intuition remain internal consequences of the modal analysis rather than detachable digressions.

identity.title: Transcendental Dialectic.

units.title: I. Of Transcendental Illusory Appearance

items.text: Truth, error, and illusory appearance arise only in judgement, where an object is related to understanding.
Error is produced when sensibility covertly supplies subjective grounds that understanding treats as objective grounds of judgement.
The inquiry excludes empirical deception in order to isolate an illusion that drives reason beyond possible experience.
The argument distinguishes immanent employment within experience from transcendent principles that authorize passage beyond experience.
Transcendental illusion is generated when subjective necessities of reason are taken as objective necessities of things.
Transcendental dialectic can expose and regulate this illusion but cannot abolish its recurrent production by human reason.
Truth and error exist only in judgement.
Sensibility does not judge and therefore does not itself err.
Understanding acting solely under its own laws produces formally lawful judgements.
Error arises when sensibility influences understanding without that influence being recognized.
Transcendental reflection can distinguish the respective contributions of sensibility and understanding within a judgement.
Principles restricted to possible experience are immanent.
Principles that authorize cognition beyond possible experience are transcendent.
A transcendent principle differs from a merely erroneous transcendental use of the categories.
Logical illusion results from inattention to logical rules.
Transcendental illusion results from subjective principles of reason appearing as objective principles.
Transcendental illusion persists after criticism has disclosed its groundlessness.
Transcendental dialectic can expose and guard against illusion but cannot terminate its natural recurrence.
Dialectic is not a doctrine of probability, because probability remains defective but non-deceptive cognition.
Phenomenon is not identical with illusory appearance.
Sensible representation is neither true nor false because it contains no judgement.
Error is not attributable to sensibility alone or understanding alone.
The inquiry is not concerned with empirical illusion occurring within otherwise valid empirical judgement.
Transcendental illusion is not identical with transcendent principles.
The legitimate principles of pure understanding are not licensed for objects beyond experience.
Transcendental illusion is not removable by the same attentive correction that dissolves logical illusion.
Error must be analyzed as a composite judgement rather than assigned to an isolated cognitive faculty.
The proper critical procedure resolves an erroneous judgement into subjective sensory influence and lawful intellectual form.
The boundary of possible experience functions as the criterion separating legitimate pure-understanding principles from transcendent claims.
Reason can experience subjective necessity as if it disclosed the necessary structure of things in themselves.
Recognition that a transcendent claim lacks objective validity does not extinguish the disposition to generate that claim.
Critique changes the status of illusion from an unrecognized source of error into a permanently monitored tendency.
The system relocates transcendental error from defective empirical evidence to a structural misattribution of rational subjectivity as objectivity.
Critical philosophy cannot deliver a final state free of metaphysical illusion, because the source of illusion is constitutive of reason’s ordinary operation.
The immanent–transcendent distinction converts the limit of experience from a mere absence of knowledge into a juridical limit on valid cognition.
Dialectic becomes a discipline of recurrent containment rather than a technique for permanently eliminating error.
No felt necessity of thought can count as immediate evidence of an objective necessity in things.
No cognition extending beyond possible experience can acquire validity merely by being generated from pure concepts or rational maxims.
No faculty-level innocence guarantees truth when faculties are combined in an unexamined judgement.
No critical disclosure can transform finite human reason into a faculty that ceases to solicit transcendent conclusions.
The system forecloses a standpoint from which reason could retain its constitutive demand for unconditioned cognition without producing transcendent illusion.
The system denies that objective reality can be secured by the mere internal coherence, subjective necessity, or formal inevitability of rational thought.
The system leaves unavailable any positive theoretical domain beyond experience in which transcendent principles could be validated.
Sensibility supplies intuition and understanding supplies judgement; their unobserved interference produces ordinary error.
Transcendental reflection decomposes the composite judgement and assigns each representation to its proper cognitive faculty.
Possible experience establishes the boundary within which pure-understanding principles retain immanent validity.
Subjective maxims of reason acquire the appearance of objective principles and generate transcendent claims beyond that boundary.
Criticism exposes the projection of subjectivity as objectivity, while dialectic continually guards against its renewed operation.
Error is relocated from objects and isolated faculties to the judgement in which sensibility and understanding become confused.
The analysis moves from ordinary error to the distinction between empirical illusion and transcendental illusion.
The distinction between immanent and transcendent principles fixes possible experience as the boundary of legitimate cognition.
Subjective rational necessity is then diagnosed as the source of an objective-seeming transcendental illusion.
The final position assigns dialectic the continuing task of exposure and restraint rather than eradication.
Illusion is reclassified from a property of objects or sensations into a defect of judgement and its attribution of grounds.
The limit of experience is reclassified from an empirical shortfall into the constitutive boundary of valid theoretical principle.
The opposition between error and critique is redrawn: critique can neutralize the authority of illusion without eliminating its appearance.
Dialectic is reclassified from sophistical failure into an unavoidable and natural tendency internal to pure reason.
Surface — The immediate object is the distinction between logical, empirical, and transcendental forms of illusory appearance.
Structural — Error is generated by an unrecognized crossing of cognitive functions, especially sensibility’s determination of understanding.
Metastrategic — Criticism operates by demarcating valid employment, exposing illegitimate extension, and instituting permanent vigilance.
Ontological/Temporal — Human reason necessarily and repeatedly projects subjective rational demands onto things beyond possible experience.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the argument’s central movement from the location of error to the necessity of critical restraint.
The system depends principally on the distinction between subjective necessity and objective validity.
The system remains underdetermined regarding how criticism reliably identifies the boundary between a merely subjective maxim and a valid objective principle.
The strongest structural relation is the distinction between correctable logical illusion and ineradicable transcendental illusion.
The system contains a productive tension because reason must employ the very subjective principles that criticism identifies as the source of its recurring illusion.
Reconstruction preserves the argument only if dialectic is treated as ongoing regulation of an unavoidable tendency rather than final removal of false appearance.

identity.title: I. Of Transcendental Illusory Appearance

units.title: II. Of Pure Reason as the Seat of Transcendental Illusory Appearance

items.text: Human cognition rises from sensibility through understanding to reason, whose proper task is the highest unity of cognition.
Reason must be distinguished from understanding because understanding unifies intuitions under rules, whereas reason unifies rules under principles.
The logical form of syllogism reveals reason’s operative demand to seek conditions for conditioned judgements until an unconditioned condition is reached.
The transition from a logical demand for completeness to an assertion that the unconditioned exists in objects is synthetic and cannot be secured by logic alone.
Transcendental illusion originates when the subjective maxim of ascending toward higher conditions is mistaken for an objective principle determining objects beyond possible experience.
Transcendental dialectic must determine whether reason’s principle has objective validity or only regulates the systematic ordering of understanding.
All human cognition begins in sensibility, is processed by understanding, and is ordered toward unity by reason.
Understanding is the faculty of rules.
Reason is the faculty of principles because it produces unity among the rules of understanding.
Cognition from principles cognizes a particular through its subsumption under a general conception.
A merely general proposition can function comparatively as a principle without being a principle by origin.
Synthetic cognition from concepts alone is required for principles in the strict sense.
The principles of understanding obtain their objective use only through the conditions of possible experience.
Reason does not directly determine intuitions or sensuous objects; it acts mediately through understanding and its judgements.
Logical reason seeks the general condition under which a conditioned judgement follows.
The repeated search for conditions leads reason to demand the unconditioned as the completion of conditioned cognition.
The claim that the whole series of conditions is given whenever the conditioned is given is a synthetic principle.
Any objective use of this principle exceeds the immanent limits of understanding and possible experience.
Reason’s demand for systematic unity is initially a subjective law governing the arrangement of cognitions.
Transcendental dialectic investigates whether reason’s subjective demand can legitimately determine objects.
Reason is not merely the faculty of mediate inference, because that definition excludes its purported real and transcendental use.
Reason is not a faculty that directly applies concepts to intuition or sensuous objects.
The unity of reason is not the empirical unity that makes experience possible.
The principle that every event has a cause is not generated by reason independently of possible experience.
A subjective requirement for conceptual economy is not an objective law of things.
Logical ascent from a conditioned cognition to its conditions does not by itself establish an unconditioned object.
Transcendent principles are not legitimately usable as immanent principles of empirical cognition.
The completeness of the series of conditions cannot be postulated as an objective feature of objects merely because reason requires completion.
Reason’s proper object is understanding itself, since rational unity orders the manifold rules and cognitions produced by understanding.
The syllogism formalizes reason’s operation by moving from a rule, through subsumption under its condition, to a determined conclusion.
The demand for the unconditioned is generated recursively because every discovered condition can itself be treated as conditioned.
Reason seeks to reduce the plurality of cognitions and rules to the smallest possible number of higher principles.
The unconditioned cannot be supplied by the understanding, because understanding cognizes only under conditions of possible experience.
The assertion of a complete unconditioned series introduces propositions that exceed what the categories and principles of understanding can establish.
Transcendental illusion is structurally possible because a necessary logical maxim can be misread as a constitutive principle of objects.
Reason produces a systematic totality-demand that is necessary for cognition’s organization but indeterminate with respect to the existence of a corresponding object.
The same rational movement that advances cognition toward systematic unity also produces transcendent claims when its formal requirement is objectified.
Dialectical error is generated not by accidental irrationality but by reason’s lawful tendency to complete the series of conditions.
The critique of reason must preserve the regulative demand for unity while suspending its unauthorized constitutive extension.
The system excludes any direct passage from the form of inference to knowledge of unconditioned being.
The system excludes the identity of subjective cognitive necessity with objective ontological necessity.
The system excludes an empirical object that could adequately exhibit or verify the totality of all conditions.
The system excludes the possibility that understanding’s experiential principles can determine what lies beyond possible experience.
The system excludes closure of rational inquiry through a final object whenever that closure is claimed as empirically knowable.
The argument is organized around the unavailable coincidence between reason’s demand for absolute completion and cognition’s capacity for objective verification.
The argument forecloses an unmediated intellectual access to the unconditioned.
The argument treats absolute totality as thinkable through reason’s demand yet inadmissible as a directly determinable object of experience.
The argument denies that human cognition can occupy a standpoint from which the entire series of conditions is simply given.
Conditioned judgement → search for its general condition.
General condition → renewed treatment of that condition as conditioned.
Recursive ascent through conditions → logical demand for the unconditioned.
Logical demand for completion → possible synthetic assertion that the complete series exists in the object.
Objectification of subjective rational demand → transcendence beyond possible experience.
Transcendent objectification → transcendental illusion and dialectical syllogism.
Dialectical critique → separation of regulative systematic unity from constitutive objective cognition.
The distinction between sensibility, understanding, and reason establishes reason as the problem of highest cognitive unity.
The distinction between rules and principles redefines reason as the faculty that systematizes understanding.
The analysis of syllogism reveals reason’s formal movement from conditioned cognition toward higher conditions.
The regress toward higher conditions generates the idea of an unconditioned completion.
The unconditioned becomes dialectically problematic when logical completion is asserted as objective totality.
Transcendental dialectic tests the legitimacy of that assertion and isolates the illusion produced by its misuse.
Reason is reclassified from a faculty that merely infers conclusions into a faculty that demands systematic unity among rules.
The distinction between logical and transcendental use separates formal inferential validity from objective validity concerning objects.
The unconditioned is recast from an immediately available object of cognition into a problem generated by rational regression.
Systematic unity is separated from empirical determination, allowing rational organization without immediate ontological commitment.
Error is reclassified as a lawful effect of reason’s own drive toward completeness rather than as a mere empirical mistake.
Surface — Reason is differentiated from understanding through its role in syllogism, principles, and the pursuit of higher unity.
Structural — Cognition is organized as a hierarchy in which sensibility supplies intuition, understanding supplies rules, and reason orders rules into a system.
Metastrategic — Critical inquiry shifts from asking whether reason can infer correctly to asking whether its demand for completion has objective authority.
Ontological/Temporal — The regress through conditions projects a totality of conditions whose completed givenness cannot be presumed within possible experience.
The axioms suffice to reconstruct the movement from the hierarchy of faculties to the dialectical problem of the unconditioned.
The structure depends principally on the distinction between a logical maxim of regression and a synthetic claim about objects.
The system is coherent insofar as it separates understanding’s immanent experiential use from reason’s demand for systematic unity.
The central fault line is that reason’s necessary pursuit of completion continually pressures cognition toward claims that its own critical limits prohibit.
The status of the unconditioned remains underdetermined until dialectic establishes whether it is objectively valid, merely regulative, or the source of unavoidable illusion.
Reconstruction preserves the argument only if the logical necessity of seeking conditions is not conflated with knowledge that an unconditioned totality is given.

identity.title: II. Of Pure Reason as the Seat of Transcendental Illusory Appearance

units.title: Transcendental Dialectic—Book I—Of The Conceptions Of Pure Reason.

items.text: The problem is to distinguish the origin, scope, and possible objective validity of the conceptions of pure reason.
The text separates conceptions of reason from conceptions of understanding by their mode of production and function.
Conceptions of understanding organize phenomena within possible experience, whereas conceptions of reason seek cognition exceeding any complete empirical attainment.
Reason is defined by its tendency toward the unconditioned underlying or governing conditioned cognition.
The objective validity of rational conceptions remains conditional and is distinguished from their merely apparent derivability.
The argument moves from distinction of faculties, through delimitation of experience, toward the classification of rational conceptions as transcendental ideas.
Conceptions of pure reason are obtained through inference or conclusion rather than reflection.
Conceptions of understanding are a priori conditions that provide the unity of reflection required for possible empirical consciousness.
Cognition and determination of an object require the conceptions of understanding.
The objective reality of conceptions of understanding depends on restricting their application to possible experience.
Rational conceptions seek a cognition of which empirical cognition and possible experience are only parts.
The aim of rational conceptions is comprehension, whereas the aim of conceptions of understanding is the understanding of perceptions.
The unconditioned is that to which all experience is subordinate but which is never itself given as an object of experience.
Reason tends toward the unconditioned in its conclusions from experience and uses it as a standard for estimating empirical cognition.
A rational conception has objective validity only if it is legitimately concluded rather than merely admitted because it appears correctly concluded.
The pure conceptions of reason are designated transcendental ideas.
Pure rational conceptions are not generated by reflection in the manner of the conceptions of understanding.
Conceptions of understanding are not derived from prior a priori conceptions of objects.
The conceptions of understanding do not possess unrestricted application beyond possible experience.
The unconditioned is not an element in an empirical synthesis.
No actual experience fully attains the cognition toward which rational conceptions tend.
Apparent derivability does not establish objective validity.
The text does not yet determine whether particular rational conceptions are legitimate or sophistical; that determination is deferred to the dialectical analysis.
Because conceptions of understanding constitute the intellectual form of experience, their objective reality is inseparable from empirical restriction.
Because rational conceptions aim at cognition exceeding empirical cognition, they cannot receive their complete object from any possible experience.
The unconditioned functions as a regulative terminus of reasoning from experience without becoming an empirical object within that reasoning.
Rational conceptions divide into legitimate conceptions and sophistical conceptions according to whether their inferred objective validity is established or merely presumed.

The distinction between understanding and reason is simultaneously a distinction between the determination of objects within experience and the comprehension of the totality or condition of such objects.
The proper classification of rational conceptions requires a later analysis of the dialectical conclusions produced by reason.
Reason is structurally oriented beyond the domain that alone can confer direct objective reality, creating a permanent distinction between its aim and its possible evidentiary ground.
The unconditioned operates as the horizon that organizes the evaluation of conditioned cognition without entering the empirical series as one more condition.
The system makes the legitimacy of reason depend on a future adjudication of inference rather than on the mere presence of an a priori conception.

The distinction between understanding and reason converts the boundary of experience from a limitation on cognition into the criterion for separating valid object-determination from speculative overreach.
The system cannot treat all a priori conceptions as having the same origin, function, or entitlement to objects.
The system excludes the identification of the unconditioned with any empirically discoverable item within the chain of conditions.
The system disqualifies unrestricted extension from the domain of possible experience as a sufficient ground of objective validity.
The system cannot infer legitimacy from the psychological or formal appearance of a conclusion alone.
The system excludes a completed empirical possession of the total cognition toward which reason is directed.
The text excludes a form of reason whose objects would be immediately available within experience while still functioning as the unconditioned.
The text excludes the possibility that the demand for total comprehension can be satisfied by extending empirical cognition without altering its epistemic status.
The text withholds any final guarantee that the content generated by reason corresponds to an objectively valid object.
The argument is organized around the absence of an empirical presentation adequate to reason’s complete object-matter.
A priori cognition divides into understanding-based conceptions and reason-based conceptions.
Understanding-based conceptions unify phenomena and thereby make object-determination within possible experience possible.
Reason-based conceptions infer a cognition that exceeds any particular empirical cognition and potentially exceeds the whole of possible experience.
The unconditioned is introduced as the terminal orientation of reasoning from conditioned experience.
The inferred conception is tested by the distinction between legitimate objective validity and sophistical appearance.
The resulting class of reason-conceptions is named transcendental ideas, whose legitimacy is reserved for subsequent dialectical examination.

A priori conceptual plurality → distinction of origin → understanding as condition of experience → reason as inference beyond experience → orientation toward the unconditioned → separation of legitimate and sophistical inference → designation as transcendental ideas → deferred dialectical adjudication.
The conceptual field is divided between object-determining cognition within experience and comprehension directed beyond the limits of experience.
The boundary of experience becomes an epistemic criterion rather than merely a restriction on the quantity of knowable objects.
The unconditioned is reclassified from a possible object among objects into the terminal standard or horizon of rational inference.
The distinction between valid and invalid metaphysical cognition is relocated from content alone to the mode by which the conception is inferred.
Pure reason is mapped as simultaneously indispensable for total comprehension and unable to obtain its aim through direct empirical presentation.
Surface: The text introduces and differentiates the conceptions of understanding and the conceptions of pure reason.
Structural: Understanding supplies the form through which phenomena become objects, while reason organizes conditioned cognition in relation to an unconditioned terminus.
Metastrategic: The text establishes a procedure for adjudicating rational concepts by separating legitimate inference from merely apparent inference.
Ontological/Temporal: The unconditioned is positioned as a non-empirical limit toward which cognition tends, while its objective status remains unresolved until later dialectical analysis.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the primary distinction between understanding and reason.
The axioms preserve the dependence of objectivity on possible experience and the orientation of reason toward the unconditioned.
The classification of rational conceptions as legitimate or sophistical remains deliberately underdetermined.
The central tension is that reason seeks cognition beyond experience while objective validity is introduced through a criterion not yet supplied.
The system is internally coherent at the level of functional distinction but incomplete at the level of validating particular transcendental ideas.
Reconstruction preserves the movement from faculty-differentiation to transcendental classification and deferred dialectical judgment.

identity.title: Transcendental Dialectic—Book I—Of The Conceptions Of Pure Reason.

units.title: Section I—Of Ideas in General

items.text: Linguistic indeterminacy threatens the preservation, communication, and scientific use of distinct conceptions.
The term “idea” must be recovered from Platonic usage and reserved for a determinate rational function rather than dispersed across representations generally.
Reason generates cognitions whose objects cannot be given in possible experience, yet whose practical operation is real.
Practical ideas function as archetypal standards by which empirical actions, persons, laws, and institutions are judged without being derived from them.
The discrepancy between an idea and its realization establishes a task of approximation rather than a refutation of the idea.
The argument moves from terminological discipline through the practical authority of ideas to a critical inquiry into the legitimate transcendental use of pure reason.
Distinct conceptions require distinct and stable terms.
A representation becomes cognitively determinate only through its place within a graduated taxonomy of representations.
An idea is a concept of reason that transcends the possibility of experience.
Ideas are not derived from the senses and admit of no perfectly corresponding empirical object.
A cognition may be real even when no object corresponding to it can be given in experience.
Practical reason, because it concerns freedom, can make ideas operative causes of actions and their objects.
Empirical instances can illustrate an idea but cannot constitute its archetype or determine its content.
Imperfect realization of an idea does not invalidate its normative authority.
The idea of a lawful constitution of mutually compatible freedom is prior to and regulative of legislation.
Ethical and juridical laws cannot be derived from empirical conduct because experience supplies what is done rather than what ought to be done.
Experience is a source of rules and truth for nature but a source of illusion when treated as the ground of ethical law.
The legitimate use, influence, and worth of ideas require transcendental critique.
Platonic insight into ideas must be separated from mystical deduction, hypostatization, and unrestricted extension into speculative cognition.
Philosophical precision is not secured by indiscriminate neologism or stylistic variation in the use of technical terms.
An idea is not a generic name for every representation.
An idea is not a sensation, intuition, empirical concept, pure concept of understanding, or category.
An empirical example is not an original model of virtue, justice, or lawful freedom.
An idea is not disqualified by the absence of complete realization in human action or political institutions.
The political end is not the greatest possible happiness as an independently grounding principle.
Adverse historical experience is not decisive evidence against a rational ideal.
Ethical obligation is not inferable from prevailing conduct, customary institutions, or observed human behavior.
A critical theory of ideas is not identical with Plato’s speculative, mystical, or hypostatizing doctrine of ideas.
The representation “idea” occupies a terminal position in the taxonomy of representations and cannot be applied to merely sensible or intellectual contents.
Moral appraisal presupposes a rational standard that precedes every comparison among empirical actions or persons.
Virtuous persons function as graded examples only because an antecedent idea of virtue measures their adequacy.
Political reform remains rationally directed by the idea of reciprocal freedom even when no state fully realizes it.
Institutional failure can indicate defective legislation or neglected rational principles rather than the impracticability of freedom.
The relation between nature and ethics divides the epistemic authority of experience: descriptive authority belongs to nature, while normative authority belongs to reason.
Reason can legitimately exceed experience in practical use only under a critique that distinguishes such use from metaphysical reification.
The impossibility of assigning the final distance between an idea and realization prevents any empirical limit from fixing the destination of freedom.
The system establishes two irreducible regimes of validity: empirical cognition governs natural actuality, while rational ideas govern practical assessment and direction.
Nonconformity to an ideal becomes the condition for moral and political judgment rather than evidence that judgment lacks an object.
Terminological taxonomy becomes an epistemic border-policing mechanism that prevents the ascent from sensation to reason from being collapsed into one undifferentiated field of representation.
The authority of practical ideals depends simultaneously on their nonempirical origin and on their capacity to order empirical transformation.
Critique is required because reason must exceed experience to ground obligation while being prevented from converting that excess into knowledge of independently existing ideal objects.
Cognition is not exhausted by the reception and synthesis of objects available in experience.
Normative universality is not produced by generalizing from examples, customs, or historical regularities.
The actuality of institutions is not the measure of their legitimacy.
The historical failure of freedom is not proof of an immutable natural limit on freedom.
No empirical state of affairs can determine the ultimate degree of approximation required by a rational ideal.
Rational standards cannot be preserved if ordinary linguistic usage is permitted to erase distinctions among modes of representation.
The system is organized around an absent empirical object that must nevertheless be present as a standard for judgment.
The system excludes any final empirical reconciliation between ideal law and its complete realization.
The system forecloses both empiricist closure, which denies rational ideals, and dogmatic metaphysical closure, which treats ideals as independently given beings.
The destination of freedom is binding precisely because no authority can assign a final boundary between freedom and its idea.
Linguistic indeterminacy produces conceptual loss; taxonomic differentiation preserves determinate thought.
Taxonomic differentiation isolates the idea as a rational concept exceeding possible experience.
The practical relation to freedom gives the nonempirical idea operational force in actions, judgments, and institutions.
The idea functions as archetype; empirical persons and institutions function as examples, approximations, or deviations.
Imperfect realization is reclassified from disproof into the measurable task of progressive approximation.
Empirical appeals to existing practice are displaced from normative grounding and confined to their proper natural-descriptive domain.
Transcendental critique limits rational excess by distinguishing practical validity from speculative hypostatization.
Lexical imprecision → loss of conceptual distinctions → preservation of technical vocabulary.
Platonic naming of ideas → critical recovery of rational archetypes → separation from Platonic metaphysical excess.
Ideas beyond experience → freedom as practical causality → ideals of virtue and reciprocal legal freedom.
Empirical inadequacy → rejection of empirical refutation → approximation under an unreached rational standard.
Practical authority of ideas → exclusion of empirical ethical grounding → transcendental examination of pure reason.
Representations are reorganized into a hierarchy in which an idea is no longer confused with perception, intuition, concept, or category.
The relation between ideal and instance is redrawn: the ideal judges the instance, while the instance can only exhibit partial practicability.
Political theory is shifted from maximizing happiness or recording existing institutions to constructing conditions of mutually compatible freedom.
Historical failure is reclassified from a veto on ideals into possible evidence of prior legislative and institutional failure.
Experience is divided into two functions: it grounds truth about nature but cannot ground laws of freedom.
Plato is reclassified from a doctrinal authority to a source of a recoverable structural insight requiring critical restriction.
Surface — The explicit task is to reserve “idea” for a concept of reason and to distinguish it from every lower mode of representation.
Structural — The text constructs a hierarchy in which reason, understanding, sensibility, experience, freedom, and legislation possess noninterchangeable functions.
Metastrategic — The argument blocks empirical objections to moral and political ideals by redescribing them as failures of realization rather than failures of principle.
Ontological/Temporal — Ideas lack complete empirical instantiation yet orient an open-ended temporal movement of freedom beyond every assigned limit of realization.
Critical — Pure reason is granted practical reach beyond experience while being subjected to a tribunal that denies it unrestricted speculative objecthood.
The axioms suffice to reconstruct the movement from semantic discipline to the practical authority and critical limitation of ideas.
The system depends centrally on the distinction between empirical objects, rational standards, and the practical causality of freedom.
The argument is internally coherent if ideas are treated as practical archetypes rather than as empirically available objects or independently existing entities.
The strongest structural operation is the conversion of nonrealization from an objection into the very condition of normative judgment and reform.
The system leaves underdetermined how a cognition without a corresponding possible object is established as real rather than merely subjective.
The system also leaves a tension between the asserted practical efficacy of ideas and the required critical prohibition on their hypostatization.
Reconstruction preserves the argument’s real movement only if the terminological taxonomy, practical application, antiempirical normativity, and critical restriction remain jointly operative.

identity.title: Section I—Of Ideas in General

units.title: Section II. Of Transcendental Ideas

items.text: The problem is to determine whether reason’s logical form generates pure a priori conceptions analogous to the categories generated from judgement.
Reason is reconstructed as the faculty that seeks the totality of conditions for every given conditioned cognition.
The demand for totality entails the conception of the unconditioned as the ground of a completed series of conditions.
The three syllogistic relations generate three transcendental ideas: the unconditioned subject, the unconditioned ground of a series, and the complete system of parts.
Transcendental ideas necessarily direct the understanding toward systematic unity but cannot determine objects within possible experience.
The argument moves from logical inference to the necessary regulative demand for unconditioned totality, then restricts that demand from transcendent cognition to the ordered use of understanding.
Logical forms of cognition can yield pure a priori conceptions when applied to the synthesis of intuitions.
The logical form of judgement yields categories that make empirical cognition possible.
The logical form of syllogism yields pure conceptions of reason.
Reason functions by subsuming a conditioned cognition under the universal condition that grounds it.
A syllogism seeks a condition under which a predicate is valid in its whole extent.
The universality of a condition in judgement corresponds to the totality of conditions in the synthesis of intuitions.
A transcendental conception of reason is the conception of the totality of conditions for a given conditioned.
The totality of conditions is possible only through the unconditioned.
The categorical, hypothetical, and disjunctive forms of synthesis require respectively an unconditioned subject, an unconditioned ground of a series, and an unconditioned system of division.
Absolute totality concerns what is unconditioned in every respect and relation.
A transcendental idea is a necessary conception of reason for which no adequate object can be presented in the world of sense.
Pure reason seeks absolute unity of the understanding’s acts rather than immediate cognition of objects of intuition.
The objective employment of transcendental ideas is transcendent because no experience contains the unconditioned.
Transcendental ideas can regulate the extended and self-consistent use of understanding without constituting further cognition of objects.
In an ascending series of conditions, reason presupposes totality as necessary for the truth of the conditioned conclusion.
In a descending series of consequences, reason requires only an indefinitely extendable progression and not a completed totality.
Transcendental ideas are not empirical concepts because no possible experience presents the unconditioned.
Transcendental ideas are not arbitrary fictions because they arise necessarily from reason’s own logical demand.
The unconditioned is not an object immediately cognized through intuition.
The objective use of reason is not immanent in the manner of the understanding’s empirical use.
Absolute possibility is not identical with intrinsic possibility.
Absolute necessity is not identical with internal necessity.
The absence of an adequate sensible object does not make an idea superfluous.
The completed totality demanded on the side of conditions is not a totality that finite cognition can fully apprehend.
Reason necessarily transforms any given conditioned cognition into a demand for its complete ground.
The forms of categorical, hypothetical, and disjunctive inference determine the exhaustive architecture of transcendental ideas.
Reason’s demand for unconditioned totality is logically necessary even where its corresponding object cannot be experienced.
The transcendental use of reason cannot add determinate objects to experience because its proper object exceeds all possible experience.
Ideas retain a legitimate use by ordering the understanding’s cognitions toward maximal systematic unity.
A conditioned conclusion is treated as necessary only through reference to an unconditionally valid totality of grounds.
The asymmetry between conditions and consequences makes completion necessary in regress but unnecessary in progress.
The distinction between absolute and intrinsic necessity blocks the inference from unrestricted necessity to necessity grounded merely in a thing’s inner constitution.
Reason is structurally compelled to exceed experience while being denied constitutive cognition beyond experience.
The system converts reason’s apparent metaphysical excess into a regulative requirement for systematic coherence.
The demand for the unconditioned is generated internally by the logic of conditioned judgement rather than imported from sensory objects.
The truth-claim of inferential cognition depends on a totality that cannot itself be given as an empirical object.
Systematic unity becomes the legitimate surrogate for unavailable knowledge of the unconditioned.
The system excludes the possibility that all legitimate cognition must be directly grounded in sensible presentation.
The system excludes the possibility that reason can be reduced to a merely formal instrument for deriving consequences.
The system excludes the possibility that the conditioned can be finally intelligible without reference to an unconditioned totality of grounds.
The system excludes the possibility that the unconditioned can be known as a determinate empirical object.
The system excludes any simple equivalence between logical necessity, intrinsic necessity, and absolute necessity.
The argument is organized around an unavailable completion: reason must posit totality precisely where no adequate presentation of totality is possible.
The argument forecloses a final coincidence between the structure required for cognition and an object that could satisfy that structure.
The system denies reason both metaphysical possession of the unconditioned and freedom from the demand for it.
Logical form of judgement → categories → conditions of possible empirical cognition.
Logical form of syllogism → search for universal conditions → demand for totality of grounds.
Given conditioned → regress through conditions → conception of the unconditioned.
Three forms of relation → unconditioned subject / unconditioned series-ground / complete systematic division.
No adequate sensible object for the unconditioned → transcendent objective use is blocked.
Necessary demand for totality + prohibition on constitutive transcendence → regulative unity of understanding.
Ascending regress requires completed grounds → descending progression remains indefinitely open.
Categories derived from judgement **→** reason examined through syllogism **→** totality of conditions identified as reason’s object.
Totality of conditions **→** unconditioned **→** three classes of transcendental ideas.
Transcendental ideas as necessary products of reason **→** absence of adequate experience **→** denial of constitutive objective use.
Denial of constitutive use **→** retention of regulative use **→** systematic unity of understanding.
Conditioned conclusion **→** required totality of premises **→** asymmetry between completed regress and open progress.
Metaphysical ideas are reclassified from candidate objects of knowledge into necessary functions of systematic orientation.
The unconditioned is relocated from empirical content to the formal horizon required by reason’s treatment of conditions.
The distinction between understanding and reason is redrawn as a distinction between possible-experience cognition and totalizing regulation.
The distinction between legitimate and illegitimate transcendence is redrawn as regulative guidance versus constitutive object-determination.
Syllogistic forms are reclassified as generators of transcendental ideas rather than merely formal patterns of inference.
Inferential regress and inferential progress are separated into structurally unequal temporal directions.
Surface — Pure conceptions of reason are defined as transcendental ideas oriented toward absolute totality.
Structural — Syllogistic inference compels reason to seek completed grounds for conditioned cognitions.
Metastrategic — Reason’s transcendent tendency is retained as a rule for organizing understanding rather than licensed as knowledge of supersensible objects.
Ontological/Temporal — The unconditioned functions as a necessary but unpresentable horizon of completed regress, while consequences remain capable of indefinite progression.
The axioms reconstruct the central transition from syllogistic form to transcendental ideas.
The axioms reconstruct the derivation of the unconditioned from reason’s demand for totality of conditions.
The system remains underdetermined concerning how a merely regulative idea can secure the specific unity it prescribes without covert objective commitment.
The system is strongest where it distinguishes the logical necessity of seeking totality from the empirical impossibility of presenting totality.
The system depends on the compressed transition from forms of syllogism to exhaustive classes of transcendental ideas.
The distinction between absolute and internal necessity blocks equivocation but leaves the positive determinations of absolute necessity deferred.
Reconstruction preserves the argument’s movement only if the regulative validity of ideas is maintained together with the prohibition on their constitutive objective use.

identity.title: Section II. Of Transcendental Ideas

units.title: Section III. System of Transcendental Ideas

items.text: Transcendental dialectic must be distinguished from formal logical dialectic because it concerns the a priori origin of reason’s non-empirical ideas.
Reason moves from conditioned syntheses toward an unconditioned that understanding cannot reach.
The possible relations of representation yield a threefold architecture of transcendental ideas.
The three ideas organize rational inquiry into soul, world, and supreme being.
The ideas can be subjectively deduced from reason’s syllogistic activity but cannot be objectively deduced from possible experience.
The chapter closes by delimiting pure reason’s proper sphere as a systematic ascent to conditions rather than an extension of empirical cognition.
Transcendental dialectic concerns a priori cognitions and ideas originating in pure reason whose objects cannot be empirically given.
Reason necessarily ascends from the conditioned to the unconditioned.
Understanding remains within conditioned synthesis and cannot reach the unconditioned.
Pure concepts of understanding concern the synthetic unity of representations, while transcendental ideas concern the unconditioned synthetic unity of all conditions.
Representations relate to the subject, to the manifold of phenomena, or to all things in general.
The first class of transcendental ideas concerns the absolute unity of the thinking subject.
The second class of transcendental ideas concerns the absolute unity of the series of conditions of phenomena.
The third class of transcendental ideas concerns the absolute unity of the condition of all objects of thought.
Pure reason relates immediately to concepts contained in understanding rather than immediately to objects.
The categorical syllogism generates the idea of the absolute unity of the thinking subject.
The hypothetical syllogism generates the idea of an absolutely unconditioned series of conditions.
The disjunctive syllogism generates the idea of a being of all beings.
Transcendental ideas admit no objective deduction because they lack objects that can be given in experience.
Transcendental ideas admit a subjective deduction from the nature and necessary activity of reason.
Pure reason seeks absolute totality on the side of conditions rather than absolute completeness on the side of the conditioned.
Reason has only logical, not transcendental, use in descending from conditions to conditioned consequences.
Pure reason collects its ideas into a system progressing from self through world to supreme being.
The analogy between logical forms and transcendental procedures remains unestablished at this stage.
Transcendental dialectic is not logical dialectic abstracted from all cognitive content.
Transcendental ideas are not concepts whose objects can be supplied in experience.
Transcendental ideas are not products that understanding can generate, even through maximal logical inference.
The rational doctrines of soul, world, and supreme being are not objective sciences constituted through empirical objects.
The totality of consequences is not a necessary presupposition of the possibility of the conditioned.
The idea of the complete series of future changes is not a transcendental idea but an ens rationis.
Logical descent from condition to conditioned is not a transcendental employment of reason.
The formal correspondence of syllogistic logic and transcendental reason is not yet demonstrated as an objective analogy.
The architecture of transcendental ideas is necessarily triadic because reason’s demand for unconditioned unity is distributed across the three fundamental relations of representation.
Rational psychology, rational cosmology, and transcendental theology are differentiated by the object-type posited by each idea rather than by empirically given domains.
The subjective deduction of transcendental ideas proceeds through the necessary synthetic use of categorical, hypothetical, and disjunctive inference.
The necessity of transcendental ideas belongs to reason’s demand for conditions and does not establish the existence or cognition of their corresponding objects.
Reason’s legitimate transcendental direction is upward toward conditions, whereas its movement toward consequences remains confined to logical ordering.
The systematic unity of pure reason is a classification of its necessary ideas, not a completed proof that their objects form a knowable totality.
Pure reason is constituted as a system-producing faculty whose necessity exceeds the limits of possible object-cognition.
Logical form supplies the generative grammar of transcendental ideas without supplying their objective warrant.
Metaphysical inquiry is reclassified from inquiry into empirically available objects to inquiry into the necessary totalizing demands of reason.
The system generates an asymmetry in which reason must posit an unconditioned ground for conditions while being barred from treating that ground as empirically knowable.
The enclosure of pure reason’s sphere simultaneously legitimates transcendental ideas as necessary products and suspends their conversion into speculative knowledge.
Empirical cognition cannot supply its own absolute totality of conditions.
The unconditioned cannot become an object of experience without ceasing to function as the unconditioned sought by reason.
The subjective necessity of reason cannot be equated with objective validity for objects.
The order of grounds and conditions cannot be replaced by an equally necessary totality of effects and consequences.
The triadic system presupposes that every transcendental demand of reason can be exhaustively situated under subject, world, or supreme condition.
No speculative procedure can transform reason’s need for unconditioned unity into direct cognition of an unconditioned object.
No established homology yet licenses the transfer of validity from logical syllogistic form to transcendental reality.
Freedom is excluded from the chapter’s operative triad of subject, world, and supreme being, although footnote 42 represents metaphysics as ordered around God, freedom, and immortality.
The system cannot provide a final metaphysical object while preserving the distinction between an idea of reason and a concept of possible experience.
The distinction between logical form and transcendental content isolates pure reason as the source of non-empirical ideas.
The ascent from conditioned synthesis to unconditioned unity establishes the functional demand governing those ideas.
The three relations of representation distribute that demand into subject, phenomenal series, and all objects of thought.
The three syllogistic forms generate the corresponding ideas of soul, world, and being of all beings.
The lack of empirical objects blocks objective deduction while permitting a subjective deduction from reason’s own necessary operation.
The restriction of transcendental use to ascent toward conditions excludes consequential totalities and encloses pure reason within a determinate system.
Formal logical dialectic is separated from transcendental dialectic.
Reason’s ascent from conditioned synthesis is identified as the source of transcendental demand.
Relations of representation are reduced to a threefold classificatory matrix.
Unconditioned unity is distributed into the ideas of self, world, and supreme being.
Syllogistic forms provide a subjective genesis for the ideas while empirical objectivity is denied.
The asymmetry between conditions and consequences restricts legitimate transcendental use to ascent.
The resulting ideas are unified as a closed system of pure reason whose logical-transcendental analogy remains provisional.
The distinction between concepts of understanding and ideas of reason redraws the boundary between empirical cognition and rational totalization.
Psychology, cosmology, and theology are reclassified as the three structural destinations of reason’s demand for unconditioned unity.
The contrast between ascending toward conditions and descending toward consequences separates necessary transcendental ideas from arbitrary rational fictions.
Logical syllogistic form becomes visible as a source of transcendental architecture without becoming evidence for transcendent objects.
Systematic unity becomes a feature of reason’s self-organization rather than a map of a directly knowable metaphysical domain.
Surface — The chapter classifies transcendental ideas as ideas of soul, world, and supreme being.
Structural — The classification is generated by the relation between conditioned synthesis, unconditioned unity, and the three forms of syllogistic inference.
Metastrategic — The argument secures a legitimate field for rational ideas by deriving them subjectively while withholding objective deduction.
Ontological/Temporal — The unconditioned functions as a required ground of conditions but cannot be treated as an empirically completed totality of objects or future consequences.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the chapter’s movement from the distinction of dialectics to the systematic triad of transcendental ideas.
The reconstruction depends on the irreducible distinction between subjective rational necessity and objective cognition.
The architecture is internally coherent insofar as the same restriction that blocks objective deduction also explains the need for subjective deduction.
The system is strongest where it derives a determinate threefold classification from the relation between conditioned synthesis and unconditioned unity.
The system compresses rather than resolves the warrant for deriving transcendental structures from logical syllogistic forms.
The unresolved status of the logical-transcendental analogy prevents the formal derivation from functioning as an objective proof.
Footnote 42 introduces a second metaphysical triad of God, freedom, and immortality that is not integrated with the chapter’s operative triad of soul, world, and supreme being.

identity.title: Section III. System of Transcendental Ideas

units.title: Transcendental Dialectic—Book Ii—Of The Dialectical Procedure Of Pure Reason

items.text: Pure reason necessarily produces transcendental ideas whose objects cannot be adequately conceived through possible experience.
The absence of adequate object-knowledge does not eliminate the ideas, because their reality as products of reason is procedurally necessary.
Pure reason converts its necessary ideas into non-empirical syllogisms that infer from something known to something unknowable.
These inferences are sophistical in result but syllogistic in origin, since their illusion arises from reason’s own laws rather than from individual fabrication.
The resulting dialectic divides into paralogism, antinomy, and the ideal of pure reason according to the unconditioned unity each argument seeks.
Critical awareness can restrain error but cannot abolish the illusion generated by pure reason.
Pure reason produces transcendental ideas according to its original laws.
An object adequate to a transcendental idea would have to be presentable and intuitable in possible experience.
No object perfectly corresponding to a transcendental idea can be adequately conceived or known.
The transcendental subjective reality of pure concepts of reason consists in their necessary generation by reason.
Pure reason generates syllogisms containing no empirical premises.
These syllogisms infer from something known to something for which no adequate conception is available.
Pure reason unavoidably attributes objective reality to the conclusions of these inferences.
The arguments are sophistical in result but syllogistic in origin.
The dialectical illusion is produced by reason’s nature rather than by accidental fiction or individual error.
The illusion cannot be eliminated, although its errors can be guarded against.
The paralogism infers the absolute unity of the subject from the transcendental conception of a subject containing no manifold.
The antinomy concerns the absolute totality of the conditions of a phenomenon and infers one unconditioned unity from the self-contradiction of another.
The ideal of pure reason infers the absolute synthetical unity of all conditions of things from the totality of conditions of thinking objects.
The ideal of pure reason culminates in the representation of a being of all beings whose unconditioned necessity cannot be conceived.
The transcendental idea is not an empirically presented object.
The object corresponding to the idea is not adequately conceivable.
The idea does not yield knowledge of an object perfectly corresponding to it.
The dialectical conclusion is not thereby an ordinary piece of valid object-knowledge.
The dialectical syllogisms are not grounded in empirical premises.
The dialectical arguments are not accidental fictions invented by individual thinkers.
The illusion is not removable through superior intelligence or completed reflection.
The absolute unity of the subject is not obtained as a concept through the transcendental conception of the subject.
The unconditioned synthetical unity of the series of conditions is not available as a coherent conception on the initially asserted side.
The being of all beings and its unconditioned necessity are not available through a transcendental conception.
The subjective reality of a rational idea is not identical with knowledge of its object.
The necessity with which reason generates an idea does not establish the knowability of the idea’s object.
Rational necessity can produce an unavoidable representation without producing an adequate object-concept.
The absence of empirical premises does not prevent pure reason from generating an objective-reality attribution.
The same reasoning process can possess legitimate syllogistic form at its origin and sophistical force in its conclusion.
Dialectical error is structural rather than merely psychological because it follows from the operation of pure reason itself.
Critique can suspend assent to dialectical conclusions without eliminating the conditions that generate them.
The three dialectical forms are differentiated by the object of unconditioned unity that each constructs.
Paralogism, antinomy, and the ideal of pure reason are distinct applications of one procedure: extending a necessary rational structure beyond possible cognition.
The progression from subject, through conditioned series, to totality of beings increases the scope of the unconditioned claim while preserving the same epistemic failure.
Pure reason is simultaneously the source of necessary rational organization and the source of unavoidable overreach beyond possible knowledge.
The objective appearance of metaphysical objects is generated by the formal demand for unconditioned unity rather than by access to an independently given object.
Paralogism, antinomy, and the ideal of pure reason form a systematic taxonomy of reason’s attempts to totalize the subject, conditions, and beings.
The epistemic boundary imposed by possible experience functions not only as a restriction but also as the condition for identifying dialectical illusion.
Wisdom changes the practical relation to dialectical illusion without changing its generative existence.

The system preserves a structural tension between the necessary legitimacy of reason’s procedure and the sophistical character of its result without fully specifying the rule that separates valid extension from dialectical overreach.
The necessity of a representation does not guarantee the existence of a correspondingly knowable object.
Pure reason is not transparent to itself in its own operation.
Empirical verification cannot adjudicate the origin of these ideas because their generating syllogisms contain no empirical premises.
Dialectical illusion cannot be reduced to defective education, individual carelessness, or intellectual weakness.
The validity of a reasoning form cannot be inferred solely from the necessity with which reason produces it.
The unconditioned is not a hidden empirical object waiting to be discovered.
The three metaphysical targets do not become knowable merely because reason can organize them as totalities.
The removal of error does not entail the removal of the conditions that make error possible.
No final object corresponding to reason’s totalizing demand is available within possible experience.
No external standpoint wholly outside pure reason is available from which its dialectical tendency could be permanently abolished.
No simple opposition between valid reasoning and irrational illusion can organize the system, because the illusion originates in reason’s own syllogistic activity.
The unconditioned remains operative as a demand even where it is unavailable as a conception.
The absence of a knowable unconditioned unity is the concealed condition underlying the production of all three dialectical forms.
Pure reason cannot attain the object it posits, but it cannot cease positing the demand for such an object.
Original laws of pure reason generate a transcendental idea.
The transcendental idea exceeds the conditions of presentation and intuition in possible experience.
The absence of possible intuition prevents adequate object-knowledge while leaving a problematic conception available.
Pure reason constructs a syllogism without empirical premises that moves from something known toward the unconditioned.
The syllogism attributes objective reality to what cannot be adequately conceived.
The resulting inference is classified as sophistical in conclusion but necessary in origin.
The same mechanism differentiates into subject-unity, series-unity, and totality-of-beings forms.
Critical reflection blocks the error of assent while leaving the underlying illusion operative.
Necessary production of transcendental ideas → absence of an adequately conceivable object.
Absence of adequate object-knowledge → reliance on non-empirical syllogistic inference.
Non-empirical inference → attribution of objective reality to the unknowable.
Objective-reality attribution → dialectical sophism generated by pure reason itself.
Common dialectical mechanism → paralogism, antinomy, and the ideal of pure reason.
Recognition of structural illusion → error-control without elimination of illusion.
The object of critique shifts from isolated false propositions to the procedure by which pure reason generates them.
Subjective transcendental reality is separated from objective knowledge of an object.
Metaphysical errors are reclassified from accidental inventions to necessary products of rational structure.
Paralogism, antinomy, and the ideal cease to appear as unrelated disputes and become forms of one totalizing operation.
The opposition between illusion and reason collapses into a model in which reason itself generates unavoidable illusion.
Critique is redefined from eradication of dialectic to regulation of its conclusions.
The boundary of possible experience becomes a diagnostic instrument for distinguishing problematic thought from knowledge.
Surface — Pure reason produces three dialectical arguments concerning the subject, the totality of conditions, and the being of all beings.
Structural — Non-empirical syllogistic reasoning converts the demand for unconditioned unity into objective-reality claims.
Metastrategic — The proper response to dialectic is to prevent error while accepting that the generative illusion cannot be removed.
Ontological/Temporal — Possible experience defines the limit of knowability, while the demand for an unconditioned totality remains continuously active beyond that limit.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the argument’s central mechanism from necessary idea-production to unavoidable dialectical illusion.
The reconstruction preserves the distinction between subjective transcendental reality, objective-reality attribution, and actual knowledge.
The classification of paralogism, antinomy, and ideal is recoverable from the three forms of unconditioned unity.
The strongest point is the linkage between reason’s intrinsic necessity and the non-accidental character of its error.
The relation between “no conception” and “problematical conception” remains compressed and depends on distinguishing inadequate object-conception from merely problematic thought.
The tension between syllogistic origin and sophistical result is asserted clearly but not fully resolved by a formal criterion of valid versus dialectical use.
The antinomy’s “opposite unity” remains directionally specified but structurally underdeveloped in this passage.
The extracted system preserves the real movement from necessary rational generation through objective illusion to limited critical containment.

identity.title: Transcendental Dialectic—Book Ii—Of The Dialectical Procedure Of Pure Reason

units.title: Chapter I. Of the Paralogisms of Pure Reason

items.text: The inquiry tests whether pure self-consciousness can yield a priori knowledge of the soul as an object.
Pure self-consciousness supplies only the formal unity of thought, not an intuition determining the subject’s mode of existence.
The argument is a transcendental diagnosis of an unavoidable illusion produced by valid logical forms used beyond their objective conditions.
Rational psychology projects the categories onto “I think” and converts logical subjecthood, simplicity, identity, and distinction into metaphysical properties of the soul.
The conversion fails because it equivocates between the subject of thought and an object given in intuition.
Rational psychology therefore survives only as a critical discipline limiting both materialist and spiritualist dogmatism.
The failure of speculative self-knowledge displaces claims concerning future existence from theoretical proof to practical reason.
A transcendental paralogism can preserve valid logical form while deriving a false conclusion from a necessary propensity of reason.
A pure rational psychology must exclude every empirical determination and therefore has only “I think” as its generative text.
“I think” is the formal accompaniment and vehicle of all concepts rather than a determinate concept of an object.
Pure thought represents the thinking subject only as a transcendental subject = x, cognizable solely through its thoughts.
Objective cognition requires a given intuition determined through concepts under the unity of consciousness.
Categories acquire objective reality only in relation to sensuous intuition and possible experience.
Self-cognition as an object requires intuition of the determinable self rather than consciousness of the determining function of thought.
The modes of pure self-consciousness are logical functions and do not themselves determine an object.
Internal intuition is sensuous and temporal and presents the self only through phenomenal data.
The objective application of the category of substance requires a permanent intuition.
Internal intuition supplies no permanent presentation corresponding to the thinking Ego.
Abstraction from empirical conditions does not establish existence independently of those conditions.
The existential occurrence of “I think” requires empirical material even though its Ego-representation is purely intellectual.
The subject cannot cognize itself through categories whose employment already presupposes its unity of apperception.
A simple being may possess intensive magnitude capable of continuous diminution.
Mere non-contradiction cannot privilege either of two opposed speculative hypotheses.
Practical warrant extending beyond experience does not constitute theoretical cognition of the soul.
Difference between internal and external appearances does not establish heterogeneity between their grounds as things in themselves.
A transcendental paralogism is not merely an argument defective in logical form.
“I think” is not a determinate transcendental concept or an intuition of the thinking subject.
Pure rational psychology is not empirical psychology based on observations of internal states.
Necessary use of the Ego as the subject of judgment is not proof that the Ego exists as substance.
Logical simplicity of apperception is not proof of a simple substance.
Analytical identity of consciousness across representations is not proof of personal identity through changing states.
Distinguishing the self from external objects is not proof that the self can exist without body or external objects.
“I think” is not a syllogistic inference from thought to existence or a universal assertion that every thinking being exists necessarily.
Mere thought presents the self neither as it is in itself nor as it appears in intuition.
Possible abstraction from empirical existence is not consciousness of a possible separate existence.
Simplicity does not entail incorruptibility, permanence, or immunity from extinction.
Freedom from contradiction is not objective knowledge that a proposed mode of existence is possible.
Rational psychology is not a positive doctrine that adds knowledge of the soul.
Critical restriction neither establishes soulless materialism nor refutes the practical admission of future life.
The exclusion of empirical predicates leaves rational psychology to generate its system by projecting the category table onto formal apperception.
Logical subjecthood, simplicity, identity, and distinction yield no corresponding determinations of substance, simple substance, personality, or separability.

The foundational syllogism of rational psychology commits a sophisma figurae dictionis by shifting from an object that can exist only as subject to the Ego’s merely formal position as subject of thought.
The category of substance cannot determine the thinking self because the permanent intuition required for its objective application is absent from inner sense.
Immateriality, incorruptibility, personality, spirituality, and immortality lose their foundation because they are combinations downstream from the invalid substantiation of the Ego.
Mendelssohn’s proof of permanence fails because exclusion of decomposition does not exclude extinction through infinitely diminishing degrees of reality and consciousness.
Speculation licensed only by non-contradiction admits contrary constructions with equal right and therefore cannot decide between rationalist and materialist hypotheses.
Treating the thinking substance as temporally determinable without external objects makes external existence gratuitous and renders problematic idealism unavoidable within rational psychology.
The real unity of apperception prevents a spatially reductive definition of the thinking subject without establishing that subject as a spiritual substance.
Self-objectification through the categories is circular because the unity to be explained is already presupposed in every categorical judgment.
Rational psychology can function only as a discipline that prohibits unsupported determinations of the soul.
The demonstrated limits of speculative reason impose the same renunciation on dogmatic denials as on dogmatic affirmations.
The failure of speculative proof leaves intact the claimed practical necessity of admitting an existence extending beyond present life.
Reclassifying space and time as forms of appearance removes the presupposed proof that soul and body are internally heterogeneous while leaving their ultimate community unknowable.
Moral consciousness may disclose practical spontaneity without supplying the theoretical predicates required for noumenal self-knowledge.
Rational psychology is generated by converting a condition of possible experience into a metaphysical property of an object purportedly existing in itself.
The attribution of substance is the load-bearing error from which the remaining ontology of the soul is produced by combinatory amplification.
The thinking subject is transcendentally indispensable as a condition of cognition and theoretically indeterminate as an object of cognition.
A successful rational psychology would license synthetic a priori knowledge of things in themselves and thereby dissolve the critical restriction of knowledge to possible experience.
Speculative underdetermination does not make arbitrary hypotheses cognitively available, because objective assertion remains constrained by the conditions of intuition.
The subject grounding the representation of time cannot derive its own substantial persistence in time from that grounding function.
Critical restriction removes both speculative proof and speculative disproof, thereby preserving a distinct domain for practical commitment without converting it into knowledge.
Conditions under which an object is represented cannot be transferred without mediation into properties of the represented object.
Self-consciousness cannot be treated as immediate self-intuition.
Formal continuity of consciousness cannot guarantee the diachronic persistence of a substantial person.
Removing empirical conditions from a representation cannot remove those conditions from the represented being’s existence.
The thinking subject cannot occupy an unconditioned standpoint from which it cognizes the ground of its own cognitive functions.
Logical thinkability cannot exhaust the conditions of real possibility.
Failure to establish one metaphysical account cannot establish its contrary.
Practical necessity cannot be converted into theoretical determination of the soul’s constitution.
An immediately self-present and theoretically transparent substantial Ego is unavailable.
The noumenal constitution of the thinking subject is excluded from speculative adjudication.
Neither immortality nor extinction beyond life is available as an object of dogmatic theoretical knowledge.
The subject cannot complete theoretical reason by turning the presupposed unity of reason into its own self-grounding object.
The purity requirement removes all empirical predicates and leaves “I think” as the sole datum of rational psychology.
The category table is projected onto that datum to generate substance, simplicity, identity, and external relation.
Combinations of those projected determinations generate immateriality, incorruptibility, personality, spirituality, communion with bodies, and immortality.
Critical analysis separates the determining unity of consciousness from the determinable self that alone could be given as an object.
Each metaphysical predicate is tested against its required intuition and fails because pure apperception supplies no corresponding object.
The central paralogism is exposed as an equivocation between existence only as subject and use only as the subject of judgment.
Auxiliary proofs are neutralized by intensive diminution, contrary possibilities, and the absence of permanent inner intuition.
The failed doctrine is converted into a reciprocal prohibition against materialist and spiritualist dogmatism.
