items.text: Cosmological antinomy arises when the logical requirement to seek conditions is converted into a claim that the total series of conditions is already given.
The conversion depends on equivocating between conditioned things in themselves and conditioned phenomena.
Phenomena are given only through successive empirical synthesis, so their full conditioned series cannot be given as a completed whole prior to regress.
Cosmological thesis and antithesis therefore conflict only because both presuppose that the world is a self-subsistent whole determined independently of empirical regress.
Once this presupposition is removed, opposed cosmological assertions become dialectically opposed judgments that may both be false.
The dissolution of antinomy supplies an indirect proof of transcendental ideality and reassigns dialectic from dogmatic knowledge-production to critical error-diagnosis.
A conditioned object necessarily refers reason to its conditions.
Reason is logically required to continue the search for conditions as far as possible.
If conditioned objects and their conditions are things in themselves, the condition-series is given with the conditioned object.
If the entire condition-series is given with the conditioned object, the unconditioned is given with that series.
Phenomena are representations rather than things in themselves.
Phenomena are given only in empirical apprehension and synthesis.
Empirical synthesis is necessarily successive and temporally conditioned.
A condition not empirically given can be required without being already given.
The cosmological syllogism uses the conditioned transcendentally in its major premise and empirically in its minor premise.
A judgment concerning the complete quantity or totality of the world presupposes that the world is a thing in itself.
A series of phenomena exists only in the regressive synthesis through which it is sought.
Opposed judgments may both be false when each predicates a determination under an invalid shared condition.
The removal of a false presupposition can transform apparent contradiction into merely dialectical opposition.
The failure of cosmological dogmatism supports the transcendental ideality of phenomena.
The logical demand for regress is not a proof that all conditions are simultaneously given.
Phenomena are not objects available to pure understanding independently of intuition and empirical cognition.
The empirical series of conditions is not an atemporal series of co-given members.
The world is not a self-subsistent whole existing independently of the regress of representations.
The world is not determinable in itself as either finite or infinite.
The negation of infinitude is not equivalent to the assertion of finitude.
Cosmological thesis and antithesis are not necessarily contradictory judgments.
The critical dissolution of antinomy is not a sceptical denial of empirical inquiry or rational regress.
Reason may require an indefinitely continued regress toward conditions without possessing the completed totality of that regress.
The cosmological inference from a given conditioned phenomenon to an absolutely complete condition-series is invalid.
The difference between things in themselves and phenomena is the decisive condition governing whether totality can be inferred from conditionedness.
No phenomenal series can be represented as a completed unconditioned whole, because its members are available only through successive regress.
The propositions that the world is finite and that it is infinite can both fail when the world is treated as a phenomenal series rather than a thing in itself.
The same critical restriction applies to quantitative, compositional, causal, and necessary-condition cosmological series.
Antinomy identifies an error in the common premise of opposed arguments rather than establishing either opposed conclusion.
The unconditioned functions within phenomenal inquiry as a regulative demand for regress rather than as an object given in experience.
Cosmological reason generates antinomy by importing the ontological conditions of things in themselves into the temporal procedure of empirical cognition.
The world is reclassified from an object possessing a determinate total magnitude into the open field of empirically executable regress.
Rational conflict becomes evidence for the limits of objectification when equally compelling opposed proofs depend upon the same illicit presupposition.
Critical reason preserves the validity of empirical investigation by denying that its procedural demands authorize transcendent conclusions.
No object of possible experience can be given as a completed absolute totality independently of the synthesis that constitutes it as experience.
No transition is licensed from the necessity of seeking conditions to the existence of a completed unconditioned object.
No temporal series can be treated as if all of its members were co-present outside temporal succession.

No cosmological predicate of finitude, infinitude, beginning, non-beginning, simplicity, composition, freedom, necessity, or contingency applies to the world as a whole independently of the conditions of representation.
No formal opposition guarantees that one of the opposed judgments corresponds to an object.
The system excludes any standpoint from which the totality of appearances could be known as an object while remaining an appearance.
The system excludes a final empirical completion of the regress that would convert reason’s demand for conditions into knowledge of the unconditioned.
The system excludes an unmediated identity between the logical form of explanation and the ontological structure of what is given in experience.
Given conditionedness, reason demands regress toward conditions.
The demand for regress becomes a claim of completed totality only if the conditioned is treated as a thing in itself.
Phenomenal conditionedness is given only through temporally successive empirical synthesis.
Successive synthesis permits required regress but forbids the prior givenness of the whole regress.
The cosmological syllogism produces antinomy by substituting the thing-in-itself model of conditionedness for the phenomenal model.
Removal of the thing-in-itself presupposition converts cosmological contradiction into a pair of jointly invalid dialectical predicates.
The collapse of the predicates finite and infinite as determinations of the world in itself establishes the ideality of the phenomenal world-whole.
Critical reason retains empirical regress while suspending every dogmatic claim to the completed unconditioned.
Given conditioned phenomenon → logical demand for conditions → illicit assertion that the entire series is given.
Illicit assertion of totality → equivocation between transcendental and empirical conditionedness → apparent cosmological proof.
Successive phenomenal synthesis → impossibility of pre-given total series → invalidation of the cosmological inference.
Invalid shared presupposition → dialectical rather than contradictory opposition → joint dissolution of thesis and antithesis.
Dissolved antinomy → transcendental ideality of phenomena → critical preservation of empirical regress without dogmatic cosmology.
The distinction between seeking every condition and possessing all conditions separates methodological infinity from an actually given infinite totality.
Cosmological oppositions are reclassified from disputes over rival world-properties into symptoms of an invalid object-model.
The world becomes thinkable as a regressive order of appearances without becoming an objectifiable whole of appearances.
The opposition between dogmatism and scepticism is displaced by a critical position that rejects transcendent assertion while retaining empirical inquiry.
Contradiction becomes diagnostically productive because it can expose a common presupposition rather than merely defeat one contestant.
Surface — The text resolves the opposed claims that the world is finite or infinite, begun or unbegun, composed or simple, and causally conditioned or unconditioned.
Structural — The text locates antinomy in the temporal and synthetic conditions under which phenomena are given rather than in the objects apparently disputed.
Metastrategic — The text replaces adjudication between opposed cosmological doctrines with diagnosis of the presupposition that generates both doctrines.
Ontological/Temporal — The text denies that phenomenal reality possesses an atemporal, self-subsistent totality and defines its objectivity through temporally successive synthesis.
Epistemic — The text confines cognition of phenomenal conditions to actual or possible regress while reserving the unconditioned from constitutive knowledge.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the transition from the logical demand for conditions to the critical rejection of cosmological totality.
The decisive reconstructive distinction is between a condition-series given with things in themselves and a condition-series sought through phenomenal regress.
The system is internally coherent if phenomenal objectivity depends on synthesis without requiring that synthesis to be complete.
The system depends on maintaining a strict distinction between logical necessity, empirical availability, and ontological givenness.
The system leaves underdetermined how indefinitely required regress can be positively characterized without reintroducing a concealed totality.

The system’s central fault line is that the indirect proof of transcendental ideality uses the failure of world-totality predicates while relying on a prior account of phenomenal representation to diagnose that failure.
The reconstruction preserves the argument’s movement only if antinomy is treated as a diagnostic instrument rather than as a set of cosmological propositions awaiting settlement.

identity.title: Section VII. Critical Solution of the Cosmological Problem

units.title: Section VIII. Regulative Principle of Pure Reason in relation to the Cosmological Ideas

items.text: Cosmological totality cannot yield knowledge of a maximum of conditions as an object existing in itself.
The idea of totality is reclassified from a claim about objects into a rule directing empirical regress from conditioned to condition.
The argument is transcendental and diagnostic: it exposes the illicit conversion of a subjective rule of inquiry into objective cosmological knowledge.
Phenomenal conditionedness requires continued regress while excluding the empirical discovery of an absolutely unconditioned condition.
The distinction between regressus in infinitum and regressus in indefinitum is determined by how the relevant series is empirically given.
The argument concludes that no empirical regress licenses a claim that the series of conditions is itself finite or actually infinite.
Sensuous objects are empirical representations rather than things in themselves.
Every condition discovered within experience is itself conditioned.
The absolutely unconditioned cannot be discovered within experience.
The idea of absolute totality belongs to reason and is not given as an object in empirical intuition.
Reason requires regress from a given conditioned through subordinate conditions toward completeness.
A principle that prescribes empirical procedure without determining its object is regulative rather than constitutive.
A constitutive cosmological principle would illegitimately attribute objective reality to absolute totality.
Empirical limits cannot be treated as absolute limits merely because regress has not yet surpassed them.
A regress through internal conditions proceeds in infinitum when the relevant whole is empirically given.
A regress toward higher external conditions proceeds only in indefinitum when the whole series is not empirically given.
Neither infinite regress nor indefinite regress establishes an actually infinite series in the object itself.
The cosmological idea is not an axiom for cognizing totality as actual in the object.
The regulative principle is not a principle of the possibility of experience or of the understanding.
The regulative principle is not authorization to extend cognition beyond possible experience.
The rule of regress does not determine whether a series of conditions is finite in itself.
The rule of regress does not determine whether a series of conditions is infinite in itself.
The empirical search for conditions must not halt at an allegedly absolute unconditioned.
The absence of a discovered limit is not evidence that an actually infinite totality is given.
A limitative perception is not identical with the series that it limits.
The demand for totality functions as an obligation to continue empirical inquiry rather than as knowledge of a completed totality.
The unconditioned operates as an unattainable terminus of regress rather than as an empirically discoverable member of the series.
Empirical cognition is enlarged by the rule of reason without being converted into transcendent cognition.
The form of permissible infinity depends on whether inquiry begins from an empirically given whole or from a single given member.
Division of a bounded body permits regress in infinitum because further internal parts are given as conditions of the whole.
Genealogical ascent permits regress in indefinitum because higher conditions must be sought without the completed series being empirically given.
The question of a series’s intrinsic numerical magnitude is displaced by the question of how inquiry must proceed.
Cosmological ideas acquire legitimate use only through their transformation from object-claims into procedural constraints on empirical synthesis.
Reason generates an indefinitely extensible task of explanation while withholding any empirical completion capable of satisfying that task.
Infinity is relocated from a property of phenomenal objects to a mode of authorized empirical continuation.
The apparent alternative between a finite world-series and an infinite world-series is structurally invalid because both alternatives presuppose objectual totality beyond empirical givenness.
Phenomena do not possess a cognizable totality independently of the empirical regress through which their conditions are sought.
Empirical inquiry cannot derive an ontological conclusion from the mere necessity of continuing inquiry.
The absence of a stopping point cannot become a positive intuition of limitless reality.
A completed explanation of phenomenal conditions cannot be available as an empirical datum.
The form of a rational demand cannot determine the ontological constitution of its empirical object.
No standpoint is available from within experience from which the total series of phenomenal conditions can be surveyed as a completed whole.
No absolute beginning, final condition, or terminal explanatory ground is admissible within the phenomenal order as empirically known.
The system excludes any direct passage from the idea of the unconditioned to the existence of an unconditioned object.
The demand for systematic completeness is organized around an end that must guide cognition without becoming cognizable.
Phenomenal representation → every encountered condition is conditioned.
Conditionedness → reason demands regress toward condition-completeness.
Idea of totality without empirical object → regulative rule rather than constitutive cognition.
Regulative rule → prohibition against arresting regress at an allegedly unconditioned condition.
Whole empirically given → regress through internal conditions in infinitum.
Only a series-member empirically given → regress toward higher conditions in indefinitum.
Either mode of regress → suspension of claims about the series’s finite or actual-infinite being in itself.
Claim to cosmological totality → denial of constitutive validity → conversion into a regulative rule → compulsory empirical regress → exclusion of empirical closure.
Mode of empirical givenness → distinction between internal decomposition and external ascent → infinitum or indefinitum as procedural forms → rejection of actual infinity in the object.
Empirical boundary encountered or absent → boundary distinguished from the series → regress continued toward its condition → no absolute empirical stopping point.
Cosmological questions are reclassified from questions about the world’s intrinsic total quantity into questions about the lawful conduct of empirical inquiry.
Infinity is divided into two non-equivalent procedural forms: infinite regression within an empirically given whole and indefinite regression beyond an uncompleted series.
The opposition between finite and infinite world-series loses legitimacy as an empirical-objectual classification.
An empirical limit becomes intelligible either as a provisional absence of further perception or as a condition requiring further regress, never automatically as absolute closure.
Reason’s legitimacy is located in the extension of experience rather than in the production of supersensible cosmological objects.
Surface — The text determines how far one may regress from a conditioned phenomenon to its conditions.
Structural — The distinction between phenomena and things in themselves blocks the transfer of rational totality into an objective property of experience.
Metastrategic — Rational ideas are preserved by changing their use from constituting objects to regulating inquiry.
Ontological/Temporal — Phenomenal series cannot be assigned a knowable completed totality, first condition, final condition, or actual infinity independently of empirical synthesis.
The axioms suffice to reconstruct the central conversion of cosmological totality from a constitutive claim into a regulative rule.
The distinction between infinitum and indefinitum is reconstructible only if empirical givenness is retained as the determining criterion.
The system is coherent insofar as it separates the demand for completeness from knowledge of a completed object.
The system depends on the compressed distinction between an empirically given whole and a totality allegedly given in the object itself.
A tension remains between reason’s demand for a complete conception of the object and the principled unattainability of the unconditioned that would complete regress.
A further tension remains because regress in infinitum is licensed for an empirically given whole while actual infinity in the object is denied.
Reconstruction preserves the argument’s movement only if procedural infinity is not silently reconverted into an ontological predicate of phenomena.

identity.title: Section VIII. Regulative Principle of Pure Reason in relation to the Cosmological Ideas

units.title: Section IX. Of the Empirical Use of the Regulative Principle of Reason with regard to the Cosmological Ideas

items.text: The cosmological demand for absolute totality arises from treating appearances as things in themselves.
Once this assumption is rejected, reason need not determine whether the world-series is absolutely finite or infinite.
Reason must instead determine how far empirical regress must proceed to answer its own questions correctly.
The principle of reason is therefore restricted from constitutive metaphysical use to regulative extension of possible experience.
This restriction dissolves the antinomial conflict by exposing the fallacy and clarifying the meaning of the ideas that produced it.

The regulative principle retains practical epistemic efficacy comparable to that of an a priori constitutive axiom because it maximizes the employment and correction of understanding within experience.
Neither reason nor understanding can be employed transcendentally to determine objects beyond possible experience.
The demand for absolute totality in the conditions of appearances results from regarding phenomena as things in themselves.
The absolute quantity of a cosmological series is not determinable as a property of things in themselves.
Reason legitimately governs the empirical regress from condition to condition as a rule for extending possible experience.
The principle of reason is regulative rather than constitutive with respect to phenomena.
The antinomy arises from a fallacious transcendental interpretation of reason’s ideas.
Clarifying the true meaning of reason’s ideas converts dialectical conflict into a valid doctrinal principle.
A regulative principle can produce epistemic effects equivalent in practical force to those of a constitutive axiom without determining objects a priori.
Reason is not entitled to transcendental knowledge of objects beyond possible experience.
Understanding is not entitled to transcendental knowledge of objects beyond possible experience.
Phenomena are not to be treated as things in themselves.
The world-series is not required to possess an empirically determinable absolute finitude or infinity.
The principle of reason is not constitutive of phenomena in themselves.
The antinomial opposition is not an irreducible contradiction between two objectively valid descriptions of the world.
Cosmological inquiry must shift from determining the absolute extent of a series to determining the necessary extent of empirical investigation.
The legitimate object of reason’s cosmological use is the procedure of regress, not the completed totality of the series as an independently existing object.
The validity of reason’s principle depends on its capacity to extend possible experience rather than on its capacity to describe noumenal reality.
Resolving the antinomy requires both rejecting the fallacious inference and reinterpreting the ideas that generated it.
The transformation of reason’s principle from dialectical to doctrinal preserves its directive function while eliminating its dogmatic object-claim.
The understanding receives a wider and more corrective field of application when reason regulates inquiry rather than constituting objects.
Critical limitation does not diminish reason’s epistemic authority; it relocates that authority from metaphysical determination to the regulation of inquiry.
The antinomy is produced by confusing a rule for indefinitely advancing knowledge with a principle that determines a completed totality of objects.
The critical solution preserves the motivating demand for systematic completeness while denying that completeness is an object already given in itself.
The system makes epistemic progress depend on an unending movement toward conditions rather than on possession of an absolute totality.
No completed metaphysical inventory of the world can serve as the legitimate endpoint of cosmological reason.
No opposition between finite and infinite totality can be treated as objectively decidable independently of the conditions of possible experience.
No epistemic gain follows from extending reason beyond the domain in which its principles can regulate experience.
No constitutive object corresponds to the totality demanded by reason when that demand is detached from empirical regress.
Absolute totality is unavailable as a completed object of knowledge.
The final ground of the cosmological series cannot function as an empirically established terminus of explanation.
The system excludes a standpoint from which reason could survey the world-series as a completed whole in itself.
Transcendental treatment of appearances as things in themselves generates the demand for absolute totality.
The demand for absolute totality generates opposed claims concerning the absolute quantity of the world-series.
Critical separation of appearances from things in themselves removes the object-domain required by those opposed claims.
Removal of the illegitimate object-domain converts reason’s demand from metaphysical determination into a rule for empirical regress.
The regulative rule extends and corrects the employment of understanding throughout possible experience.
The resulting expansion of empirical cognition supplies the practical force formerly attributed to a constitutive a priori axiom.

Transcendental misclassification of appearances → demand for absolute totality → cosmological antinomy → critical restriction of reason → empirical-regulative rule → expanded employment of understanding.
Absolute object-question → procedural question about the necessary extent of regress → dialectical principle → doctrinal principle.
Cosmological totality is reclassified from an object of determination into a horizon governing inquiry.
The finite-versus-infinite opposition is displaced from an absolute ontological dispute to a question concerning the legitimate progress of empirical regress.
Antinomy is transformed from a conflict within the objects of reason into a conflict generated by the misuse of reason’s ideas.
Limitation of metaphysical reach becomes a condition for the wider and more exact use of the understanding.
Surface — The issue is how far empirical inquiry must proceed through a series of conditions.
Structural — The argument distinguishes constitutive principles that determine objects from regulative principles that organize the extension of experience.
Metastrategic — Reason’s apparent defeat in antinomy is converted into a method for correcting the scope and direction of inquiry.
Ontological/Temporal — Totality is denied as a completed thing in itself and retained as an indefinitely approached horizon of regress.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the movement from transcendental error to empirical regulation.
The reconstruction preserves the distinction between constitutive object-knowledge and regulative guidance of inquiry.
The dissolution of the antinomy follows from denying that appearances possess the status of things in themselves.
The system remains dependent on the compressed identification of dialectical reason with a misapplied demand for totality.

The strongest point is the conversion of limitation into epistemic productivity; the unresolved tension is that a merely regulative principle is claimed to possess force comparable to a constitutive axiom without determining any object.

identity.title: Section IX. Of the Empirical Use of the Regulative Principle of Reason with regard to the Cosmological Ideas

units.title: I. Solution of the Cosmological Idea of the Totality of the Composition of Phenomena in the Universe

items.text: Cosmological totality poses a problem because reason seeks an unconditioned limit for an empirical series whose members are always conditioned.
The problem is reframed from determining the world’s completed magnitude to determining the legitimate rule of empirical regress.
No experience can exhibit an absolutely unconditioned condition, because such exhibition would require intuition of a boundary against empty time or space.
The world is represented only through a possible empirical regress and is never given as a completed intuition of totality.
The absence of an empirically discoverable absolute limit requires continued ascent from each conditioned appearance to a further condition.
The legitimate cosmological conclusion is an indefinite regress governed by a rule, not an assertion that the world is either finitely bounded or actually infinite.
Every condition reached in empirical regress is itself empirically conditioned.
No experience can present an absolutely unconditioned condition.
An absolute temporal or spatial limit of phenomena would have to be experienced as a boundary against void time or void space.
Experience of a boundary against mere void is impossible because such an experience has no content.
The world of sense is a totality of appearances and is not given as a whole in intuition.
The conception of cosmical totality is constituted through possible empirical regress.
The magnitude of the world cannot be determined before the empirical regress through which it is represented.
A claim of actual infinite regress presupposes a determinate infinite cosmical quantity already given.
A claim of finite cosmical magnitude presupposes an empirically possible absolute limit.
Reason’s proper cosmological use is to regulate empirical inquiry by requiring ascent from each conditioned phenomenon to a further condition.
The regulative rule requires no termination of possible empirical extension, not an actually unceasing series of perceptions.
The unconditioned is not an object discoverable within empirical regress.
The world is not a thing in itself given in totality prior to all regress.
Cosmical magnitude is not an independently intuited quantity from which the extent of regress can be inferred.
The regress is not regressus in infinitum, understood as a determinate infinite series or quantity.
The world is not finitely bounded by an empirically accessible beginning in time or limit in space.
The rule of regress is not a demand that every empirical lineage or phenomenal sequence lack a relative beginning or endpoint.
The regulative principle is not a constitutive determination of the world’s magnitude in itself.
Every attained empirical condition remains subject to further conditioning and therefore cannot terminate inquiry.
An absolute beginning in time or absolute spatial boundary cannot be empirically established.
The world cannot be classified as either finite or infinite by means of empirical knowledge.
Cosmical quantity is generated only through the activity of regress and is never available as a completed object before that activity.
The appropriate designation of cosmological regress is indefiniteness rather than actual infinity.
Relative empirical limits may occur within experience without constituting an absolute limit of the world.
Cosmological reason changes status when it ceases to determine a completed object and instead governs the open continuation of empirical synthesis.
The antinomy of finite versus infinite world arises from treating a rule for possible inquiry as a predicate of a completed object.
The world has no absolute empirical quantity because the conditions under which it is represented cannot yield a completed totality.
Empirical openness is compatible with locally completed investigations because indefinite regress governs the form of inquiry rather than the duration of every factual sequence.
No standpoint external to possible experience can supply the world as a completed object of cognition.
No determinate cosmical magnitude can precede the synthesis through which magnitude is empirically constructed.
No empirical datum can function as an absolutely final condition.
No inference from the inexhaustibility of inquiry to the actual infinity of its object is licensed.
No local boundary within appearances can become a boundary of appearance as such.
The completed world-whole is unavailable as an object for theoretical cognition.
The unconditioned remains unavailable as an empirical terminus even while it structures reason’s demand for conditions.
Cosmological closure is foreclosed because the condition of representing totality is the regress that prevents its completed presentation.
Conditioned appearance → demand for its condition → further empirically conditioned appearance.
Supposed absolute limit → required intuition of void boundary → contentless experience → impossibility of empirical confirmation.
World-whole treated as prior object → determinate finite-or-infinite magnitude → illegitimate anticipation of unreached synthesis.
World-whole treated as possible regress → nonterminal rule of conditioning → regressus in indefinitum.
Regulative continuation of inquiry → denial of absolute cosmical limits → suspension of finite/infinite predication.
Demand for an unconditioned cosmical totality → impossibility of experiencing an absolute boundary.
Impossibility of absolute boundary → every attained condition remains subordinated to a further condition.
World not given in collective intuition → cosmical magnitude cannot precede empirical regress.
No pre-given finite or infinite magnitude → rejection of regressus in infinitum and absolute finitude.
Regress governed by nontermination → cosmological totality designated as indefinite rather than determinate.
The finite/infinite opposition is reclassified from an exhaustive cosmological alternative into a shared misuse of totality as a completed object.
The world is relocated from an object presumed to possess a knowable total magnitude to a horizon represented through possible empirical synthesis.
The unconditioned is relocated from an obtainable empirical item to the negative boundary regulating the search for conditions.
Empirical inquiry is distinguished from dogmatic cosmology by its capacity for indefinite extension without commitment to actual infinity.
Relative beginnings and limits become compatible with the absence of an absolute beginning or limit of the world.
Surface — The text determines the proper answer to whether the world has a temporal beginning, a spatial limit, or an infinite magnitude.
Structural — The text grounds cosmological judgment in the conditions of possible empirical regress rather than in properties attributed to a completed world-whole.
Metastrategic — The text converts reason from a faculty that declares cosmical facts into a faculty that legislates the nonterminal procedure of inquiry.
Ontological/Temporal — Appearances are temporally and spatially conditioned, while the world as their totality lacks a determinable absolute magnitude within experience.
Epistemic — Totality is cognizable only as the rule-governed openness of synthesis, not as an intuition or concept determinative of a completed object.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the transition from the impossibility of empirical absolute limits to indefinite empirical regress.
The structure depends principally on the distinction between appearances and a world treated as a thing in itself.
The decisive compression is the inference that all absolute limits would require experience of void, whose impossibility carries the anti-finitist conclusion.
The system is internally coherent when “no beginning” and “no absolute limit” are read as restrictions on empirical determination rather than predicates of a completed world.
A residual tension remains because the text formulates negative claims about the world while denying that the world as a whole is an object available for determination.
A further tension remains between the demand for continued conditioning and the allowance that particular empirical series may possess relative initial members or terminal limits.
Reconstruction preserves the argument only if regressus in indefinitum is maintained as a regulative form of possible inquiry rather than converted into an ontological thesis of infinite reality.

identity.title: I. Solution of the Cosmological Idea of the Totality of the Composition of Phenomena in the Universe

units.title: II. Solution of the Cosmological Idea of the Totality of the Division of a Whole given in Intuition

items.text: Division of an intuitively given whole regresses from a conditioned whole to its constitutive conditions.
Infinite divisibility entails an infinite regress of subdivision, not an actually given infinite multitude of parts.
The distinction between continuous magnitude and discrete multiplicity determines whether infinite division is coherent.
Phenomenal substance cannot secure an indivisible remainder because it is not an absolute subject or thing in itself.
Mathematical antinomies arise from treating a homogeneous phenomenal series as if it admitted completed unconditioned totality.
Dynamical antinomies may permit a non-sensuous intelligible condition outside the phenomenal series, allowing qualified satisfaction of reason without interrupting empirical regress.
Division of a whole given in intuition is a regress from the conditioned to its conditions.
In a continuous decomposition, every attained part remains divisible.
Conditions contained together with a given whole generate a regress in infinitum rather than a merely indefinite empirical search.
An infinite regress of division does not contain a completed infinite series of divided members.
Space is a continuum, and every limited space is divisible to infinity.
Bodies, as extended phenomena, are divisible to infinity because their divisibility derives from space.
Phenomenal substance is a permanent sensuous intuition rather than an absolute subject cognized by a pure category.
Infinite divisibility belongs only to a quantum continuum whose parts are determined through progressive division.
A quantum discretum contains a determinate numerical multitude of distinct units.
An organized whole presupposed as already divided into infinitely many determinate organized parts is self-contradictory.
Mathematical cosmological ideas concern homogeneous sensuous conditions whose members all belong to one phenomenal series.
No homogeneous phenomenal series can contain a mathematically unconditioned member without falsely treating a conditioned member as unconditioned.
Dynamical synthesis may admit a heterogeneous intelligible condition that is not a member of the phenomenal series.
An intelligible condition can be empirically unconditioned only if its admission leaves empirical regress regular and uninterrupted.
Infinite divisibility is not equivalent to an infinite number of parts actually composing a whole.
The regress of decomposition is not a regressus in indefinitum grounded in conditions merely discoverable through subsequent experience.
A body as phenomenon is not an independently subsisting substance that remains after all spatial composition is removed.
Infinite division is not applicable to an organized discrete whole as an already determinate infinite organization.
A determinate multitude of units is not infinitely large merely because its material can be further divided.
Mathematical antinomies are not resolved by awarding truth to either contradictory assertion.
An unconditioned mathematical condition is not admissible within the phenomenal series.
An intelligible dynamical condition is not a sensuous member inserted into the empirical chain.
The given whole contains every part reachable through division, but it does not contain the complete infinite division as an accomplished series.
The infinity of spatial division signifies inexhaustible determinability of parts through regress rather than actual infinite composition.
The divisibility of bodies licenses no inference to an actually infinite aggregate of bodily parts.
No indivisible substantial residue can be inferred from the removal of bodily composition in thought.
Experience can determine only how far organization has been encountered, not the transcendental endpoint of the regress of division.
The principle of reason forbids treating empirical analysis of an extended body as absolutely complete.
Contradictory mathematical totality claims are both false when each presupposes a completed homogeneous phenomenal series.
Dynamical contradiction can be conditionally reframed because its unconditioned ground need not belong to the phenomenal series it conditions.
The text relocates infinity from the ontology of completed parts to the rule-governed procedure of regress.
The apparent conflict between finite given whole and infinite divisibility dissolves once the whole is distinguished from the never-completed operation of division.
The legitimacy of a cosmological idea depends on the kind of synthesis underlying it, not on a uniform demand for totality.
Mathematical and dynamical antinomies require non-identical resolutions because homogeneous and heterogeneous conditions have different admissibility structures.
Reason can seek an unconditioned ground without converting that ground into an empirically discoverable terminus of natural explanation.
Phenomenal intuition cannot present a completed infinite multiplicity as an object.
The categories cannot establish the nature of a phenomenal object as though it were a thing in itself.
Empirical regress cannot culminate in an absolutely first or unconditioned phenomenal member.
The same model of totality cannot govern both spatial quantity and dynamical dependence.
The unconditioned required by reason cannot be supplied by a completed sensuous series.
No final phenomenal inventory can coincide with the idea of absolute totality.
No intelligible ground may be admitted if it functions as a hidden empirical object or disrupts the continuity of empirical explanation.
The demand for unconditioned explanation is foreclosed as an object-level demand within mathematical intuition.
Absolute completion is unavailable wherever the conditions are constituted only through the regress that seeks them.
Given intuitive whole → division into conditions → each condition remains divisible → infinite regress of determination.
Infinite regress of determination → absence of completed division → rejection of an actually infinite aggregate of parts.
Spatial continuity → infinite divisibility of extended phenomena → no indivisible phenomenal substance.
Continuous division versus discrete organization → indeterminate progressive parts versus determinate numerical plurality → exclusion of infinitely pre-organized composite wholes.
Homogeneous phenomenal series → impossibility of mathematical unconditioned totality → reciprocal falsity of opposed mathematical theses.
Heterogeneous dynamical synthesis → possible intelligible non-member condition → empirically uninterrupted regress with conditionally satisfied rational demand.
Given whole in intuition → regress of division → distinction between infinite regress and infinite aggregate.
Spatial continuum → infinitely divisible body → denial of an absolute phenomenal substratum.
Continuous magnitude versus discrete organization → contradiction in completed infinite organization.
Mathematical homogeneity → both totality claims invalid → dynamical heterogeneity → conditional admissibility of an intelligible ground.
Infinity is reclassified from a property of a completed object into a structure of permissible regress.
Bodies are reclassified from substances with potentially surviving simple cores into spatial phenomena whose analysis lacks an absolute internal terminus.
The distinction between continuum and discrete multiplicity prevents infinite divisibility from being transferred to determinate organized plurality.
Antinomies are divided into mathematical conflicts requiring reciprocal rejection and dynamical conflicts permitting qualified bilateral validity.
The unconditioned is repositioned from the head of a phenomenal sequence to a possible intelligible ground outside that sequence.
Surface — Limited spaces and bodies are divisible without yielding an actually infinite stock of constituent parts.
Structural — The status of a series depends on whether its conditions are given simultaneously in intuition, constituted through regress, or heterogeneous to the series.
Metastrategic — Contradictions of reason are resolved by diagnosing the illicit form of totality presupposed by a claim rather than by selecting a victorious thesis.
Ontological/Temporal — Completed infinity is denied to phenomenal composition, while infinity is retained as an unending temporal-procedural regress of determination.
Transcendental — The admissibility of an unconditioned condition is determined by whether it is represented as phenomenal or intelligible and whether it preserves empirical lawfulness.
The axioms reconstruct the central distinction between infinite divisibility and an actually infinite plurality of parts.
The axioms also reconstruct the exclusion of an indivisible phenomenal substance and of infinitely pre-given organization.
The transition from mathematical to dynamical antinomies is reconstructible only if homogeneous and heterogeneous synthesis remain distinct.
The dynamical resolution remains conditional because the text permits an intelligible condition only under the requirement that empirical regress remain intact.
The system is coherent at the level of phenomenal series, but it leaves the positive status of the intelligible condition underdetermined.
The argument depends on a strict separation between completed totality, procedural regress, phenomenal conditions, and intelligible grounds.

identity.title: II. Solution of the Cosmological Idea of the Totality of the Division of a Whole given in Intuition

units.title: III. Solution of the Cosmological Idea of the Totality of the Deduction of Cosmical Events from their Causes

items.text: The central problem is whether one action can be universally necessitated as a phenomenon and free in relation to its cause without contradiction.
The apparent contradiction arises when phenomena and their temporal causal series are treated as things in themselves.
The argument is transcendental, reconstructive, and critical rather than empirical or physiological.
The distinction between appearance and nonphenomenal ground reindexes causality into empirical and intelligible relations.
Empirical character secures complete natural determination, while intelligible character permits timeless spontaneity with respect to the same effect.
Practical ought and blame motivate the representation of reason as causally free without establishing freedom as an object of knowledge.
The argument moves from causal antinomy through standpoint differentiation and practical application to the restricted conclusion that nature and freedom are not mutually contradictory.
Causality is cogitable only as causality through nature or causality through freedom.
Every phenomenal event, including a cause’s action, is temporally determined by a preceding phenomenal event.
Unbroken phenomenal causation is a condition of possible experience and admits no exception within experience.
Cosmological freedom is the faculty of originating a causal series without determination by a preceding sensuous cause.
Practical freedom from sensuous coercion depends on the possibility of transcendental spontaneity.
Phenomena are representations rather than things in themselves.
Phenomena require a nonphenomenal transcendental ground.
The same causal subject can be represented through an empirical character as appearance and an intelligible character as thing in itself.
Empirical character is the stable causal rule by which every action of a phenomenal subject is integrated into nature.
An intelligible character, if ascribed, is exempt from time, change, and sensuous determination.
Any effect attributed to intelligible causality must remain fully conditioned and explicable within the empirical causal series.
Intelligible character cannot be cognized directly and can be thought only through its empirical manifestation.
Ought expresses a necessity grounded in a pure conception rather than in the course of nature.
Ought presupposes that reason can produce effects in the phenomenal world according to ideas.
Human self-consciousness represents reason as a nonempirical faculty distinct from sensuous receptivity.
The transcendental argument can establish only the non-opposition of freedom and nature, not freedom’s actuality or real possibility.
No third mode of causality is admitted beyond nature and freedom.
Natural causality admits no exceptional phenomenon within possible experience.
Freedom is not an empirical property, event, or object of possible experience.
Freedom is not merely the absence of empirical determination but a positive power of causal origination.
Free causality is not an absolute temporal beginning within the phenomenal series.
Phenomena are not things in themselves.
Nature and freedom are not exclusive predicates of an action when attributed under different causal relations.
Intelligible causality is not an additional phenomenal cause cooperating with natural causes.
Ought is not a description, prediction, or modification of what occurs in nature.
Intelligible character is not available to theoretical cognition.
The compatibility argument is not a proof that freedom exists or is really possible.
The phenomenal causal chain admits neither an absolute beginning nor an attainable absolute totality of conditions.
Treating phenomena as things in themselves makes natural necessity ontologically exhaustive and thereby excludes freedom.
The disjunction between nature and freedom ceases to be exclusive at the level of a single event once causal attribution is indexed to empirical and intelligible relations.
Complete empirical knowledge of an agent’s character and conditions would make every phenomenal action predictable as naturally necessary in principle.
An intelligible cause can condition the temporal beginning of an empirical series without itself beginning in time.
Physical inquiry can explain actions completely through empirical causes while omitting their unknowable intelligible ground.
Practical freedom collapses if phenomenal natural causality is treated as the exhaustive form of causality.
Normative necessity both exceeds natural description and presupposes the causal efficacy of rational ideas.
Rational imputation brackets empirical antecedents for purposes of blame without denying their explanatory necessity.
No empirical observation can prove freedom because observation reaches only temporally conditioned effects and empirical character.
Freedom and natural necessity can coexist because each governs the action under a different kind of condition.
The cosmological antinomy is generated by converting the empirical validity of natural causality into a claim about reality in itself.
The two-character model assigns complete natural explanation and complete rational attribution to the same action without construing them as competing empirical causes.
Freedom is relocated from a gap within nature to a nonempirical relation underlying an uninterrupted natural series.
Normative judgment functions as a practical reason for representing rational causality, not as theoretical evidence of a noumenal fact.
Natural causality is constitutive and knowable within experience, whereas freedom remains regulative and merely thinkable beyond empirical determination.
The framework licenses practices of imputation while withholding knowledge of the actual proportion attributable to freedom, nature, error, or temperament.
The system preserves the conceptual availability of both physical determinism and responsibility by assigning them noninterfering explanatory jurisdictions.
The causal form governing possible experience does not govern things in themselves.
Empirical explanatory completeness is not ontological completeness.
Temporal priority is not a necessary form of every conceivable causality.
Normative necessity is not reducible to natural necessity.
An intelligible cause is not itself an event requiring a prior temporal cause.
Coexistence of nature and freedom does not require causal competition within one phenomenal series.
Establishing noncontradiction does not require cognition of the mechanism linking intelligible character to empirical effects.
Freedom occupies the epistemically unavailable ground left when phenomenal causality is denied ontological exhaustiveness.
No cognizable bridge connects timeless intelligible determination to its temporally determinate empirical manifestation.
An absolute beginning is unavailable both as a first phenomenal event and as a temporal act within reason.
The system supplies no answer to why an intelligible character produces one empirical character rather than another.
Perfect knowledge of moral merit and demerit remains structurally foreclosed because the contribution of freedom cannot be separated from natural determination.
Exceptionless phenomenal causality → every causal action becomes a conditioned event → no absolute empirical beginning.
Reason’s demand for an unconditioned condition → idea of spontaneous causality → conflict with the phenomenal causal law.
Absolute reality of phenomena → single causal series → mutual exclusion of nature and freedom.
Appearance–thing-in-itself distinction → empirical–intelligible character distinction → dual causal attribution.
Empirical character → temporal conditioning → complete natural necessity.
Intelligible character → exemption from time and sensuous conditions → spontaneous rational causality.
Same phenomenal effect → full physical explanation plus nonempirical rational imputation → compatibility without causal interference.
Ought and blame → practical representation of rational causality → epistemic limitation → conclusion restricted to non-opposition.

Universal natural causality → impossibility of an empirical first cause → transcendental idea of freedom → antinomy under absolute phenomenal reality → dual-character reframing → compatibility of nature and freedom.
Human action as phenomenon → empirical determination → rational ought → attribution to intelligible reason → blame without denial of natural explanation.
Compatibility established → intelligible ground remains unknowable → actuality and real possibility remain unproved.
The exclusive opposition between nature and freedom is replaced by relation-indexed coexistence.
Natural determinism is reclassified as exhaustive within experience but not exhaustive of reality in itself.
Freedom is relocated from interruption of natural law to the intelligible grounding of law-governed effects.
The human subject is reclassified as both a naturally explicable phenomenon and a rationally imputable agent.
Physical explanation and practical imputation become distinct operations directed at the same action.
Ought is reclassified from a possible natural predicate into the mark of a nonempirical rational order.
Logical compatibility, real possibility, actuality, and empirical provability become distinct epistemic statuses.
Surface: The argument asks whether natural necessity and freedom can apply to the same human action.
Structural: The empirical and intelligible characters distribute causal determination across phenomenal and nonphenomenal relations.
Metastrategic: The antinomy is dissolved by exposing absolute phenomenal reality as the assumption that falsely makes causal modes exclusive.
Ontological/Temporal: Phenomena exist under temporal succession, whereas intelligible causality is represented as timeless and unchanging.
Epistemic/Practical: Knowledge remains confined to empirical character, while practical reason requires the representation of a causality it cannot theoretically cognize.
The axiom set is sufficient to reconstruct the causal antinomy, the dual-character resolution, the practical application, and the restricted conclusion.
The relation by which intelligible character determines empirical character remains underdetermined.
The structure is internally coherent only if the appearance–thing-in-itself distinction and the domain restriction of natural causality are accepted.
The structure is strongest where it preserves exceptionless empirical causality without allowing empirical causality to become ontologically exhaustive.
The transition from an unknowable transcendental ground to the attribution of genuine intelligible causality depends on modal compression rather than demonstration.
The claim that freedom is not opposed to nature does not by itself establish the real possibility that the text expressly declines to prove.
Complete empirical determination remains in tension with the practical claim that the agent could and ought to have acted otherwise.
Decisive blame remains in tension with the admitted impossibility of knowing the actual moral contribution of freedom.
The isolated phrase “illusion of transcendental idealism” conflicts with the argument’s reliance on transcendental idealism and its rejection of the absolute reality of phenomena.
Reconstruction from these elements preserves the movement from antinomy to standpoint differentiation, practical instantiation, and epistemic closure.

identity.title: III. Solution of the Cosmological Idea of the Totality of the Deduction of Cosmical Events from their Causes

units.title: IV. Solution of the Cosmological Idea of the Totality of the Dependence of Phenomenal Existences

items.text: The apparent antinomy arises when the contingent existences of phenomena are treated as requiring an unconditioned existent within their own empirical series.
The dynamical regress differs from the mathematical regress because its condition need not be a homogeneous member of the series it conditions.
A necessary condition can be thought without contradiction only as purely intelligible and extramundane, not as the highest phenomenal condition.
Empirical reason must continue to seek empirical conditions for every phenomenon despite the admissibility of an intelligible ground of the whole series.
The solution establishes only compatibility between phenomenal contingency and an intelligible necessary being, not the being’s existence or determinable nature.
The fourth antinomy drives reason from cosmological inquiry toward transcendent ideas and the projected investigation of a necessary being.
All objects in the sensuous world are phenomena and are conditioned in their existence.
No phenomenal existence possesses unconditioned necessity.
If condition and conditioned belong to one phenomenal series, every condition is itself conditioned.
A dynamical condition need not belong to the empirical series of the conditioned existence.
A necessary condition of phenomenal existence must be purely intelligible if it is not to fall under phenomenal contingency.
A purely intelligible necessary being is not a member, including a highest member, of the phenomenal series.
Phenomenal contingency is compatible with an intelligible condition independent of empirical conditions.
Reason is required to seek an empirical condition for every empirical member of the series.
The empirical regress may proceed without limit through further empirical conditions.
No existence may be inferred from a condition outside the empirical series by means of empirical reasoning.
The absence of empirical explanatory use cannot demonstrate the impossibility of the intelligible.
An intelligible object outside possible experience cannot be cognized through determinate predicates or affirmed as existent.
Transcendent ideas arise when the unconditioned is placed outside possible experience and treated as an object of cognition.
The necessary being functions initially as a limiting thought required to resolve an antinomy, not as an established object of knowledge.
The necessary being is not a phenomenal substance, a worldly cause, or the highest member of an empirical causal sequence.
The solution is not an assertion that a necessary being exists.
Phenomenal contingency is not evidence that an intelligible necessary condition is impossible.
The unrestricted demand for empirical conditions is not permission to seek an empirical cause beyond the empirical world.
The intelligible is not invalidated merely because it cannot explain or be exhibited within phenomena.
A transcendent intelligible object is not determinable by predicates borrowed from empirical cognition.
The unconditioned is not obtainable as a completed object through the empirical regress.
The fourth antinomy dissolves when its opposed claims are assigned to heterogeneous relations: empirical dependence within phenomena and intelligible independence outside them.
The necessary being can be conceived as unconditioned only by being excluded from the domain in which every existence is empirically conditioned.
The empirical investigation of nature remains methodologically unchanged by the thought of an intelligible ground.
The possibility of an intelligible ground is defensible only negatively, through the failure of empirical contingency to disprove it.
Reason may admit an unknown transcendental ground of phenomena without possessing knowledge of its existence or inner constitution.
The transition from cosmological ideas to transcendent ideas occurs when the unconditioned is relocated from the totality of empirical conditions to an object beyond possible experience.

The antinomy is transformed from a dispute about competing objects into a jurisdictional dispute about whether empirical and intelligible conditions may occupy the same explanatory field without belonging to one series.
The system protects empirical science by making its regress indefinitely exhaustive within experience while preventing that regress from deciding the status of what lies beyond experience.
The necessary being is preserved as a permissible boundary-concept precisely by being deprived of empirical membership, empirical causal efficacy, and determinate cognition.
The fourth antinomy becomes the threshold at which a merely regulative restriction on reason prepares a new transcendent inquiry whose object cannot yet be known.
The system excludes the assumption that empirical dependence and absolute dependence are one and the same relation.
The system excludes any inference from the incompleteness of empirical explanation to the existence of a supersensible explanation.
The system excludes the converse inference that the empirical world’s self-contained methodological order exhausts all possible being.
The system excludes a necessary being that could be empirically located, empirically conditioned, or empirically known.
The system excludes the conversion of the unconditioned from a limiting demand of reason into a presented object of experience.
The discourse is organized around the unavailable object of an unconditioned existence that reason must think in order to close dependence but cannot know in order to avoid transcendence.
The resolution depends on the foreclosure of any single domain in which phenomenal contingency and absolute necessity could confront one another as properties of the same object.
The projected cognition of intelligible things is structured by an absence of intuition, leaving analogy and pure conception without constitutive access to their object.
Phenomenal existence → universal empirical conditioning → impossibility of an unconditioned phenomenal member.
Dynamical regress → non-homogeneity of condition and conditioned → admissibility of a condition outside the empirical series.
Intelligible relocation of the unconditioned → removal from contingency → formal compatibility with phenomenal dependence.
Empirical regulative law → unbounded search for empirical conditions → prohibition on empirical transcendence.
Compatibility without proof → intelligible ground as permissible but indeterminate → suspension of ontological assertion.
Relocation beyond experience → transcendent idea → projected inquiry into the necessary being.

Conditioned phenomenal series → impossibility of necessary phenomenal existence → distinction between mathematical and dynamical regress → intelligible extramundane condition → coexistence of empirical contingency and possible necessity → restriction of empirical inference → transition to transcendent investigation.
The necessary being is reclassified from a missing empirical cause into a possible intelligible ground that cannot enter empirical explanation.
The opposition between universal phenomenal contingency and necessary existence is recoded as non-contradictory because the claims concern different orders of conditioning.
Infinite empirical regress becomes compatible with a non-empirical ground, rather than functioning as evidence either for or against such a ground.
Empirical reason and pure reason receive distinct jurisdictions: the former investigates conditions of appearances, while the latter may think a limiting intelligible condition without knowing it.
The fourth antinomy is converted from a cosmological impasse into a passage toward rational theology, while retaining the prohibition on constitutive knowledge.
Surface — The text resolves whether a necessary being can coexist with the universal contingency of phenomenal existence.
Structural — The resolution depends on separating empirical causal series from an intelligible condition that does not belong to their membership.
Metastrategic — The text limits both dogmatic rationalism, which infers supersensible existence, and empirical exclusivism, which declares the supersensible impossible.
Ontological/Temporal — Phenomena are constituted as endlessly conditionable representations, whereas the unconditioned can be thought only as outside the temporal-empirical order of dependence.
Epistemic — Thinkability exceeds knowability: an intelligible ground may be admitted as possible while its existence and predicates remain unavailable to cognition.
The axioms reconstruct the argument if phenomenal contingency, the non-membership of dynamical conditions, and the restriction of empirical inference are retained together.
The system is coherent at the level of compatibility because it does not derive necessary existence from phenomenal dependence.
The system is strongest where it distinguishes the methodological infinity of empirical regress from an ontological assertion about what may lie beyond it.
The system remains underdetermined concerning how an intelligible ground can be positively conceived without importing empirical predicates by analogy.
The movement toward a subsequent investigation of a necessary being strains the prior prohibition against affirming the existence or determinate nature of transcendent objects.
The distinction between permissible thought and illicit cognition bears the full burden of the resolution and cannot itself be established by empirical evidence.

identity.title: IV. Solution of the Cosmological Idea of the Totality of the Dependence of Phenomenal Existences

units.title: Section I. Of the Ideal in General

items.text: Pure conceptions provide forms of thought but require sensuous conditions for objective presentation.
Ideas exceed possible phenomenal presentation and organize experience through a unity that experience never fully attains.
An ideal is an idea individualized and completely determined by a priori principles.
Unlike a merely formal idea, an ideal has practical force as an archetype for judging and perfecting action.
The ideal remains non-objective and unattainable, yet functions as a standard for measuring empirical incompleteness.
The argument preserves rational ideals by excluding both empirical embodiment and indeterminate imaginative representation.
Objective presentation to the mind requires sensuous conditions.
Pure conceptions contain the form of thought without independently containing objective reality.
Pure conceptions can acquire concrete application when related to phenomena.
Ideas cannot be presented in concreto by any phenomenon.
Ideas provide a perfection unattainable by empirical cognition and a unity toward which experience can only approximate.
An ideal is an idea considered as an individual object determined by the idea alone.
Complete ideal determination requires selecting one conforming predicate from each set of contradictory predicates.
Human reason contains ideals in addition to ideas.
Ideals possess practical and regulative power.
An idea provides a rule, while an ideal provides an archetype for the complete determination of its copy.
An ideal can lack objective reality without being a chimera.
An ideal enables reason to estimate the incompleteness of objects through comparison.
Empirical realization of the ideal as an exemplary object is impracticable and absurd.
Ideals of imagination lack determinate rules and cannot function as standards of production or appreciation.
Reason conceives its ideal object as completely determinable by a priori principles despite the absence of empirical conditions.
Pure conceptions are not independently objective objects.
Ideas are not phenomenal contents available in concrete intuition.
The ideal is not merely an abstract rule but an idea individualized as a complete object of determination.
Rational ideals are not creative or constitutive objects in the Platonic sense.
Lack of objective reality does not reduce the ideal to a chimera.
The ideal is not realizable as a perfect empirical example.
The rational ideal is not an indeterminate image produced by imagination.
Imaginative ideals are not rules or standards for explanation, examination, production, or appreciation.
Moral conceptions are not perfectly pure conceptions insofar as empirical pleasure or pain enters their foundation.
The movement from pure conception to idea to ideal progressively withdraws objective presentation while increasing systematic and determinative function.
An ideal converts a general rational rule into an individual archetype against which copies can be judged.
The ideal can measure empirical deficiency without itself being an empirical object.
Unattainability does not cancel practical efficacy because the ideal operates as a regulative standard rather than as an attainable state.
Moral action can be regulated by an ideal even when moral concepts retain empirical elements.
Attempted empirical embodiment destroys the ideal’s perfection by introducing conditions that the ideal excludes.
Imaginative representation cannot perform the rational function of an ideal because it lacks determinate rule-governed structure.
The ideal is transcendent because it lacks empirical conditions but remains non-arbitrary because its determination follows a priori principles.
Rational judgment can possess objective standardizing force without possessing an objectively given standard-object.
The ideal’s distance from empirical realization is what preserves its function as a universal measure of incompleteness.
Perfectibility is constituted as an indefinite orientation toward a standard rather than as the achievement of a final empirical condition.
The ideal separates normative validity from ontological existence: it lacks actuality while retaining critical and practical authority.
The system makes the absence of a sensible image a condition for preserving the rational ideal’s determinacy.
The ideal is simultaneously an individual object of thought and a non-objective standard, with the tension contained by locating its individuality in rational determination rather than intuition.
The validity of the ideal does not depend on its being given in intuition.
No completed empirical cognition can supply the perfection or unity prescribed by the ideal.
No empirical specimen can ground the ideal’s normative authority.
No sensible image can preserve complete rational determination.
Normative force does not require creative, constitutive, or object-producing causality.
Empirical content cannot be allowed to determine the formal structure of the rational ideal.
The empirical world is structurally incapable of containing the ideal as a completed object.
Experience cannot become the self-sufficient ground of rational normativity.
The permanent gap between ideal and experience cannot be closed without abolishing the ideal’s function.
A sensible representation cannot substitute for a determinate a priori archetype.
The ideal cannot be converted from a regulative standard into a constitutively existing entity without contradiction.
Sensuous condition → objective presentation; absence of sensuous condition → pure form of thought.
Phenomenal application → concrete empirical conception; impossibility of phenomenal presentation → idea beyond empirical cognition.
Idea + individuation + exhaustive a priori determination → ideal.
Ideal + archetypal function → comparison, criticism, and practical perfectibility.
Denial of objective reality + retention of regulative function → non-chimerical transcendence.
Attempted empirical embodiment or imaginative depiction → loss of determinate perfection and failure of standardization.

Sensuous condition of objectivity → formal conception → idea beyond possible intuition → individualized ideal → archetypal comparison → practical perfectibility → exclusion of empirical embodiment and imaginative substitution.
Objective reality is progressively withdrawn while systematic unity, determination, criticism, and practical regulation are retained.
The ideal is reclassified from a possible object of knowledge into a regulative standard of judgment.
Non-attainment is reclassified from failure into the condition of practical perfectibility.
Empirical incompleteness becomes measurable through comparison with a non-empirical archetype.
The rational ideal is separated from the sensible prototype and the imaginative image.
Individuality is detached from empirical existence and relocated in complete rational determination.
The attempted representation of perfection is exposed as a degradation of the standard it seeks to exhibit.
Surface — The passage distinguishes pure conceptions, ideas, ideals of reason, and ideals of imagination.
Structural — The argument organizes the relation between sensibility, phenomenal cognition, understanding, and reason according to degrees of objective presentation and determination.
Metastrategic — The passage converts unattainable perfection into a governing standard for criticism, comparison, and self-reformation.
Ontological/Temporal — The ideal is transcendent and non-objective, while experience remains an indefinitely incomplete approximation to rational unity and perfection.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the hierarchy from pure conception through idea to ideal.
The extracted system preserves the distinction between objective reality and regulative validity.
The reconstruction preserves the exclusion of both empirical exemplification and imaginative indeterminacy.
The system remains underdetermined concerning whether the ideal’s individuality is epistemic, ontological, or a deliberately suspended hybrid.
The central unresolved tension is that the ideal must be sufficiently individual for complete determination while lacking the objective reality of an individual empirical object.
The argument is internally coherent once the ideal’s authority is assigned a regulative rather than constitutive status.
Reconstruction depends on retaining the text’s distinction between rational determination and sensible depiction; collapsing that distinction dissolves the machine.

identity.title: Section I. Of the Ideal in General

units.title: Section II. Of the Transcendental Ideal (Prototypon Trancendentale)

items.text: Complete determination appears to require a total field of possible predicates rather than merely the logical exclusion of contradictories.
The material condition of complete determination is represented as the sum-total of reality, because negations are intelligible only as limitations of affirmative reality.
The sum-total of reality becomes an individual transcendental ideal, the ens realissimum, only within reason’s demand for complete determination.
Reason analogically treats the ideal as the prototype and ground of the possibility of determinate things.
The ideal supplies a regulative condition for thinking objects but supplies no warrant for asserting an objectively existing primal being.
Transcendental illusion arises when a principle valid for empirical objects is extended to things in general.
The reified totality of empirical reality is successively objectivized, hypostatized, and personified as a supreme intelligence or God.
Logical determinability requires that only one predicate of each contradictory pair belong to a conception.
Complete determination requires that a thing be related to the whole domain of possible predicates.
Complete determination concerns the material content of possibility, not merely the logical form of judgement.
The totality required for complete determination cannot be given in concreto and therefore has the status of an idea of reason.
Transcendental affirmation signifies reality or being, whereas transcendental negation signifies privation, absence, or limitation.
Negative determinations are cognizable only through their relation to corresponding affirmative determinations.
The material of all possibility is therefore the sum-total of reality.
The idea of the sum-total of reality determines an individual ideal of pure reason, the ens realissimum.
Determinate things are thinkable through partial participation in, and limitation of, the totality of reality.
The transcendental ideal is a condition for the thought of complete determination, not an assertion of the existence of its object.
The ideal must be thought as simple because derivative beings cannot constitute the primal condition from which they derive.
Sensuous objects are possible for cognition only in relation to the unified whole of possible experience.
Reason naturally mistakes the empirical condition of possible experience for a transcendental condition of things in general.
The conversion of distributive empirical unity into a collective individual whole produces dialectical hypostatization.
Complete determination is not identical with the principle of contradiction or the law of excluded middle.
Logical negation is not transcendental negation.
A negative predicate is not a positive representation of an independent non-being.
The sum-total of reality is not a genus containing predicates as subordinate species.
The ens realissimum is not an aggregate composed from derivative beings or partial realities.
The transcendental ideal is not evidence that a corresponding being objectively exists.
Empirical totality is not an individual object containing all reality.
The regulative unity of experience is not a property inhering in phenomena independently of understanding.
Complete knowledge of a thing would require its positive and negative determination against the total field of possibility.
Every determinate negation presupposes a prior affirmative reality of which it is a limitation.
The totality of possibility is represented as omnitudo realitatis rather than as a totality of positive and negative items of equal rank.
The ens realissimum functions as an archetype from which finite things are conceived as imperfectly determined copies.
The logical form of disjunctive determination supplies the analogue through which reason thinks finite determination by exclusion from a total field.
The predicates of unity, simplicity, sufficiency, and eternity can be attached to the ideal only after it is treated as an individual being.
The demand for an unconditioned ground of possibility exceeds the legitimate use for which the ideal is required.
Finite plurality is structurally subordinated to a prior affirmative totality because difference is construed as graduated limitation rather than independent positivity.
The transcendental ideal mediates between the logical demand for exhaustive determination and theology’s representation of a supreme being.
The same structure that permits systematic empirical determination also generates the illusion of an ontologically supreme object.
The ideal is indispensable as a condition of reason’s systematic completion while invalid as an object of theoretical knowledge.
Transcendental theology is generated by a category error in which a subjective condition of complete determination is converted into an objectively existing cause.
The critique of the ideal does not abolish the idea of totality but relocates it from constitutive ontology to regulative reason.
Possibility is not grounded by a collection of independent determinations lacking a common material condition.
Negation is not ontologically co-original with affirmation.
Empirical conditions of objectivity are not licensed to determine the structure of supersensible being.
A conceptual necessity for totality is not a proof of an object corresponding to that totality.
The unity required by cognition is not thereby a unity possessed by reality independently of cognition.
