The system requires the falsity of the assumption that reason’s prestige guarantees the validity of its concepts.
The system requires the falsity of the assumption that unrestricted development of a power is always beneficial.
The system requires the falsity of the assumption that validity established in one cognitive domain transfers automatically to another.
The system requires the falsity of the assumption that interconnected fallacies can be neutralized through isolated objections.
The system requires the falsity of the assumption that regulating cognitive content and regulating cognitive method are the same operation.
The argument is organized around the absence of an external empirical or intuitive test for pure concepts.
It forecloses the possibility that reason can certify its transcendental products merely by generating them.
It excludes a seamless continuity between the positive expansion of knowledge and the control of error.
It renders unrestricted transcendental speculation inadmissible as a secure route to knowledge.
It denies the possibility of a discipline-free autonomy of reason in the transcendental sphere.
Logical negativity is separated from content-negative judgment, isolating error prevention as the operative function of the latter.
Restricted cognition, deceptive illusion, and consequential error elevate error prevention above positive accumulation.
The elevated negative function is formalized as discipline, while positive development is assigned to culture and doctrine.
The requirement of discipline is extended from ordinary powers to reason itself.
Empirical observation and pure intuition partition domains where reason is externally constrained from the transcendental domain where it is not.
The absence of external constraint produces a tendency toward overstepping possible experience.
Overstepping is treated as a connected system of fallacies rather than as a collection of independent mistakes.
A connected system of fallacies generates the need for a general negative code of examination.
The code is directed at the method of pure cognition and functions by preventing illegitimate methodological transfer and transcendental overreach.

Negative judgment as error prevention → heightened value under epistemic risk → discipline as corrective restraint → reason subjected to discipline → separation of externally constrained and transcendental cognition → method-directed code against systematic illusion.
Negativity is reclassified from an impediment to knowledge into a condition of epistemic security.
The conceptual field is divided between positive power formation and negative power regulation.
Reason’s exemption from criticism is removed; reason becomes an object of critique.
Cognitive domains are reclassified according to the presence or absence of empirical and intuitive constraint.
Error is reclassified from a local defect into a system generated by general principles.
Critique shifts from correcting propositions to governing the methods by which propositions are produced.
Surface: Negative judgments are assigned the function of preventing error rather than adding knowledge.
Structural: Discipline organizes the relation between mental powers, cognitive domains, and permissible methods.
Metastrategic: Critique becomes a regulatory operation that blocks the misuse of reason-generated methods.
Ontological/Temporal: Possible experience establishes the boundary of legitimate cognition, while transcendental reason tends toward an ungrounded extension beyond that boundary.
The extracted axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the movement from the limited value of negative judgment to the necessity of disciplining pure reason.
The system is internally coherent because the distinction between positive cognition and negative error-control governs every major transition.
Its strongest structural point is the distinction between externally constrained cognition and transcendental cognition lacking such constraint.
The system contains a productive tension because discipline must regulate reason while being founded on reason’s own nature and principles.

A second tension arises because the discipline of pure reason is methodologically necessary, while the text does not specify its concrete tests with the precision available in empirical or mathematical cognition.
The relation between the positive construction of cognition in the doctrine of elements and the negative regulation of cognition in discipline remains partially underdetermined.
Reconstruction preserves the original argument’s movement because systematic illusion, domain separation, and method-directed restriction jointly generate the final position.

identity.title: Chapter I. The Discipline of Pure Reason

units.title: Section I. The Discipline of Pure Reason in the Sphere of Dogmatism

items.text: Mathematical success induces pure reason to expect an equally secure extension into the transcendental sphere.
The governing problem is whether mathematical demonstration and philosophical dogmatism employ the same method.
Mathematical cognition constructs concepts in a priori intuition, whereas philosophical cognition proceeds discursively through concepts.
This methodological division arises because space and time are available a priori for construction, while the matter of appearances is available only through experience.
Definitions, axioms, and demonstrations depend in their mathematical form upon construction and therefore lack strict philosophical equivalents.
The argument is diagnostic, transcendental, and disciplinary, moving from methodological temptation through formal differentiation and evidential testing to prohibition.
Philosophy may remain systematic, but its proper procedure is deduction, conceptual exposition, limit-detection, and correction rather than mathematical dogmatism.
Objects are presented to cognition only through possible intuitions.
Philosophical cognition is rational cognition through concepts.
Mathematical cognition is rational cognition through the construction of concepts.
Construction is the a priori presentation of an intuition corresponding to a concept.
An individual construction yields universal cognition when only its universal conditions of construction determine the result.
Philosophical and mathematical cognition can both possess universality and an a priori origin.
The difference between philosophy and mathematics lies in their cognitive form rather than their subject matter.
Space and time are the only a priori intuitions and constitute the pure form of appearances.
The matter of appearances is given only a posteriori through perception.
Analysis clarifies a concept but does not extend cognition beyond its contained marks.
Synthetic extension requires passage beyond a concept to an intuition corresponding to it.
A concept is constructible only insofar as its corresponding intuition can be presented a priori.
Transcendental concepts represent rules for synthesizing possible empirical intuitions rather than a priori intuitions of objects.
Transcendental principles possess objective validity only as conditions of possible experience.
The completeness of an analysis of a given concept cannot be established with demonstrative certainty.
A synthetic connection made through concepts requires mediating cognition and deduction.
A strict definition can initiate cognition only when it generates a concept that can be constructed a priori.
Demonstration is apodeictic proof grounded in intuition.
Philosophy and mathematics are not distinguished by an opposition between quality and quantity.
Shared universality and a priori origin do not establish methodological identity.
Mathematical success does not warrant transferring mathematical procedure into transcendental philosophy.
The matter, reality, or existence of an object cannot be constructed a priori.
Conceptual analysis does not produce synthetic cognition.
Empirical cognition does not possess necessity or strict universality.
Empirical concepts cannot receive complete and permanently bounded definitions.
Given a priori concepts cannot receive demonstrably complete definitions.
The definition of an arbitrary project does not establish the existence or possibility of its object.
Philosophy contains no immediately certain synthetic principles in the mathematical sense of axioms.
Discursive philosophical proofs are not demonstrations.
Transcendental principles are not direct synthetic dogmata grounded in concepts alone.
Rejection of the dogmatic method does not entail rejection of philosophical system.
Mathematical construction converts an individual a priori presentation into universally valid synthetic cognition by retaining only universal construction conditions.

Mathematics concerns quantity because quantities admit a priori construction; quantity is therefore an effect of mathematical form rather than the original basis of the mathematics–philosophy distinction.
Common objects and common a priori validity do not erase the difference between construction and conceptual consideration.
Discursive reflection confined to a concept can reorder or clarify cognition but cannot discover properties not already contained in that concept.
Recourse to empirical intuition can produce synthetic propositions, but it forfeits necessity and strict universality.
Transcendental propositions determine rules for the unity of possible experience without presenting their objects in a priori intuition.
Mathematical definitions can generate their concepts at the beginning of inquiry, whereas philosophical definitions remain uncertain expositions that properly approach completion only at the end.
Philosophy possesses no axioms because synthetic connections between concepts require mediation and deduction.
Philosophy possesses no demonstrations because it cannot present its transcendental concepts through constructed a priori intuitions.
Speculative pure reason contains no dogmata because its objectively valid synthetic principles are mediated through their relation to possible experience.
Philosophy can form a systematic investigation under principles of unity even though experience supplies its material and deduction supplies its authority.
Philosophy’s proper transcendental task is to establish validity, delimit legitimate employment, detect illusion, and revise defective principles.
Importing mathematical evidence into philosophy suppresses the mediations through which philosophical claims must be justified and thereby conceals error.
A priori cognition is internally heterogeneous: common origin and universality divide into intuitive construction and discursive conditioning rather than forming one transferable method.
Mathematical mastery is confined to formal objects whose determinations the subject can construct; it does not extend to empirical matter, existence, or reality.
Possible experience functions simultaneously as the limit of transcendental principles and as the ground through which their objective validity is established.
Philosophical inquiry must operate with incompletely exposed concepts before it can approach complete exposition, making its order of cognition inverse to mathematical definition.
Philosophical certainty, where attainable, is deduced and mediated rather than self-evident, so apodeictic force does not entail mathematical form.
The dogmatic method is structurally error-preserving because it treats revisable conceptual premises as though they possessed intuitive transparency.
The absence of constructible intuitions for transcendental concepts blocks mathematical passage from possible experience to a supersensible intellectual world.
No intellectual intuition beyond space and time is available to speculative reason.
No method remains invariant when transferred between constructed intuition and discursive concepts.
No concept guarantees the existence, possibility, or determinate reality of its object merely by being clearly formed.
No material content of appearance can be generated from pure reason.
No transcendental principle is entitled to acceptance through self-evidence alone.
No complete philosophical vocabulary can be secured before philosophical inquiry begins.
No idea of pure reason produces objectively valid synthetic knowledge of a supersensible object.
No technical success within mathematics exempts mathematical reason from philosophical determination of its limits.
The unavailable intuition of transcendental objects is the central absence around which the prohibition of dogmatic metaphysics is organized.
Philosophy lacks an Archimedean beginning composed of complete definitions, self-evident axioms, and intuitive demonstrations.
The system forecloses a universal apodeictic method capable of moving unchanged from mathematics to every object of thought.
Pure reason cannot erect a speculative edifice from self-supplied material because the material of cognition remains dependent upon experience.
The intellectual world promised by transcendental dogmatism remains structurally inaccessible rather than merely undiscovered.
Mathematical success generates analogical expectation, which generates the question of methodological transfer.
Object-presentation divides into pure formal intuition and empirically given matter, thereby producing two legitimate employments of reason.
Pure intuition → a priori construction → individual schema under universal conditions → synthetic universality → mathematical cognition.
Empirical matter → transcendental rule of synthesis → relation to possible experience → mediated deduction → philosophical cognition.
The distinction yields three evidential oppositions: concept-generation versus exposition, immediate construction versus deduction, and intuitive demonstration versus discursive proof.
Failure of philosophical construction eliminates mathematical definitions, axioms, demonstrations, and direct synthetic dogmata from speculative philosophy.
The resulting closure redirects philosophy from transcendental expansion toward systematic criticism, boundary-determination, error detection, and revision.

The argument moves through mathematical success → transcendental imitation → method-identity question → construction–concept distinction → pure-form–empirical-matter division → test of definitions, axioms, and demonstrations → elimination of speculative dogmata → critical-systematic discipline.
Mathematics and philosophy are reclassified by their modes of cognition rather than by separate inventories of objects.
Quantity becomes a consequence of constructibility rather than the primitive definition of mathematics.
The a priori divides into constructible intuition and discursive conditions of experience.
Certainty divides into immediate intuitive evidence and mediated validity established through deduction.
Definitions, axioms, and demonstrations cease to function as universal norms of rational proof and become domain-specific effects of construction.
Transcendental principles are reclassified from direct dogmata into conditions governing possible experience.
Philosophy’s inability to imitate mathematics is reclassified from cognitive deficiency into the condition of its critical function.
Dogmatism is reclassified as an illicit transfer of evidential form rather than merely excessive confidence in particular doctrines.
Surface: The text tests whether philosophical reasoning can employ mathematical definitions, axioms, and demonstrations.
Structural: The legitimacy of each method is determined by the relation among concepts, pure intuition, empirical matter, and possible experience.
Metastrategic: Philosophy is redirected from imitating mathematical expansion toward policing validity, limits, and inferential error.

Ontological/Temporal: Appearances divide into the a priori forms of space and time and the a posteriori matter of sensation, while causality and other transcendental concepts govern temporal synthesis without presenting objects independently of experience.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the methodological distinction, its transcendental ground, the tripartite evidential test, and the critical conclusion.
The exclusivity of space and time as a priori intuitions and the objective validity of the categories remain underdetermined because their proofs are imported from earlier stages of the Critique.
The structure is coherent only if direct synthetic cognition from concepts is distinguished rigorously from mediated synthetic principles validated through possible experience.
The system is strongest where differences in available intuition generate differences in method, evidence, and legitimate scope.
The claim that mathematics alone possesses definitions depends on restricting strict definition to object-valid, a priori constructible concepts, despite admitting definitions of arbitrary projects.

The coexistence of apodeictically certain philosophical principles with the denial of philosophical demonstrations depends upon a distinction between deduced certainty and intuitive evidence whose full defense is not supplied here.

The use of possible experience both as the proof-ground of transcendental principles and as what those principles make possible creates a reflexive dependence that requires the prior transcendental deduction to avoid circularity.
The assertion that dogmatic methods merely conceal error is stronger than the demonstrated conclusion that mathematical evidence cannot be transferred unchanged into philosophy.

Reconstruction preserves the actual movement from temptation to restriction, but it cannot reproduce the argument’s full warrant without the antecedent accounts of intuition, categories, and experience.

identity.title: Section I. The Discipline of Pure Reason in the Sphere of Dogmatism

units.title: Section II. The Discipline of Pure Reason in Polemics

items.text: The governing problem is how pure reason can confront unavoidable disputes over supersensible claims without dogmatic proof, censorship, or terminal scepticism.
Unrestricted criticism, rather than partisan victory, secures reason’s legitimate domain and the possibility of lasting intellectual peace.
Objective speculative validity is restricted to possible experience, rendering both affirmative and negative transcendent claims indemonstrable.
Polemical success is reduced from proving a transcendent proposition to showing that its contrary cannot establish itself.
Free contest corrects reason by exposing dialectical illusion, whereas coercive protection preserves dogmatic fragility.
Scepticism functions as censure and preparation but must yield to systematic a priori determination of reason’s necessary limits.
The argument is juridical-critical, diagnostic, and reconstructive, moving from speculative conflict through jurisdictional diagnosis and sceptical interruption to bounded rational self-possession.
Every exercise of reason must remain open to unrestricted criticism.
Universal human reason is the sole legitimate tribunal for rational claims.
Critique determines reason’s rights and limits by examining reason’s own sources and powers.
Possible experience supplies the only objective criterion of speculative truth available to human cognition.
The understanding possesses synthetic a priori principles whose objective validity consists in governing possible experience.
Ideas of supersensible objects cannot determine either the actuality or the impossibility of their objects for human cognition.
A polemical defence establishes at most the failure of a dogmatic counterclaim, not the truth of the defended proposition.
Phenomena are not things in themselves.
Treating phenomena as things in themselves and demanding their unconditioned completion generates apparent rational contradiction.
Practical rational interest can warrant faith in transcendent propositions without increasing their speculative demonstrability.
Free reciprocal testing advances reason by exposing illusion and restricting unjustified claims.
Rational adjudication requires honesty concerning doubts, proof deficiencies, and actual convictions.
Sceptical censure of failed dogmatic attempts produces doubt but cannot establish necessary limits to cognition.
Necessary limits and unavoidable ignorance can be established only through systematic a priori investigation of reason itself.
No claim, institution, interest, or sacred doctrine is exempt from criticism.
Reason is not a despotic authority and cannot be legitimately governed by foreign coercive powers.
Refuting an opponent is not equivalent to proving one’s own transcendent assertion.
Phenomena must not be interpreted as independently existing things in themselves.
Speculative pure reason cannot demonstrate the existence of God, an immortal soul, or freedom.
Speculative pure reason cannot demonstrate the nonexistence or impossibility of those objects.
Rational faith is not speculative knowledge.
Practical usefulness does not legitimate deceptive proof, concealment of doubt, or censorship.
Protective guardianship and dogmatic instruction do not produce durable rational conviction.
Scepticism is not a permanent dwelling-place for reason.
Empirical awareness of ignorance is not knowledge of cognition’s necessary boundaries.
The necessity of causal law is not reducible to habitual association among observed events.
Opposed assertions concerning supersensible objects are symmetrical in speculative undecidability, even when one side has greater practical interest.
A transcendent affirmative may be preserved against dogmatic refutation without thereby receiving a satisfactory speculative title.
No proper object-level polemic is possible beyond experience because neither party possesses a criterion capable of fixing the disputed object.
Cosmological antinomy is dissolved by correcting the status assigned to phenomena rather than by selecting one dogmatic proposition over its contrary.
Speculative attacks cannot overthrow practically warranted commitments when those commitments are not misrepresented as speculative knowledge.
Suppressing opposition deprives reason of its corrective mechanism and leaves inherited convictions vulnerable to later dialectical attack.
Critique replaces the unstable victories of dogmatic warfare with jurisdictional decisions concerning which claims reason is entitled to make.
Scepticism is a necessary interruption of dogmatism but becomes illegitimate when it converts failed attempts into a universal verdict on reason.
Accidental ignorance motivates further inquiry, whereas only critically demonstrated necessary ignorance can terminate inquiry as knowledge of limits.

The contingency of particular causal determinations does not entail the contingency of causal law, because the law is a condition of possible experience rather than an inference from repeated experience.
Critical education must expose students to opposed speculative arguments and train them to detect the dialectical defects shared by both sides.
Critique transforms metaphysical warfare over supersensible objects into constitutional inquiry concerning the conditions under which any claim may possess authority.
Rational freedom and rational limitation become mutually constitutive because reason remains autonomous only by submitting itself to universally valid self-criticism.
Supersensible doctrines survive critique only through a change of status from speculative cognition to practically grounded rational commitment.
The dogmatic opponent becomes an internal instrument of reason’s self-correction rather than an external danger to be silenced.
Lasting speculative peace is produced by terminating illegitimate jurisdiction, not by answering questions about supersensible objects.

Epistemic symmetry between transcendent affirmation and negation coexists with a practical asymmetry favouring affirmation, while the criterion separating rational faith from interest-driven preference remains incompletely formalized here.
Critique claims necessary and enduring jurisdiction while requiring unrestricted criticizability, so its final authority remains conditional on demonstrations supplied outside this section.
The functionalization of error, conflict, and hypocrisy as purposive contributions to humanity invokes a teleological assurance that the restriction on supersensible cognition cannot itself certify.
Human cognition possesses no intellectual intuition through which supersensible objects could be directly presented.
A rational idea cannot generate or certify the existence of its corresponding object.
No criterion of objective speculative truth is available independently of possible experience.
Repeated failure or observed limitation cannot establish necessary incapacity.
Synthetic a priori cognition cannot be wholly reducible to empirical habit without destroying the possibility of critique itself.
Anticipated social benefit or harm cannot determine the speculative truth of a proposition.
Reason cannot acquire durable security through insulation from opposition.
A completed theoretical metaphysics of God, freedom, and immortality is structurally foreclosed.
No standpoint external to reason is available from which reason can be authoritatively judged.
Final object-level victory in transcendent dispute is unavailable because the disputed object can never enter the common evidential field.
Stable dogmatic innocence is impossible once reason encounters opposed arguments generated by its own structure.
The possibility that critique is merely another revisable combatant rather than the final tribunal is structurally inadmissible to the chapter’s juridical closure.
The practical foundation expected to secure supersensible commitments remains deferred beyond the speculative argument developed here.
The constitutional mechanism is unrestricted criticizability → universal rational tribunal → determination of rights and limits → lawful possession of a bounded domain.
The polemical mechanism is transcendent assertion → absence of experiential criterion → reciprocal inability to prove → defensive invalidation of the contrary → dissolution of proper polemic.

The antinomy mechanism is appearance treated as thing in itself → demand for unconditioned completion → contradictory inference → restoration of the transcendental distinction → dissolution of contradiction.

The civic-pedagogical mechanism is perceived doctrinal threat → censorship or deceptive apologetics → dogmatic fragility, whereas free exposure → critical testing → resistance to dialectical illusion.
The developmental mechanism is dogmatism → sceptical censure → recognition that failed facta do not determine necessary bounds → systematic a priori self-investigation → criticism.

The correction of Hume proceeds from separating contingent empirical causal determination from the necessary causal form of possible experience and thereby restoring limited synthetic a priori validity.
Strategic closure proceeds through boundary determination → renunciation of transcendent knowledge → retention of practical rational orientation → cessation of speculative war.

Unrestricted criticism → dogmatic antithetic → experiential criterion of validity → reciprocal speculative impotence → polemic reduced to counter-refutation → critique established as jurisdiction → free contest and critical education → scepticism subordinated → Humean overreach corrected → bounded certainty and legal peace.
Supersensible disputes are reclassified from contests over objects into inquiries concerning the jurisdiction of cognitive faculties.
Affirmation and negation cease to form a speculative winner-loser opposition because both exceed the available criterion of truth.
Faith and knowledge become formally separable modes of assent rather than competing degrees of the same speculative proof.
Freedom and discipline cease to be opposites because criticism limits reason through reason’s own universal legislation.
Scepticism is repositioned from philosophical conclusion to transitional instrument between dogmatism and criticism.
Ignorance is divided into indefinite empirical lack and determinate critical knowledge of necessary limits.
Hostile argument is reclassified from a danger to doctrine into an exercise that reveals reason’s legitimate possessions.
A priori cognition is separated from transcendent speculation and reassigned to the formal conditions of possible experience.
At the surface level, the argument governs disputes concerning God, the soul, freedom, immortality, causal necessity, and freedom of speculative expression.
At the structural level, criticism functions as a juridical institution that replaces intellectual war, censorship, and doctrinal guardianship with lawful adjudication and critical education.
At the metastrategic level, the argument refuses partisan entry into transcendent disputes and redirects inquiry toward the conditions that make claims valid or inadmissible.
At the ontological-epistemic level, the system distinguishes phenomena from things in themselves and confines objective cognition to possible experience.
At the temporal level, rational maturity develops from dogmatic assertion through sceptical interruption to critical knowledge of a permanently bounded domain.
The extracted axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the chapter’s transition from free polemic to critical jurisdiction and from scepticism to bounded cognition.
The objective validity of synthetic a priori principles remains dependent on transcendental demonstrations supplied elsewhere in the work.
The practical warrant for faith in God, freedom, and immortality is invoked but not established within this section.
The structure is internally coherent if possible experience is accepted as the exclusive criterion of objective speculative validity.
The system is strongest in distinguishing reciprocal transcendent unprovability from critical knowledge of necessary limits.
The juridical analogy and the teleological treatment of conflict perform argumentative work not fully reducible to the stated epistemic premises.
The principal fault lines are the practical preference for affirmative doctrines despite speculative symmetry, and the tribunal’s claim to finality despite the universal requirement of criticism.
Reconstruction preserves the real movement only if Humean scepticism is retained as the necessary middle stage rather than treated as the chapter’s final adversary.

identity.title: Section II. The Discipline of Pure Reason in Polemics

units.title: Section III. The Discipline of Pure Reason in Hypothesis

items.text: The failure of pure speculation to extend knowledge creates an apparent opening for unrestricted hypothesis.
Hypothesis is legitimate only where an object’s possibility is secured and the supposition explains what is certainly given.
The conditions of possible experience delimit both theoretical objecthood and admissible explanatory causes.
Transcendental hypotheses are excluded from explanation because they replace inquiry with incomprehensible grounds beyond experience.
Hypotheses concerning transcendent matters retain a strictly defensive use against equally ungrounded dogmatic objections.
Reason achieves durable discipline only by eliciting, confronting, and neutralizing its own dialectical objections.
Pure speculative reason cannot extend cognition beyond the bounds of possible experience.
A legitimate hypothesis presupposes certainty of the possible object to which it refers.
A legitimate hypothesis must connect its explanatory ground to something actually given and certain.
The categories determine dynamical connections only when such connections are or can be given in experience.
The conditions of possible experience are the only theoretical conditions under which things can be cognized as possible.
Ideas of reason are problematical regulative principles for systematizing experience rather than cognitions of objects.
The explanation of phenomena may employ only grounds connected with them through known laws of experience.
A hypothesis is sufficient only if it determines in advance the experienced consequences attributed to it.
Auxiliary hypotheses weaken a hypothesis when their necessity lacks independent justification.
Pure reason can issue either necessary cognition or a declaration of non-cognition, but not theoretical opinion beyond experience.
A hypothesis may defend against a transcendent assertion without serving as proof of its contrary.
Equal speculative ignorance of opposed transcendent claims prevents either party from claiming theoretical superiority.
Speculative reason is inherently dialectical and must subject its own claims to adversarial examination.
Hypothesis is not permission to invent objects, powers, properties, substances, relations, durations, or presences unavailable to experience.
Logical non-contradiction is not sufficient to establish the objective possibility of a thing.
Ideas of reason are not representations of imaginary, merely possible, or independently knowable objects.
A transcendental hypothesis is not an explanation of natural phenomena.
Hyperphysical grounds are not admissible substitutes for empirical causal investigation.
The absolute totality of explanatory conditions is not a requirement that may obstruct empirical inquiry.
Probable judgement and opinion are not valid forms of pure speculative cognition.
Defensive hypotheses are not personal opinions, dogmatic theses, or proofs of transcendent reality.
External controversy is not the primary source of transcendental conflict, because the opposition originates within reason itself.
Theoretical hypotheses are restricted to empirical possibilities whose explanatory relation to given appearances can be specified.
The soul may be treated as a regulative unity for investigating mental appearances without being asserted as a simple substance.
Natural order and purposiveness must be investigated through natural laws even when a hyperphysical ground appears explanatorily tempting.
The multiplication of ad hoc auxiliaries functions as evidence that an original hypothesis lacks demonstrated sufficiency.
Neither the existence nor the non-existence of intelligible entities can be established by speculative reason.
A counter-hypothesis may exhibit the incompleteness of an opponent’s appeal to empirical conditions without acquiring positive theoretical validity.
The philosopher must abandon a defensive transcendent hypothesis once the opposing dogmatic assertion is withdrawn.
The discipline of hypothesis divides reason into three non-interchangeable functions: empirical explanation, regulative systematization, and polemical self-defence.
Explanatory closure is reclassified as a methodological danger when it is achieved by appeal to a ground that terminates rather than advances inquiry.
The inability to prove transcendent claims generates a relative equality in speculative conflict rather than a licence for either affirmation or denial.
Reason’s permanent security depends not on suppressing objections but on making their strongest form visible and dissolving their source.
Transcendental fictions acquire conditional legitimacy only as instruments for preventing the conversion of empirical limitation into absolute impossibility.
The system excludes any theoretical route from a merely thinkable predicate to an objectively possible object.
The system excludes the demand that empirical explanation must culminate in an unconditioned explanatory ground.
The system excludes the inference that the absence of empirical conditions proves the impossibility of what exceeds them.
The system excludes a protected doctrine that may evade the objections it would direct against its opponent.
The system excludes the conversion of methodological usefulness into ontological proof.
No theoretical possession of transcendent reality is available to either affirmative metaphysics or its empirical negation.
No final speculative peace is available through external victory, because the adversary is the self-dividing structure of reason.
No positive knowledge of an intelligible order can be extracted from the inadequacy of sensuous explanation.
No absolute validity may attach to a hypothesis whose only role is to neutralize an opponent’s unwarranted certainty.
Speculative cognitive failure produces an apparent surplus of hypothetical freedom.
Secured object-possibility, empirical connection, and anticipatory sufficiency convert supposition into an admissible physical hypothesis.
Absence of experiential objecthood converts transcendental supposition into fiction without explanatory entitlement.
Hyperphysical explanation terminates empirical causal inquiry and is therefore methodologically excluded.
Symmetrical ignorance concerning transcendent claims permits a relative counter-hypothesis solely for defensive refutation.
Defensive counter-hypothesis is withdrawn when dogmatic opposition ceases, preventing polemic from becoming doctrine.
Reason internalizes opposition, intensifies its objections, and seeks settlement through critique rather than suppression.
The failure of speculative extension leads to the question of whether hypothesis can occupy the space left by knowledge.
The question is constrained by the distinction between empirically grounded physical hypotheses and transcendental explanatory inventions.
The exclusion of transcendental explanation leads to standards of sufficiency, predictive consequence, and suspicion toward auxiliary repair.
The prohibition on dogmatic transcendent assertion is converted into a limited right of polemical counter-supposition.
Polemical symmetry culminates in a discipline requiring reason to stage and overcome its own dialectical opposition.
The distinction between possible experience and bare thinkability becomes the boundary between legitimate hypothesis and empty invention.
The distinction between regulative ideas and constitutive objects separates systematic inquiry from metaphysical object-assertion.
The distinction between physical and hyperphysical explanation reclassifies appeals to ultimate grounds as impediments to inquiry rather than explanatory achievements.
The distinction between dogmatic proof and defensive counter-hypothesis creates a narrow polemical space without reopening speculative metaphysics.
Opposition is relocated from an external adversary to the internal dialectical operations of reason.
Surface — The text establishes conditions under which hypotheses concerning natural and transcendent matters may be used.
Structural — The possibility of objects, the authority of categories, and the scope of explanatory laws are all subordinated to possible experience.
Metastrategic — The text distinguishes inquiry from closure, defence from proof, and self-critique from merely external controversy.
Ontological/Temporal — Phenomenal existence is conditioned by space, time, and sensibility, while intelligible existence remains neither theoretically cognizable nor theoretically disprovable.
The axioms suffice to reconstruct the central restriction of hypothesis to empirically possible objects and empirically connected explanations.
The system is strongest where it distinguishes regulative use, explanatory use, and polemical use without allowing one to substitute for another.
The criterion of secured object-possibility remains dependent on prior critical doctrine concerning the limits of categories and possible experience.
The defensive use of transcendental fictions creates a controlled tension with the general prohibition on hypotheses lacking experiential objects.
The claimed equality of speculative ignorance suspends dogmatic verdicts but cannot itself determine which practical suppositions may be admitted.
The announced practical exception remains structurally necessary but is not developed within this argument.
Reconstruction preserves the argument’s movement only if polemical hypotheses remain relative, retractable, and incapable of becoming positive doctrine.

identity.title: Section III. The Discipline of Pure Reason in Hypothesis

units.title: Section IV. The Discipline of Pure Reason in Relation to Proofs

items.text: Transcendental synthetic proof must establish the objective validity of its concepts before it can establish a proposition formed from them.
The proof-problem is reframed from deriving predicates out of concepts to showing the conditions under which experience and its objects are possible.
Pure reason is disciplined by requiring a deduction of the source, right, and objective scope of every principle used in speculative proof.
The uniqueness of the conceptual condition of an object entails the uniqueness of any valid transcendental ground of proof.
Indirect proof is excluded from transcendental inquiry because subjective conditions can be mistaken for objective conditions and can invalidate both opposed propositions.
Criticism converts the failure of dogmatic proof into a restriction of speculative reason and a relocation of reason to practical principles.
A transcendental synthetic proposition requires prior proof of the objective validity of its concepts and of the possibility of their synthesis.
No cognition can pass a priori beyond a concept without a guide not contained in that concept.
Possible experience guides transcendental cognition when concepts of the understanding are in question.
A transcendental proof establishes a conceptual connection by showing that experience and its object would be impossible without it.
Principles of the understanding have validity only for objects of possible experience.
Principles of pure reason employed as objectively constitutive are dialectical and lack objective validity.
Subjective association and subjective conditions of thought can be mistaken for objective cognition.
A proof using pure ideas must first establish the possibility of the proposed synthetic extension of cognition.
A transcendental proposition has only one possible ground of proof because its concept alone determines its possible object.
A direct proof discloses the ground of a proposition’s truth, whereas an indirect proof can at most establish truth through the falsity of its opposite.
Indirect proof is valid only where subjective representation cannot be confused with objective cognition.
Where an object-conception is impossible, both its affirmative and negative predicates are equally invalid.
A transcendental deduction of the principles used is the necessary tribunal for every speculative proof.
Transcendental proof is not an immediate transition from one concept to another concept.
Conceptual simplicity in abstraction is not objective simplicity of the thing represented.
The unity of apperception is not a proof that the soul is a simple substance.
Principles of the understanding are not grounds for cognition of objects beyond possible experience.
Ideas of pure reason are not objectively valid principles of speculative cognition.
A plurality of persuasive arguments is not a plurality of valid transcendental proofs.
The falsity of a counter-proposition is not sufficient to prove a transcendental proposition.
The sensible world considered as a totality given in itself is not a coherent object of determination as either finite or infinite.
Causality is established transcendentally only as a condition under which an event can be temporally determined within experience.
A proof of a supersensible object fails unless it first justifies the possibility of extending cognition through the idea of that object.
The demand for a deduction can reject an entire class of dialectical proofs without locating the particular sophism in each proof.
Multiple proofs of the same transcendental thesis signal that none has isolated the unique objective condition determined by its concept.
An indirect disproof in transcendental inquiry may reveal only an incompatibility with subjective reason rather than an impossibility in the object.
Antinomial alternatives can both be false when they predicate opposed determinations of an object constituted by an impossible presupposition.
Speculative reason must renounce claims whose proof depends on treating regulative ideas as constitutive knowledge.
The proper object of transcendental proof is not a supersensible thing but the lawful possibility of experience as the field in which concepts acquire objective reference.
Critique changes proof from an accumulation of conclusions into a jurisdiction over the conditions under which conclusion-making can claim objectivity.
Dialectical conflict is structurally produced when reason converts the subjective demand for the unconditioned into an objective determination of things.
The discipline of proof displaces dogmatic victory over an opponent with critical determination of the admissible domain of reason.
Logical coherence of a representation is not sufficient for objective reference to an object.
The subjective necessity with which reason seeks completion is not evidence that an unconditioned object is given.
Contradictory predicates do not necessarily divide a real object into exhaustive alternatives.
Speculative reason has no self-authorizing capacity to determine what lies beyond the conditions of possible experience.
The defeat of an opposing proof is not identical with the objective establishment of its contrary.
No theoretical procedure can transform the idea of the unconditioned into cognition of an unconditioned object merely by formal inference.
No speculative proof can occupy a standpoint outside the subjective conditions whose unnoticed operation generates transcendental illusion.
The absolute totality sought by dogmatic metaphysics is unavailable as an object for determinate theoretical predication.
The final restriction of speculative reason silently forecloses the identification of rational demand with theoretical possession.
Conceptual claim → demand for objective validity → demand for possible synthesis.
Possible synthesis → identification of its guide → possible experience as the condition of objective reference.
Objective-reference condition → single legitimate transcendental ground → direct proof of the condition’s necessity.
Failure to deduce the principle’s source and right → classification as dialectical appearance → suspension of speculative assent.
Exposure of dialectical appearance → abandonment of constitutive speculative pretension → confinement of reason to regulative and practical employment.
Transcendental proposition → prior validation of concepts → possible experience as mediating ground.
Pure idea → unproved synthetic extension → paralogism or dialectical assertion.
Demand for deduction → invalidation of unsupported principles → economy of critical refutation.
Conceptual determination of an object → unique ground of proof → exposure of dogmatic proof-plurality.
Subjective-objective confusion → failure of indirect proof → necessity of ostensive procedure.
Failure of dogmatic proof → critical self-limitation → practical destination of reason.
Proof is reclassified from a relation among propositions into a demonstration of the conditions that make objective reference possible.
Causality, substance, soul, deity, and world-whole are separated according to whether their concepts can receive objective validity through possible experience.
The opposition between direct proof and refutation is reorganized: refutation becomes subordinate to prior critique of the principles used by both sides.
The apparent opposition between finite and infinite world-totality collapses when the allegedly given total object is withdrawn.
Dogmatic metaphysical controversy is redescribed as a conflict generated by shared subjective conditions rather than by rival knowledge of objects.
Surface — Transcendental propositions require special rules governing their proof, number of proofs, and permissible form of inference.
Structural — Objective cognition depends on conditions of possible experience, while dialectic arises from the misattribution of subjective conditions to objects.
Metastrategic — Critical reason does not defeat every dogmatic claim individually but tests the legitimacy of the principles from which all such claims proceed.

Ontological/Temporal — Objects are determinable only within conditions that permit experiential temporal ordering; unconditioned totalities and supersensible substances lack this theoretical mode of determination.
The axioms suffice to reconstruct the transition from proof as inference to proof as deduction of objective validity.
The structure depends principally on the distinction between subjective representation and objective cognition.
The system is coherent if possible experience is accepted as the exclusive court of objective validity for theoretical cognition.
The argument is strongest where it derives causal necessity from the possibility of temporal experience rather than from conceptual association or contingent observation.
The claim that every transcendental proposition has only one proof-ground compresses the distinction between a unique objective ground and potentially diverse valid expositions of that ground.
The transition from speculative restriction to practical reason is asserted as the final destination of discipline but is not independently derived within this section.
Reconstruction preserves the argument’s movement only if the critique of indirect proof is retained as a consequence of subjective-objective subreption rather than as a general rejection of reductio.

identity.title: Section IV. The Discipline of Pure Reason in Relation to Proofs

units.title: Chapter II. The Canon of Pure Reason

items.text: Pure reason cannot securely discover truth through speculation and therefore requires discipline against its own deviations and illusions.
Self-imposed limits both restrain reason and protect its legitimate cognitive possessions from rival claims.
The primary use of philosophy of pure reason is negative: it determines the limits of speculative employment and guards against error.
Reason nevertheless contains a positive orientation toward cognitions beyond experience, whose mischaracterization produces speculative error.
Speculative reason fails to attain its desired knowledge, whereas practical reason remains the possible site of reason’s proper employment.
A canon can govern only a faculty with a possible proper use; because speculative pure reason has no such use, its canon belongs to practical rather than speculative reason.
Pure speculative reason is incompetent to establish truth by speculation alone.
Pure reason requires discipline to restrain its deviations and expose its self-generated illusions.
The discipline of pure reason is exercised by reason itself rather than by an external authority.
The limitation of speculative claims protects whatever legitimate cognition remains from opposing usurpation.
The principal use of philosophy of pure reason is negative and consists in guarding against error.
Pure reason contains positive cognitions whose misidentified status becomes a source of error.
Human reason is oriented toward knowledge beyond the limits of possible experience.
Speculative reason cannot successfully satisfy this orientation.
A canon is a set of a priori principles governing the proper employment of a cognitive faculty.
A canon can exist only where a proper employment of the relevant faculty is possible.
The synthetic cognition of pure speculative reason is impossible.
The speculative exercise of pure reason is dialectical rather than cognitively legitimate.
The proper employment of pure reason, if it exists, belongs to its practical rather than speculative use.
Pure reason is not a self-sufficient instrument for extending knowledge through speculation.
Philosophy of pure reason is not primarily an organon for discovering new truths.
Speculative limitation is not an external suppression imposed by another cognitive authority.
Pure speculative reason is not capable of a valid synthetic canon.
Transcendental logic, insofar as it concerns speculative reason, is not a canon.
The dialectical activity of speculative reason is not a proper employment of the faculty.
The failure of speculation does not eliminate reason’s positive orientation toward supersensible cognition.
Practical reason is not treated as merely another unsuccessful route of speculation.
Because speculative reason generates illusions through its own activity, critique must function as internal self-discipline rather than as external correction.
Because limiting speculative claims removes illegitimate pretensions, critique converts restriction into protection of legitimate cognition.
Because the positive content of pure reason is misused rather than simply absent, critique must distinguish its proper character from its speculative distortion.
Because reason’s desire exceeds experience while speculation cannot satisfy it, the failure of speculative knowledge does not terminate reason’s orientation.
Because a canon presupposes a possible proper employment, the impossibility of speculative synthetic cognition excludes a speculative canon.
Because speculative reason has no legitimate synthetic use, transcendental logic can discipline its speculative activity but cannot prescribe it as a canon.
Because practical employment remains the only possible proper use of pure reason, the search for a canon must be redirected from speculation to practice.
Reason’s limitation is simultaneously epistemic restraint, internal self-government, and protection of a residual domain of legitimate cognition.
The critique of pure reason transforms failure to know beyond experience into a criterion for distinguishing legitimate from illegitimate uses of reason.
The absence of a speculative canon does not abolish rational normativity; it relocates normativity from speculative cognition to practical employment.
Pure reason is structurally divided between a negative speculative function that limits error and a possible practical function that supplies its proper positive employment.
The system preserves reason’s aspiration beyond experience by denying speculative possession of its object while retaining the aspiration as a motive for practical inquiry.
Legitimate cognition cannot be secured by unrestricted speculative confidence.
Rational autonomy does not mean unrestricted permission for reason to legislate beyond its competence.
The existence of rational concepts does not entail the possibility of speculative knowledge of their objects.
The persistence of metaphysical desire does not validate the speculative method used to satisfy it.
A faculty’s possession of cognitive content does not by itself establish a proper rule for using that content.
The failure of speculative reason cannot be interpreted as the failure of reason as such.
Practical legitimacy cannot be inferred merely from speculative aspiration; it must arise from a distinct mode of employment.
The system excludes the possibility that speculation can provide final metaphysical security on its own terms.
The system excludes an external tribunal capable of disciplining reason more fundamentally than reason’s own critique.
The system excludes the reduction of reason’s supersensible orientation to an error that can simply be discarded.
The system excludes the identity of reason’s desire for supersensible knowledge with an actual speculative possession of it.
The system leaves unavailable a positive speculative science of the supersensible while preserving the demand for a non-speculative completion of reason.
Speculative aspiration exceeds experience → speculation generates illusion → self-discipline becomes necessary.
Self-discipline limits speculative claims → illegitimate pretensions are removed → legitimate cognition is secured against attack.
Pure reason’s negative function is established → reason’s positive orientation remains unexplained by speculation alone → practical reason becomes the alternative site of fulfillment.
Canon is defined as a rule for possible proper employment → speculative synthetic cognition is declared impossible → no speculative canon can exist.
Speculative reason is classified as dialectical → transcendental logic functions as discipline rather than canon → the canon of pure reason is sought in practical employment.
Speculative incompetence → internal discipline → limitation of claims → protection of legitimate cognition.
Negative critique → persistence of supersensible aspiration → failure of speculative satisfaction → redirection toward practical reason.
Definition of canon → requirement of possible proper employment → impossibility of speculative synthesis → exclusion of a speculative canon.
Dialectical status of speculation → disciplinary role of transcendental logic → practical canon of pure reason.
The boundary of reason becomes a positive epistemic instrument rather than a mere deprivation.
Critique reclassifies philosophical success from acquiring metaphysical truths to preventing illegitimate claims.
The distinction between cognition and aspiration becomes necessary: reason may be oriented toward what speculation cannot know.
The concept of canon is separated from the general activity of critique and restricted to a faculty’s possible proper employment.
The failure of speculative metaphysics redirects the normative center of pure reason toward practical use rather than toward abandonment of reason.
Transcendental logic is repositioned as a boundary-discipline for speculative reason rather than a source of speculative extension.
Surface — Speculative reason fails to establish truth and must be disciplined by limits.
Structural — Reason’s self-critique separates legitimate cognition from dialectical overreach and distinguishes discipline from canon.
Metastrategic — Philosophical authority is relocated from the production of new speculative truths to the regulation of claims and the protection of reason’s legitimate domain.
Ontological/Temporal — Reason is constituted by an enduring orientation beyond experience whose speculative fulfillment is impossible but whose practical fulfillment remains open.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the movement from speculative failure to practical redirection.
The decisive hinge is the definition of a canon as a rule for a possible proper employment.
The system is internally coherent in distinguishing the negative task of critique from the positive possibility of practical reason.
The relation between positive cognitions and their practical status remains underdetermined within the passage.
The transition from the persistence of supersensible desire to the promise of practical reason is asserted more than demonstrated.
The argument depends on maintaining a tension between reason’s aspiration beyond experience and the impossibility of speculative access to its object.
Reconstruction preserves the real movement: speculative limitation → protection of legitimate cognition → distinction between discipline and canon → practical relocation of reason’s proper use.

identity.title: Chapter II. The Canon of Pure Reason

units.title: Section I. Of the Ultimate End of the Pure Use of Reason

items.text: Reason naturally exceeds experience in pursuit of a self-subsistent systematic unity of cognition.
The ideas of freedom, immortality, and God constitute reason’s highest speculative problems but yield no immanent knowledge of experience.
The practical interest of reason, rather than its speculative interest, supplies the real significance of these transcendent ideas.
Practical reason divides into empirically conditioned prudence and pure moral legislation determined a priori.
Moral law converts the ultimate question of reason into the question of what ought to be done under the ideas of freedom, God, and a future life.
Practical freedom is admissible through experience as reason’s causal determination of the will, while transcendental freedom remains a speculative problem excluded from the practical canon.
Reason possesses a natural drive to transcend experience and organize cognition into systematic unity.
The highest ends of reason must possess complete unity if they are to serve the highest interest of humanity.
Transcendental speculation is concentrated on freedom of the will, immortality of the soul, and the existence of God.
Transcendent ideas cannot serve as immanent principles for explaining objects of possible experience.
Experience must be explained through natural causes and unchangeable laws rather than through transcendent grounds.
The speculative cognition of freedom, immortality, and God is without practical utility for physical or empirical investigation.
The value of the cardinal transcendent ideas therefore belongs primarily to the practical interest of reason.
Practical cognition concerns what is possible through free will.
Empirically conditioned willing permits reason only a regulative role in unifying inclination-based ends and their means.
Pure practical laws are determined a priori by reason and command absolutely rather than conditionally.
Moral laws alone constitute a canon of pure practical reason.
Practical freedom consists in the will’s capacity to be determined by rational motives independently of sensuous impulses.
Experience establishes practical freedom by displaying reason as a causal power in the determination of the human will.
Transcendental freedom concerns independence from every sensuous determining cause and remains a speculative problem.
Transcendental philosophy excludes empirical psychological and affective elements because it concerns pure a priori cognition alone.
Speculative reason is not authorized to use freedom, immortality, or God as explanatory principles of experience.
Knowledge of an incorporeal soul is not positive knowledge of either present life or future life.
The existence of a supreme intelligence is not a warrant for inferring particular natural arrangements where experience does not disclose them.
Transcendent explanation is not permitted to displace natural causal explanation.
Prudential unification of happiness-seeking inclinations is not pure moral legislation.
A will determined solely by sensuous impulse is not free will but animal arbitrium.
Practical freedom is not identical with transcendental freedom.
The practical canon is not required to resolve whether rational causality itself belongs to a higher natural causal order.
Empirical feeling is not an element of transcendental philosophy.
The three cardinal ideas retain rational importance only after their theoretical employment has been converted into a practical concern.
Reason’s practical use separates conditional guidance toward happiness from unconditional moral command.
Only moral law can supply the pure practical canon because only moral law originates entirely a priori in reason.
The ultimate end of pure reason is reordered from theoretical completion to moral deliberation concerning what ought to be done.
Practical agency can be treated as rationally law-governed without settling the metaphysical origin of rational causality.
The practical canon narrows its remaining transcendent questions to God and a future life because practical freedom is already established in the relevant practical sense.
The text subordinates metaphysical speculation to morality without converting morality into a branch of empirical explanation.
The system preserves the autonomy of the practical standpoint by assigning causal explanation and moral obligation to distinct rational functions.
Reason’s demand for systematic unity survives the failure of speculative cognition by relocating final unity in the moral end of humanity.
The argument permits practical commitment to questions whose theoretical objects remain unavailable as objects of empirical cognition.
The ultimate interest of reason is not exhausted by the expansion of theoretical knowledge.
Moral obligation is not reducible to the empirical coordination of pleasure, pain, inclination, or happiness.
The legitimacy of practical law is not dependent upon a prior speculative proof of transcendental freedom.
Systematic unity is not obtainable through unrestricted metaphysical explanation of empirical phenomena.
The rational subject is not treated solely as a phenomenon governed by natural law, even though its actions as phenomena must be so explained.
No theoretical standpoint is available from which rational causality can be reconciled with the total causal order of nature.
No positive speculative cognition is available of the transcendent objects that orient reason’s highest practical questions.
No final speculative system can fulfill reason’s demand for totality without exceeding the limits of possible experience.
No empirical account of motivation can supply the unconditional authority claimed by moral law.
Natural demand for systematic totality → transcendence beyond experience through ideas.
Transcendent ideas → attempted speculative cognition of freedom, immortality, and God.
Speculative non-immanence → prohibition on using transcendent ideas to explain experience.
Speculative impotence → transfer of the ideas’ significance to practical reason.
Practical reason → division between empirical prudence and pure moral legislation.
Pure moral legislation → canon of what ought to be done.
Empirical proof of practical freedom plus suspension of transcendental freedom → restriction of the practical canon to God and future life.

Reason’s demand for totality → transcendent ideas → speculative non-usefulness → practical revaluation → distinction between prudence and moral law → moral primacy → practical freedom → suspension of transcendental freedom.
Natural-law explanation of phenomena → exclusion of transcendent causal explanation → preservation of empirical inquiry alongside practical obligation.
Sensuous determination of the will → rational resistance to impulse → practical freedom → objective laws of what ought to occur.
Freedom, immortality, and God are reclassified from possible theoretical explanations into practical objects of reason’s highest interest.
The distinction between what happens and what ought to happen redraws the boundary between natural law and practical law.
Freedom is divided into an empirically established practical capacity and a metaphysically unresolved transcendental condition.
Happiness is reclassified as the terminal end of prudence rather than the source of pure moral legislation.
The demand for systematic unity is redirected from speculative completion toward the moral end of humanity.
Surface — The text determines the ultimate end served by pure reason’s concern with freedom, immortality, and God.
Structural — The text partitions reason into speculative, empirical-practical, and pure-practical uses with distinct evidentiary and legislative powers.
Metastrategic — The text blocks metaphysical explanations of experience while preserving transcendent ideas as practically indispensable questions.

Ontological/Temporal — Human action is simultaneously treated as phenomenal nature subject to causal law and as practically attributable to rational freedom, while the reconciliation of these orders is deferred.
The axioms reconstruct the argument if the central operation is understood as a transfer of ultimate rational interest from speculation to morality.
The system remains underdetermined concerning how practical freedom can be empirically established without resolving its relation to transcendental freedom.
The system is coherent insofar as it separates empirical explanation from practical legislation rather than requiring one to derive from the other.
The system is strongest where it establishes the non-immanent status of transcendent ideas and the a priori status of moral law.
The system depends on a compression where the practical authority of moral law is asserted before the later grounding of its relation to God and future life.
Reconstruction preserves the argument’s movement only if the unresolved problem of transcendental freedom remains suspended rather than silently solved.

identity.title: Section I. Of the Ultimate End of the Pure Use of Reason

units.title: Section II. Of the Ideal of the Summum Bonum as a Determining Ground of the Ultimate End of Pure Reason

items.text: Pure reason’s highest interest requires an account of how moral obligation can authorize hope when speculative cognition cannot reach the required supersensible objects.
The argument performs a practical-transcendental deduction in which moral law, rather than theoretical knowledge, becomes the route to reason’s ultimate end.
The distinction between prudential happiness and moral worthiness separates duty from inclination while making hope a distinct rational problem.
The supreme good is defined as happiness distributed in exact proportion to moral worthiness.
Nature supplies no cognizable causal order that guarantees proportionality between virtue and happiness.
The required unity of morality and happiness therefore produces the practical hypotheses of God and future life, and thereby moral theology and teleology.
The argument closes by subordinating theology to antecedent moral law and restricting its legitimate use to immanent moral practice.
Speculative reason cannot establish theoretical knowledge of the supersensible conditions of reason’s highest ends.
Pure moral laws determine rational freedom a priori, categorically, and independently of happiness.
Happiness concerns the satisfaction of desires, whereas morality concerns worthiness to be happy.
The moral disposition must be the condition of participation in happiness, not an effect of the prospect of happiness.
The highest good requires happiness to correspond exactly with the moral worthiness of rational beings.
Natural causality cannot establish that morally worthy action will produce happiness proportionate to worthiness.
A moral world is an intelligible systematic unity of free rational beings under moral laws and a practical idea for transforming the world of sense.
The ideal of the supreme good requires a morally perfect and supremely blessed intelligence to cause happiness in proportion to moral worthiness.
God and future life are practically necessary hypotheses inseparable from the complete realization of moral obligation’s final end.
Practical necessity does not yield theoretical cognition, demonstrated dogma, or intuitive access to supersensible objects.
Moral law is prior to the representation of God and determines the sense in which divine commands can be recognized as binding.
Moral unity of ends gives natural inquiry a teleological orientation without authorizing transcendent theoretical use.
Moral theology has legitimate force only insofar as it preserves reason’s legislative authority in moral action.
The highest objects of reason are not available as speculative knowledge.
Happiness alone is not the complete good.
Morality is not prudence directed toward the acquisition of happiness.
Moral worthiness is not produced by the expectation of reward.
The moral world is not an empirically given order or an object of intelligible intuition.
Nature alone is not a sufficient ground for hope that virtue and happiness will coincide.
God and future life are not theoretical discoveries or demonstrated metaphysical objects.
Moral obligations are not binding because they are externally commanded by God.
Moral theology is not permitted to replace moral legislation with transcendent religious authority.
Moral obligation entails the practical possibility of free action and of a systematic moral unity among rational beings.
Hope is rational only as hope for happiness conditioned by prior moral worthiness rather than as expectation generated by desire.
The highest good cannot be completed within nature alone and therefore requires the practical assumption of a supersensible moral order.
The representation of a single supreme will arises from the requirement that one universal order coordinate moral laws, natural conditions, and the distribution of happiness.
Divine attributes are inferred functionally from the requirements of the highest good rather than known independently through speculative theology.
Moral theology gives nature a teleological interpretation because moral ends require nature to be thinkable as compatible with freedom.
Moral law remains the source of obligation even when reason represents morally required action as conformity with divine will.
Practical reason extends rational orientation beyond speculative limits without converting its postulates into objects of knowledge.
The three questions of reason form a hierarchy in which the unconditional “ought” governs the conditional “may I hope,” and practical necessity thereby directs speculative orientation.
The moral world has a double status: it lacks theoretical objecthood while possessing practical reality as the rule for transforming sensible conditions.
Theology is structurally dependent on autonomous morality because it is required to make the highest good thinkable yet forbidden to legislate the moral law from which it was derived.
Practical teleology totalizes nature under moral ends while withholding any theoretical warrant for asserting that this totality is known as actual.
The future becomes the temporal form of the highest good because its required harmony is absent from present sensible experience but demanded by practical reason.
No immanent empirical relation can guarantee the final coincidence of moral worth and happiness.
No desire, reward, punishment, observed consequence, or external command can constitute the ground of moral obligation.
No practical need can be converted into theoretical cognition of the object postulated to satisfy that need.
No merely natural order contains enough intrinsic teleological unity to validate the final ends of moral reason.
No plurality of independent supreme wills can secure the complete unity of ends required by the highest good.
The system is organized around the absence of any empirically accessible world in which the moral law’s ultimate end is visibly fulfilled.
Finite reason cannot close the gap between unconditional duty and conditioned happiness; it can only postulate their unifying ground.
The divine ground of the highest good is unavailable as an external source of moral authority because such a source would displace reason’s own legislation.
The complete moral order required by reason is unavailable as present knowledge and can appear only as a future intelligible horizon.
Speculative limitation removes theoretical cognition as the route to reason’s highest supersensible ends.
Pure moral law supplies an unconditional practical norm independent of inclination and empirical reward.
Moral law generates the idea of worthiness, which combines with happiness to define the highest good.
Nature fails to guarantee the required proportion between worthiness and happiness.
The failure of nature generates the practical postulation of a supreme moral cause and a future moral world.
The postulate yields moral theology and a teleological orientation of nature without producing speculative knowledge.
The priority of moral law returns as a limiting condition that prevents theology from becoming the source of obligation.

Speculative boundary → three interests of reason → categorical moral law → distinction between happiness and worthiness → highest good → natural insufficiency → God and future life as practical hypotheses → moral theology and teleology → restoration of moral autonomy through immanent use.
Happiness is reclassified from the final good to one required component of the highest good, subordinate to moral worthiness.
God and future life are reclassified from speculative objects of proof to practically necessary hypotheses of hope.
The moral world is reclassified from a possible object of knowledge to a practical idea governing the transformation of sensible life.
Theology is subordinated to morality, so divine will is interpreted through moral law rather than moral law derived from divine will.
Natural teleology is reclassified as an effect of practical reason’s demand for systematic moral ends rather than an independent proof of theology.
The relation between freedom and nature is redescribed as a coordination problem requiring a postulated unity rather than as a theoretically solved causal relation.
Surface — The text answers how one should act and what one may rationally hope after speculative reason has reached its limits.
Structural — The argument constructs the highest good by linking free moral agency, distributive happiness, natural causality, and a supreme causal ground.
Metastrategic — Practical reason gains priority over speculative reason by supplying the regulative conditions under which theology and teleology may be employed.
Ontological/Temporal — The required unity of freedom and happiness belongs to an intelligible moral order represented as future relative to sensible experience.
Juridical — Moral law retains legislative sovereignty by treating divine commands as recognizable only through independently binding rational obligation.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the movement from speculative limitation through moral law to the practical postulation of the highest good.
The system depends on the unproven transition from the practical need for proportional happiness to the assumption of a supreme causal ground capable of realizing it.
The structure remains coherent only if practical necessity and theoretical cognition are held apart as different modalities of rational validity.
A persistent tension arises because moral law is declared independently binding while the complete efficacy of moral maxims is said to require God and a future world.
A second tension arises because the unity and attributes of a sole supreme being are functionally required by moral teleology but cannot be independently known by speculative reason.
The architecture is most determinate at the sequence moral law → worthiness → highest good → postulate, where each transition performs a distinct structural function.
Reconstruction preserves the argument’s real movement only if the final restriction on transcendent theology is retained as constitutive rather than appended.

identity.title: Section II. Of the Ideal of the Summum Bonum as a Determining Ground of the Ultimate End of Pure Reason

units.title: Section III. Of Opinion, Knowledge, and Belief

items.text: Holding a proposition true must be divided according to whether its ground is objectively sufficient for every rational being or merely subjectively compelling for an individual.
The possibility of universal communication functions as the external test that distinguishes conviction from private persuasion.
The degrees of holding true are ordered by subjective and objective sufficiency into opinion, belief, and knowledge.
Where theoretical certainty is unavailable, belief can be legitimate only insofar as an idea is required for practical or regulative rational guidance.
Moral obligation transforms belief in God and a future life from a speculative hypothesis into morally necessary subjective certainty.
Critique limits transcendent knowledge while preserving universally available practical orientation beyond experience.
Holding a proposition true has both objective grounds and subjective causes.
A judgement is conviction when its ground is objectively sufficient for every rational being.
A judgement is persuasion when it rests on the particular character of the judging subject.
Truth consists in agreement of judgement with its object.
Judgements that agree with an object must be mutually communicable and mutually consistent.
