Reconstruction preserves the argument’s real movement only if the missing-shade anomaly and the deferred theory of causation remain explicit structural fault lines.

identity.title: Sect. I. Of The Origin Of Our Ideas

units.title: Sect. II. Division Of The Subject

items.text: The argument is classificatory, genealogical, and methodological.
The problem is to determine the proper order for examining impressions and ideas.
The general priority of simple impressions over correspondent ideas initially requires impressions-first inquiry.
The division of impressions into sensation and reflection replaces undifferentiated priority with a stratified genealogy.
The operative sequence is sensation → idea-copy → reflective impression → reflective idea → possible recurrence.
Because sensations are disciplinarily deferred and reflective impressions mostly arise from ideas, the inquiry must begin with ideas.
Simple impressions generally precede their correspondent ideas, notwithstanding rare exceptions.
Impressions divide into impressions of sensation and impressions of reflection.
Impressions of sensation arise originally in the soul from unknown causes.
An idea is a mental copy that remains after its originating impression ceases.
Returned ideas of pleasure and pain produce desire, aversion, hope, and fear as impressions of reflection.
Memory and imagination copy impressions of reflection into correspondent ideas.
Resulting ideas may generate further impressions and ideas.
An impression of reflection is posterior to and derived from sensation while antecedent to its own correspondent idea.
Passions, desires, and emotions are the principal objects of the present inquiry.
Impressions of reflection arise mostly from ideas.
Examination of sensations belongs to anatomy and natural philosophy rather than the present moral inquiry.
Method requires the operative antecedents of the focal object to be examined before that object.
Ideas are not ordinarily prior to their correspondent simple impressions.
The original causes of sensory impressions are not known.
Impressions of reflection are not original sensory occurrences.
Reflective impressions are not prior to the sensations from which they derive.
Ideas are not causally inert copies; returned ideas can produce new impressions.
The present inquiry is not an anatomical or natural-philosophical investigation of sensation.
General impression-priority does not require every kind of impression to precede ideas in the order of exposition.
Impressions-first inquiry is the default method when simple impressions and their correspondent ideas are considered without further division.
Priority cannot be assigned uniformly to impressions as an undifferentiated class.
Ideas mediate the derivation of reflective impressions from sensory impressions.
The copy relation can enter a recursive production sequence rather than terminate in a single idea.
Sensations can be deferred without abandoning the principal objects of the inquiry.
Ideas must be examined before the reflective impressions principally under investigation.
Ideas are derivative relative to sensation but productive relative to reflection.
Temporal priority is relational: each item may be posterior to one stratum while anterior to another.
The methodological reversal changes the relevant reference class rather than contradicting the priority of simple impressions.
The perception-chain is recursively extensible but asymmetrically grounded in sensation.
Moral inquiry begins from an intermediate representational mechanism while leaving the ultimate sensory origin unexplained.
Explanation of reflective life must not require prior resolution of the unknown causes of sensation.
The principal reflective impressions cannot be predominantly independent of antecedent ideas.
Chronological firstness alone cannot determine method once the object and disciplinary scope are restricted.
Rare exceptions must not invalidate the general precedence of simple impressions.
Recursive production must not be mistaken for a self-originating circle detached from sensation.
A complete account of the first cause of perception is unavailable within the system.
A purely immediate and representation-free account of passion is foreclosed as the primary moral model.
A single invariant order governing every relation between impressions and ideas is inadmissible.
Exceptionless closure is withheld by the qualifiers governing priority, derivation, and recurrence.
General precedence: simple impression → correspondent idea → default impressions-first method.
Class division: impression → sensation or reflection.
Genetic sequence: unknown cause → sensory impression → idea-copy → returned pleasure-or-pain idea → reflective impression.
Recursive extension: reflective impression → memory-or-imagination copy → reflective idea → possible further impression or idea.
Scope filter: sensation → anatomy and natural philosophy; reflection → present moral inquiry.
Local methodological output: ideas as antecedents of reflection → ideas-first exposition.
General impression-priority → division of impressions → stratified genealogy → relative-priority correction → disciplinary exclusion of sensation → concentration on reflection → ideas-first method.
“Impression” is reclassified from a uniform category into kinds distinguished by origin and dependency.
“Idea” is reclassified as both a copy of an antecedent impression and a cause of subsequent reflective impressions.
Priority becomes indexed to a specific correspondence and genealogical stratum rather than assigned absolutely to a whole class.
Order of exposition is detached from absolute origin and governed by the dependencies of the selected object.
Surface: impressions are divided, and ideas are selected as the starting point of inquiry.
Structural: copying and return mediate a recursive sequence between sensation, idea, reflection, and further ideas.
Metastrategic: disciplinary jurisdiction converts the natural impressions-first order into an ideas-first method.
Ontological/Temporal: perception has an unknown sensory origin, layered temporal precedence, and recursively productive mediation.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the classification, genealogy, and methodological reversal.
The causes of sensation and the rare exceptions to impression-priority remain underdetermined.
The mechanism by which an idea “returns” and produces reflection is asserted rather than explained.
The structure is coherent if genetic order, correspondent order, and expository order remain distinct.
The strongest inferential joint is the derivation of ideas-first inquiry from the idea-dependence of the focal reflective impressions.
The principal fault line is that sensation supplies the indispensable foundation while being excluded from present analysis.
The argument depends on compressed qualifiers—rarely, mostly, and perhaps—that prevent universal closure.
Reconstruction preserves the real movement only if the final reversal is treated as local and methodological rather than as a denial of sensory precedence.

identity.title: Sect. II. Division Of The Subject

units.title: Sect. III. Of The Ideas Of The Memory And Imagination

items.text: The problem is to distinguish memory from imagination when both consist of impressions returning as ideas.
The argument is empirical-taxonomic and reconstructive: experienced differences among ideas are assigned to distinct faculties.
Both faculties remain subject to a common antecedent-impression constraint.
The first differential is vivacity: memory retains considerable force, whereas imagination loses it.
The second differential is relational fidelity: memory conserves original form and order, whereas imagination can transpose them.
Imaginative liberty is generated from copy-dependence combined with distinction, separability, and simple-complex composition.
The movement is recurrence → common origin → force distinction → order distinction → combinatorial explanation.
A previously present impression can later reappear in the mind as an idea.
Every idea is copied from a corresponding impression.
Memory repeats an impression as an idea retaining a considerable degree of its original vivacity.
Imagination repeats an impression as an idea after its original vivacity has been lost.
Proper memory preserves the original form, order, and position of its objects.
A departure in recollection from the original arrangement arises from defect or imperfection in memory.
Imagination is free to transpose and change copied ideas.
No two impressions are perfectly inseparable.
Any difference perceived by imagination among ideas permits their separation.
Ideas are divided into simple and complex forms.
Neither memory nor imagination can supply an idea without a prior corresponding impression.
Memory is not free to alter the original relations among remembered objects.
Imagination is not bound to reproduce the original conjunction or order of impressions.
Imaginative freedom is not the creation of unprecedented simple ideas.
An altered order of exposition is not an altered remembered order when the original positions remain acknowledged.
Memory and imagination differ by mode of recurrence rather than by the origin of their contents. (from Axioms CH_THN_SIIM:A1 + CH_THN_SIIM:A2 + CH_THN_SIIM:A3 + CH_THN_SIIM:A4)
Memory ideas are more forceful, lively, distinct, and stable than imagination ideas. (from Axioms CH_THN_SIIM:A3 + CH_THN_SIIM:A4)
Memory’s characteristic work is preservation of relational order and position rather than preservation of simple contents as such. (from Axioms CH_THN_SIIM:A2 + CH_THN_SIIM:A5 + CH_THN_SIIM:A10)
Deliberate narrative reordering remains compatible with memory when due positions are retained. (from Axioms CH_THN_SIIM:A5 + CH_THN_SIIM:A6)
Imagination can form unexperienced complexes by separating and rearranging impression-derived components. (from Axioms CH_THN_SIIM:A2 + CH_THN_SIIM:A7 + CH_THN_SIIM:A9 + CH_THN_SIIM:A10)
Perceived difference becomes compositional liberty because distinguishable components are separable rather than necessarily conjoined. (from Axioms CH_THN_SIIM:A7 + CH_THN_SIIM:A8 + CH_THN_SIIM:A9)
Mental recurrence is organized along two axes—vivacity and relational fidelity—rather than by differences in elemental source.
Memory conserves experienced temporal and positional order, while imagination releases copied contents from that order.
Imagination is dependent at the level of elements but free at the level of arrangement.
The faculty boundary is maintained asymmetrically: mnemonic disorder counts as failure, while imaginative disorder counts as successful liberty.
Copy-dependence is not relational determinism; derivation from impressions does not require preservation of their conjunctions.
A component idea’s identity is not constituted by the complex whole in which its impression originally appeared.
Distinguishability cannot coexist with an unbreakable necessary union among ideas.
Mnemonic variation cannot count as an equally proper mode of memory without dissolving the fidelity criterion.
Absolute mental spontaneity is unavailable: productivity begins only after impression-given materials.
Necessary continuity between experienced world-order and thinkable world-order is foreclosed.
Mixed cases in which vivacity and order-fidelity point toward different faculties remain unformalized.
Independent access to the original arrangement by which mnemonic fidelity is judged is absent from the system.
Present impression → later recurrence as corresponding idea.
Recurrence with considerable retained vivacity → memory → force, distinctness, and relative stability.
Recurrence after loss of original vivacity → imagination → faintness and instability.
Preservation of original form, order, and position → proper memory; altered remembered order → mnemonic defect.
Perceived difference + absence of perfect inseparability → separable idea-components.
Separable components + simple-complex composition → transposition and changed conjunction.
Copy-fixed elements + variable arrangement → imaginative fiction without novel elemental content.

Experienced return of impressions as ideas → bifurcation by vivacity → common copy constraint → bifurcation by fidelity to original order → memory as positional conservation → imagination as transposition → separability as the ground of fiction.
Ideas are reclassified from a homogeneous derivative class into faculties differentiated by force and operation.
Common provenance is separated from divergent treatment: identical source materials can support conservation or recombination.
Memory is reclassified as an archive of relations and positions rather than merely a repository of simple ideas.
Imaginative liberty is localized in arrangement rather than in the origination of content.
Unnatural fictional objects become evidence of recombination rather than exceptions to impression-origin.
Surface: Memory and imagination are distinguished by vivacity and fidelity to original arrangement.
Structural: The mind applies conservation or separation-recombination to common impression-derived materials.
Metastrategic: The faculty distinction is secured by coding mnemonic variation as defect and fictional anomaly as lawful recombination.
Ontological/Temporal: Ideas are posterior copies; memory preserves experienced succession and position, while imagination detaches contents from that succession without escaping derivation.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the two faculties, their dual criteria, and the bounded liberty of imagination.
The vivacity threshold remains underdetermined; memory is both an idea and intermediate between impression and fully diminished idea.
The relation between vivacity and order-fidelity is unspecified, leaving mixed cases unresolved.
The structure is coherent if copy-dependence governs elements while separability governs arrangements.
The tightest inference is the derivation of novel complexes from copied but rearrangeable components.
The memory principle depends on compressed appeal to common phenomena rather than an independent derivation.
The move from perceived difference and non-inseparability to easy separation is asserted without specifying limits.
Mnemonic fidelity lacks an independent standard for recovering original order, while the classification of deviations as defects partially insulates the principle.
Reconstruction from this system preserves the text’s movement from experiential recurrence through dual differentiation to combinatorial closure.

identity.title: Sect. III. Of The Ideas Of The Memory And Imagination

units.title: Sect. IV. Of The Connexion Or Association Of Ideas

items.text: The central problem is how freely separable and recombinable ideas nevertheless form regular sequences and complexes.
Uniformity requires universal associative principles that guide imagination without determining it.
The argument is empirical, reconstructive, taxonomic, and methodologically anti-speculative.
Free combination → inadequacy of chance → non-necessary associative force → three relational operators.
Direct association expands into attenuated relational chains, with causation extending from production to power and social influence.
Inquiry terminates at original qualities of human nature and redirects itself from unknown causes to complex ideational effects.
Every simple idea is separable and recombinable by imagination.
The regular recurrence of simple ideas in complex formations requires a universal bond rather than chance.
Association is a gentle prevailing tendency that introduces one idea through another without compelling the transition.
Resemblance, contiguity in time or place, and cause and effect are the three associative qualities.
Resemblance alone is sufficient to facilitate an imaginative transition.
Custom transfers the regular contiguity of sensory succession into the imagination’s method of transition.
Cause and effect produce the strongest and most extensive associative relation.
Association propagates through relational intermediaries while weakening at each remove.
Causal association includes the production of an object’s existence, action, or motion.
A power to produce action establishes causal relation because its exertion through will remains possible and often probable.
Relations of interest, duty, government, and subordination arise from powers by which persons influence one another.
Associative cohesion supplies within imagination the role played by inseparable connexion within memory.
The causes of associative attraction are mostly unknown and terminate here in original qualities of human nature.
Once a principle is experimentally established, inquiry should examine its effects rather than pursue obscure ultimate causes.
Complex ideas, as the common objects of thought and reasoning, generally arise from associative union among simple ideas.
Complex ideas divide into relations, modes, and substances.
Association is not an inseparable or necessary connexion.
Association is not a condition without which imagination becomes unable to join ideas.
Regular ideational composition is not attributable to chance alone.
Associative connexion is not confined to objects standing in an immediate relation.
Causation is not restricted to actual production or to the production of existence.
The theory does not claim to explain the ultimate causes of associative principles.
Philosophical inquiry should not continue into obscure and uncertain speculation after experimental sufficiency is reached.
Mental order is compatible with combinatorial freedom because association governs probabilistically rather than necessarily.
Correspondence among languages follows from shared associative tendencies toward similar complex formations.
Relational proximity is inversely proportional to the number of intermediaries, making kinship distance representable as causal-chain length.
Social offices and hierarchies become associatively causal wherever positional power can be converted into another person’s action.
Association is admissible as an experimentally supported original principle even when its underlying mechanism remains unknown.
The investigation must proceed from the associative mechanism to the classes of complex ideas it generates.
The imagination is neither mechanically determined nor randomly discontinuous; it is free under recurrent natural tendencies.
The ideational field forms an attenuating network in which relation type and relational distance jointly regulate recall.
Causation becomes a bridge between natural production, counterfactual capacity, and institutional authority.
A science of mind can map the production of complex thought through observable associative effects without possessing an ultimate metaphysics of mental connexion.
Radical cross-contextual idiosyncrasy in the succession of ideas must be false.
The opposition between necessary determination and pure chance must be false.
No independent fourth principle may be required to explain ordinary associative transitions.
Relational force cannot remain unchanged across indefinitely extended mediation.
Social interest and duty cannot require an irreducibly normative bond wholly outside causal power.
Adequate empirical explanation cannot depend upon access to the ultimate mechanism of every observed principle.
The system is organized around the absence of necessary mental connexion, whose functional place is occupied by gentle attraction.
The origin of associative attraction remains unavailable; “original qualities of human nature” names the terminal explanatory absence.
The possibility of further primitive associative sources is excluded by the triadic taxonomy without being independently refuted.
The nature of causation remains deferred even while causation carries the greatest explanatory scope within the chapter.
Free separability and recombination + recurrent complex formations → demand for a non-random ordering principle.
Ordering without compulsion → gentle associative force.
Associative force → resemblance / contiguity / cause and effect.
Immediate relation + intermediary relations → extended but progressively weakened associative chains.
Causal production → action and existence → power to produce → social influence and hierarchy.
Observable effects + unknown ultimate causes → methodological arrest at original human qualities.
Associative cohesion → complex ideas → relations / modes / substances.

Freedom of combination → recurrent uniformity → insufficiency of chance → gentle universal association → triadic operators → mediated attenuation → causal expansion into power → methodological limit → taxonomy of complex effects.
Imagination is reclassified from an arbitrary combinatorial faculty into a free faculty regulated by natural tendencies.
Necessary connexion and random succession cease to exhaust the possible models of mental order.
Ideational connexion becomes graded and transmissible rather than merely present or absent.
Causation expands from actual event-production to latent power and institutional command.
Complex ideas become generated effects of associative operations rather than primitive mental units.
Philosophical explanation is redirected from inaccessible origins toward experimentally observable effects.
Surface: One idea regularly recalls another, and simple ideas regularly form complexes.
Structural: Three relational operators organize transitions through direct and attenuated chains.
Metastrategic: The inquiry expands causation into social power while restricting philosophy to experimentally warranted effects.
Ontological/Temporal: Human nature supplies universal but non-necessary tendencies, while sensory succession and custom sediment spatial-temporal order into imagination.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the chapter’s central account of regularity within a freely combinatorial imagination.
The core structure is coherent insofar as gentle tendency mediates between necessity and chance.
The exhaustiveness and universality of the three associative relations remain underdetermined rather than demonstrated.
Causation is assigned maximal explanatory force before its own nature is examined.
Contiguity is explained through acquired custom, while associative causes are classified as original qualities; the relation between acquisition and originality remains unresolved.
The argument is strongest in its graded model of mediated association and its separation of regularity from necessity.
Its extension into social relations depends on compressing interest, duty, authority, and obedience into causal power.
Reconstruction from this system preserves the movement from combinatorial freedom through associative regulation to complex ideational effects.

identity.title: Sect. IV. Of The Connexion Or Association Of Ideas

units.title: Sect. III. Of The Other Qualities Of Our Idea Of Space And Time

items.text: Problem — Determine the impression-origin and internal composition of the ideas of space and time.
Thesis — Space and time are not distinct impressions but ordered manners in which sensible or perceptual contents appear.
Argument type — Empiricist genealogy joined to eliminative, separability, and compositional tests.
Spatial movement — Sensible points → disposition → extension → abstraction across variable sensible qualities.
Temporal movement — Successive perceptions → noncoexistent order → duration → exclusion of time without change.
Closure — Indivisible spatial and temporal components remain conceivable only when filled by sensible quality or real existence.
Every idea is preceded by a correspondent impression that it copies.
Only sight and touch supply impressions from which extension can be derived.
An extended sensible impression consists of indivisible colored or tangible points disposed in a determinate order.
Every abstract idea is a particular idea considered under a shared aspect and attached to a general term.
The idea of time originates in the succession of perceptions of every kind.
Time is the manner in which successive perceptions appear, not an additional impression.
The parts of duration are noncoexistent.
The parts of extension are coexistent.
Whatever is different is distinguishable.
Whatever is distinguishable is separable in idea.
What is not distinguishable cannot be separated in idea.
An idea can properly represent only the objects or impressions from which it derives.
The compound ideas of extension and duration resolve into simple indivisible component ideas.
A real compound idea cannot be composed of nonentities.
An indivisible spatial point is conceivable only through retained color or tangibility.
The idea of extension is not derived from passions, emotions, desires, or aversions.
Extension is not an impression additional to colored or tangible points and their disposition.
An abstract idea is not an indeterminate or contentless universal.
Time cannot appear to the mind alone.
A steady and unchangeable object cannot originate the idea of time.
Time is neither an additional sensation nor an additional impression of reflection.
Duration cannot properly be predicated of an unchangeable object without fiction.
A simple spatial point is neither itself extended nor a nonentity.
A point deprived of every visible or tangible quality is unavailable to thought.
The idea of extension copies sensible points together with their relative disposition.
Abstract extension suppresses variable sensible peculiarities only while retaining their shared disposition in a particular sensible representation.
One abstract idea of extension can represent both visible and tangible configurations because their parts share a disposition.
Abstract time ranges over sensations, reflections, impressions, and ideas while remaining represented by a determinate succession.
Without successive perceptions there is no notion of time, even where objects undergo real succession.
Apparent duration varies with the rate and discriminability of successive perceptions.
Coexistence and noncoexistence provide the constitutive distinction between extension and duration.
Time may be abstracted from particular successive objects but cannot be separated from some succession of objects.
Applying duration to an unchangeable object exceeds the impression from which duration derives and is therefore fictional.
The indivisible component of extension must be qualitatively sensible rather than extended or nonexistent.
No idea of space or extension remains when all visible and tangible content is removed.
An indivisible moment must be filled by a real object or existence whose succession makes duration conceivable.
Space and time are higher-order arrangements of content rather than additional contents: space orders coexistent sensible points, while time orders successive existences.
Abstract universality is representational rather than imagistic: a determinate particular represents heterogeneous cases through selective regard and general denomination.
Experienced temporality is constrained by the mind’s resolution and rate of perception rather than determined immediately by objective succession.
Pure spatial and temporal minima are conceptually unavailable because every minimum must retain sensible quality or existential filling.
The genealogy of an idea functions as a limit on its legitimate application: predication cannot properly outrun the originating impression.
Space and time cannot be innate or independently given ideas.
Repeated contemplation cannot generate a new simple idea unless a new original impression occurs.
Abstraction cannot remove every particular determination while leaving a positive idea intact.
A manner of appearance cannot be reified as an additional constituent of what appears.
Common linguistic application cannot establish conceptual legitimacy independently of impression-origin.
Objective occurrence alone cannot furnish an idea when the corresponding order is not perceivable.
Pure empty spatiality is the absent object around which the spatial argument is organized.
Bare duration without successive existence is excluded from possible conception.
Absolute time capable of measuring changeless being is foreclosed except as fiction.
Direct cognitive access to space or time independently of perceptual content is unavailable to the system.
Copy principle → impression audit → elimination of reflective sources → restriction to sight and touch.
Sensible minima → relative disposition → compound extension → spatial idea.
Recurrent disposition across variable qualities → selective omission → particular representative → abstract space.
Heterogeneous perceptions → perceivable succession → noncoexistent order → temporal idea.
Absence of distinct temporal impression → non-distinguishability → non-separability from succession.
Genetic restriction → absence of temporal source in changeless objects → fictional application of duration.
Compound decomposition → indivisible component → exclusion of nonentity → sensible or existential filling.

Copy principle → source elimination → spatial derivation → abstraction mechanism → temporal derivation → separability test → exclusion of changeless duration → indivisible-component test → content-filled space and time.
Space is reclassified from an independent receptacle into the disposition of visible or tangible minima.
Time is reclassified from an independent medium into the perceivable succession of changing contents.
Abstraction is reclassified from production of a contentless universal into selective use of a particular idea.
Coexistence and noncoexistence replace independent substances as the primary distinction between space and time.
Changeless duration and qualityless spatial points are relocated from proper ideas to fiction or nonconception.
Questions concerning space and time are made answerable through impression-tracing rather than through unrestricted metaphysical postulation.
Surface — The immediate inquiry identifies the impressions and component qualities represented by ideas of extension and duration.
Structural — Copying, abstraction, separability, and decomposition govern the formation and limits of both ideas.
Metastrategic — Conceptual disputes are adjudicated by tracing ideas to impressions and rejecting applications that exceed that genealogy.
Ontological/Temporal — Spatiality and temporality become orders of existent content: coexistence for sensible points and succession for changing objects.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the parallel genealogies of extension and duration.
The claim that the senses present only sensible points and their disposition is asserted phenomenologically rather than independently demonstrated.
The terminal argument depends on the prior establishment of indivisible component ideas.
Internal coherence is strongest where the copy principle, absence of a distinct impression, and inseparability test converge.
The exact-copy principle strains against abstraction: abstract extension omits determinate color while every spatial representative must retain color or tangibility.
Temporal abstraction separates time from particular perceptions while denying its separation from some perceptions; the type-token mechanism remains compressed.
The denial of duration to changeless objects depends on treating genetic origin as a binding semantic limit.
The argument establishes conditions of conception more securely than conditions of independent existence; its closing language partially compresses that distinction.
Reconstruction preserves the chapter’s movement only if spatial disposition and temporal succession remain parallel but nonidentical structures.

identity.title: Sect. III. Of The Other Qualities Of Our Idea Of Space And Time

units.title: Sect. VI. Of The Idea Of Existence, And Of External Existence

items.text: Problem: determine the origin and content of the ideas of existence and external existence.
Argument type: empiricist genealogy conducted through an exhaustive dilemma, elimination, and conceptual boundary test.
The impression-copy principle and the universal conception of perceptions as existent force existence to be either a distinct accompanying perception or identical with the object conceived.
The absence of a distinct impression inseparably accompanying every perception eliminates the first alternative.
Existence is identical with the idea of the object and adds nothing to its conceived content.
Because only perceptions are present to the mind, no positive idea can represent an existence specifically different from perceptions.
Impression-origin test → exhaustive dilemma → elimination of distinct existence-content → identity thesis → perceptual closure → relative conception of externality.
Every idea arises from a similar antecedent impression.
Every impression or idea available to consciousness or memory is conceived as existent.
No distinct impression is inseparably conjoined with every perception.
The idea of existence is identical with the idea of the object conceived as existent.
A distinction without real difference requires one simple idea to bear different resemblance-relations to other ideas.
Nothing is present to the mind except perceptions: impressions and ideas.
External objects are known only through the perceptions they occasion.
An external object supposed specifically different from perceptions can be conceived only relatively, without comprehension of its intrinsic nature.
External objects are ordinarily differentiated from perceptions by attributed relations, connections, and durations rather than by a specifically different content.
Existence is not derived from a distinct impression attached to every perception.
Existence is not an additional quality inserted into an object-idea.
Reflecting on an object simply is not distinct from reflecting on it as existent.
Existence cannot be rescued as a distinction without difference, because presented objects supply no differential resemblance with respect to existence.
Loving, hating, thinking, feeling, and seeing are not modes of mental presence beyond perception.
No specifically extra-perceptual kind of existence can be positively represented.
Directing attention outward does not move conception beyond the universe of perceptions.
Relative reference to external objects is not comprehension of those objects.
Conscious awareness supplies the maximal idea and assurance of being available within the argument.
The idea of existence must arise either from a distinct impression universally conjoined with perception or from the perception itself.
The distinct-impression alternative fails, leaving identity between existence and the conceived object.
Conjoining existence with an object-idea produces no conceptual enlargement.
No contrast class permits existence to function as a distinction of reason.
Every positive conception remains composed of perceptual content already available within the mind.
Knowledge of external objects is necessarily mediated and cannot become direct presence of those objects to the mind.
Externality is available either as an uncomprehended relative correlate or as a redistribution of relations, connections, and durations.
Being functions at the conceptual level as the universal status of presentation rather than as discriminating content.
Conceivability guarantees existence-as-conceived but supplies no additional content establishing independent external actuality.
Positive ontology is bounded by the inventory of possible perceptions; whatever exceeds that inventory cannot be conceived according to its specific nature.
External realism remains thinkable only through mediation, relational attribution, or an intrinsically unfilled correlate.
An intellectual idea of being independent of impressions is excluded.
Existence cannot be both universally attached to perceptions and positively distinguishable from them.
Presented objects cannot differ in kind merely through possession or absence of conceived existence.
Attention and imagination cannot generate access to a domain specifically heterogeneous to perception.
Merely positing a specifically different external object cannot generate positive content for that object.
The requirement that relative reference comprehend its relatum is excluded by the permitted conception of external existence.
The positive essence of mind-independent being is the governing absence: external existence is retained only where intrinsic comprehension is withdrawn.
No bare existential marker separates an imagined object from an independently existing object.
No representational passage connects the perceptual universe to a positively conceived heterogeneous realm.
The external source said to occasion perceptions remains named through relation but unavailable as a comprehended kind of being.
The intrinsic nature of external objects remains neither positively affirmable nor eliminable within the chapter’s conceptual resources.
Copy principle + universal existential conception → exhaustive origin dilemma.
Candidate universal existence-impression → test for distinctness and inseparability → failure.
Elimination of distinct impression → identity of existence with object-conception → zero conceptual addition.
Proposed distinction without difference → differential-resemblance test → absence of an existence contrast class → rejection.
Perceptions alone present + ideas copied from prior perceptions → closure of positive conception within perception.
Specifically different external object posited → no qualitative comprehension → relative idea only.
Ordinary external attribution → altered relations, connections, and durations → no specifically different object-content.

Question of existence-content → impression-origin dilemma → elimination of a distinct existence-impression → identity and non-addition → rejection of distinction by resemblance → perception-only horizon → impossibility of specifically external conception → relative or relational externality.
Existence is reclassified from a detachable predicate or quality into identity with conceived content.
Existential predication loses the power to enlarge an idea or distinguish kinds of conceived objects.
The internal/external distinction is displaced from specific qualitative difference to mediation and relational organization.
The universe of imagination becomes the boundary of all positive conceptual content.
External-object discourse divides into comprehensible relations and an incomprehensible related term.
Surface: the chapter determines what the ideas of existence and external existence contain and from which impressions they derive.
Structural: the copy principle, separability test, and perception-only presence rule regulate admissible concepts.
Metastrategic: metaphysical claims are converted into demands for an originating impression, with unsupported positive content eliminated.

Ontological/Temporal: being adds no further essence to conceived objects, while external objects are ordinarily differentiated through relations, connections, and durations rather than through a separately conceived ontological kind.
CH_THN_SVIE:A1 through CH_THN_SVIE:A9 are sufficient to reconstruct both the existence argument and its extension to external existence.
The legitimacy of a relative idea whose relatum cannot be positively conceived remains underdetermined.
The structure is internally coherent if the copy principle, perceptual presence rule, and separability test are granted.
The strongest operation is the elimination of a distinct existence-impression through the demand for a universal inseparable source.
The argument compresses the difference between existence-as-conceived and independent actuality into an unresolved shift in the use of “existent.”
The claim that external objects occasion perceptions invokes a causal relation to the very term whose specific nature cannot be conceived.
Because existence adds nothing to an idea, the criterion distinguishing fiction from external actuality is unavailable within this chapter.
Reconstruction preserves the movement from conceptual genealogy through eliminative identity to the negative boundary of external conception.

identity.title: Sect. VI. Of The Idea Of Existence, And Of External Existence

units.title: Sect. VII. Of The Nature Of The Idea Or Belief

items.text: Central problem: belief contains an object-idea yet exceeds mere conception; its surplus must be identified without adding representational content.
Scope: matter-of-fact assent, whose contrary remains conceivable, rather than demonstrative determination.
Elimination: neither existence nor belief contributes a distinct idea or changes the composition of the object-idea.
Argument type: diagnostic elimination → phenomenological reconstruction → taxonomic revision.
Core thesis: belief is an idea conceived with superior force, vivacity, firmness, or steadiness through relation to a present impression.
Direction: conception–belief gap → content invariance → modal difference → intensive definition → collapse of the scholastic taxonomy → experiential confirmation.
The idea of an object is necessary but insufficient for belief in that object.
Conceiving an object as existent adds nothing to the simple conception of the object.
Believing an object to exist adds no idea and changes no part of the object-idea.
Both sides of a question concerning matter of fact remain intelligibly conceivable.
Intuition and demonstration determine conception by rendering the contrary unintelligible.
Believer and disbeliever can understand a proposition through the same constituent ideas.
Factual opinion requires a principle that fixes one conceivable alternative as the object of assent.
Because the fixing principle adds no idea, it can alter only the manner of conception.
All mental perceptions are impressions or ideas, distinguished only by degrees of force and vivacity.
Ideas copy impressions and represent their constituent parts.
An idea can vary while representing the same object only through a change in force and vivacity.
Belief is a strong, lively, and steady idea related or associated with a present impression.
Matter-of-fact inference requires a perception present to sense or memory as its foundation.
The transition from a present perception to a believed idea is determined by custom or association, not reason.
Superior force gives believed ideas greater presence, weight, persistence, and influence over passion, imagination, and action.
Conception, judgment, and reasoning resolve into different ways of conceiving objects rather than compositionally distinct acts.
The distinctive manner of belief is ultimately given as a feeling that philosophical vocabulary can only approximate.
Belief is not the mere possession or comprehension of an object-idea.
Existence is not a separable idea added as a predicate to an object.
Assent does not add ideas to the proposition assented to.
Matter-of-fact belief is not demonstrative necessity.
Disbelief is not an inability to understand or conceive the rejected proposition.
Judgment does not necessarily consist in uniting or separating two distinct ideas.
Reasoning does not necessarily require a third idea mediating between two others.
Imaginative recombination and circumstantial completeness cannot by themselves produce belief.
Belief and fiction are not distinguished by the nature, number, or order of their represented parts.
From CH_THN_SVNI:A2 + CH_THN_SVNI:A3 + CH_THN_SVNI:A6: bare conception, existential conception, and existential belief can preserve identical object-content.
From CH_THN_SVNI:A4 + CH_THN_SVNI:A5 + CH_THN_SVNI:A6: factual assent cannot be identified by contradiction, intelligibility, or semantic content.
From CH_THN_SVNI:A7 + CH_THN_SVNI:A8 + CH_THN_SVNI:A11: the principle fixing opinion must operate through scalar intensification rather than representational modification.
From CH_THN_SVNI:A2 + CH_THN_SVNI:A16: existential judgments can contain only one object-idea, invalidating the universal model of judgment as the union of two ideas.
From CH_THN_SVNI:A13 + CH_THN_SVNI:A14 + CH_THN_SVNI:A16: causal inference can pass directly from a present perception to a correlative idea without an interposed third idea.
From CH_THN_SVNI:A12 + CH_THN_SVNI:A15: belief distinguishes experienced reality from fiction by cognitive weight and practical influence despite representational identity.
From CH_THN_SVNI:A9 + CH_THN_SVNI:A11 + CH_THN_SVNI:A12: belief is not a third species of perception but an idea intensified toward the condition of an impression.
From CH_THN_SVNI:A12 + CH_THN_SVNI:A17: force, vivacity, solidity, firmness, and steadiness are approximate names for one felt mode rather than separate constituents of belief.
The experienced distinction between fact and fiction is relocated from representational content to the felt intensity and stability of conception.
Conceptual enrichment cannot convert the possible into the actual because actuality contributes no detachable representational content.
The architecture of understanding becomes operationally monistic: conception is the base act, differentiated by necessity, association, and intensity.
Matter-of-fact commitment depends on present experiential anchoring and associative determination rather than insight into necessary connection.
The epistemic authority and practical efficacy of belief arise from the same intensification that makes an idea persistent and action-governing.
The system excludes an independent faculty of judgment that stamps truth onto an otherwise complete idea.
The system excludes any content-internal marker by which an idea announces the actual existence of its object.
The system requires that reason disclose no necessary existential connection between distinct matters of fact.
The system excludes the possibility that imaginative detail or coherence alone can generate factual assent.
The system excludes non-intensive changes in the manner of conception that would preserve the identity of the represented object.
The system denies irreducible boundaries between conception, judgment, and reasoning as fundamental mental operations.
The system requires vivid fiction to remain distinguishable from belief when it lacks the steadiness and experiential relation characteristic of assent.
The foreclosed possibility is a purely conceptual passage from the idea of an object to its actual existence.
No intrinsic representational sign separates the actual from the merely conceivable.
A self-sufficient reason capable of constructing the factual world through necessity is structurally unavailable.
Complete discursive capture of belief is unavailable; explanation terminates in a commonly recognizable but indefinable feeling.
The absent criterion is an exact threshold separating exceptionally vivid fiction from genuine belief.
Conception of object O is required for belief in O, but conception of O does not entail belief in O.
Content of simple conception = content of existential conception = content of existential belief; therefore belief cannot be an added idea.
Conceivable P + conceivable not-P + non-demonstrative selection of P → difference located in mode of conception.
Same represented object + permissible variation only in force and vivacity → belief as intensified and stabilized conception.
Present perception → customary or associative transition → intensified related idea → factual assent.
Intensified idea → greater felt reality → increased influence on passion and imagination → governance of action.
Conception as base operation / demonstration as necessary determination / factual judgment as conception plus belief / reasoning as transition among conceptions.

Conception insufficient for belief → existence adds no idea → factual contraries remain conceivable → content cannot explain assent → difference relocated to manner → manner reduced to force and vivacity → belief defined through present-impression relation → judgment and reasoning reduced to modes of conception → definition confirmed by felt and practical effects.
Existence is reclassified from an added predicate into the object as conceived under a mode of assent.
Belief is reclassified from a content-producing judgment into an intensive modification of an idea.
Belief and disbelief become compatible with identical semantic comprehension.
The boundary between judgment and imagination is redrawn through force, firmness, and influence rather than representational capacity.
The scholastic division of conception, judgment, and reasoning collapses into variations of one conceiving operation.
Demonstrative and factual assent are separated by their determining principles: unintelligibility of the contrary versus associative vivacity.
The connection between cognition and action becomes intrinsic to belief’s degree of force rather than dependent on additional content.
Surface: the immediate object is the difference between merely conceiving a proposition and believing it.
Structural: the distinction is generated within an impression–idea economy governed by force, vivacity, present perception, and association.
Metastrategic: the conventional taxonomy of understanding is displaced by a unified theory of conception differentiated by modal intensity.
Ontological/Temporal: existence has no separable idea, while belief concerning absent objects depends on their present experiential or mnemonic anchoring.
CH_THN_SVNI:A1–CH_THN_SVNI:A17 are sufficient to reconstruct the movement from representational invariance to the intensive definition of belief.
The eliminative argument is strongest where identical content is shown to occur under conception, disbelief, and assent.
The positive reconstruction depends on the exclusivity of the impression–idea taxonomy and the claim that same-object variation is limited to force and vivacity.
The mechanism by which a present impression communicates vivacity through association remains compressed and is deferred beyond the section.
No exact degree or threshold distinguishing belief from exceptionally vivid imagination is supplied.
The claim that imagination cannot produce belief is asserted through felt difference more than independently demonstrated.
The vocabulary of force, vivacity, firmness, solidity, and steadiness marks an acknowledged explanatory compression.
The structure remains coherent only if intensification preserves representational identity while experiential relation preserves the distinction between belief and vivid fiction.

Reconstruction from the extracted system preserves the section’s real sequence: elimination of added content, relocation to manner, intensive definition, taxonomic revision, and phenomenological confirmation.

identity.title: Sect. VII. Of The Nature Of The Idea Or Belief

units.title: Sect. X. Of The Influence Of Belief

items.text: Central problem: explain how custom and habit produce belief-effects extending across reasoning, action, passion, and imagination.
Core thesis: belief is a simple idea intensified toward the force and vivacity of an impression.
Belief mediates between motivationally insufficient present impressions and the intolerable activation of the will by every passing idea.
Belief, passion, and imagination reciprocally transmit vivacity and thereby reinforce one another.
Poetry and madness test the mechanism by producing impression-like vivacity without the customary basis of serious conviction.
Argument type and movement: reconstructive naturalistic psychology; scale objection → motivational dilemma → scalar mechanism → reciprocal confirmation → counterfeit cases → rule-governed correction.
Pain and pleasure are the chief moving principles of human action.
Impressions and ideas differ originally in their degrees of force and vivacity.
Differences in the effects of perceptions arise from differences in their force and vivacity.
Present impressions actuate the mind more strongly than mere ideas.
Belief is almost necessary for an idea to excite the passions.
Ideas of objects believed to exist or to be forthcoming influence action and passion in the same manner as impressions, but ordinarily in a lesser degree.
Belief is a more vivid and intense conception of an idea.
Serious conviction arises when customary conjunction conveys vivacity from a present impression to a related idea.
An excited passion transfers its vivacity to the idea of its object.
Forceful and vivid ideas are agreeable to the imagination.
Truth and reality affect imaginative enjoyment by securing easy reception and mental acquiescence.
Vivacity can diffuse from one idea to other ideas related to it.
Repetition and familiarity can facilitate imaginative reception without producing judgmental belief.
A vigorous imagination can vivify ideas sufficiently to procure assent and authority.
Extraordinary bodily ferment can raise loose ideas to impression-like vivacity.
Poetical vivacity arises from present temperament rather than customary connections among objects.
Reflection and general rules regulate assent by discounting vivacity recognized as accidental or disconnected from reality.
Education is not a philosophically valid ground of assent, despite its power to produce assent.
The magnitude of an effect does not require an apparently substantial psychological principle.
The will is not governed exclusively by present impressions.
The will is not activated by every passing idea of good or evil.
Belief is not additional representational content attached to an idea.
Literal truth and absolute assurance are not necessary conditions of imaginative satisfaction.
Historical anchoring within fiction is not necessarily an attempt to deceive judgment.
Vivacity transmitted through accidental poetic relations does not amount to perfect assurance.
Poetical enthusiasm is not serious conviction, even when it produces stronger apparent agitation.
Apparent mental vehemence is not a reliable measure of genuine cognitive force.
Every increase in an idea’s occurrent vivacity does not require a corresponding increase in settled belief.
Selective vivification permits absent and future goods or evils to motivate action without allowing every fiction to disturb the will.
Because believed ideas imitate the effects of impressions, they must approach impressions in force and vivacity.
A prevailing passion increases assent to representations suited to that passion by transferring its vivacity to them.
Belief pleases the imagination by making represented objects enter the mind forcefully and without reluctance.
Familiarity can replace literal truth as a mechanism of imaginative admission.
A believed or familiar narrative component can vivify connected fictional components without converting the whole fiction into assured belief.
Eloquence can generate assent by transferring imaginative vivacity into judgment.
When bodily ferment gives every fiction impression-like force, truth and falsehood become operationally indistinguishable and act equally on the passions.
Poetically induced passions can entertain even when their real counterparts are painful because counterfeit belief excites the spirits without the weight of reality.
Reflection can dissipate poetical illusion by identifying its vivacity as accidental and reality-disconnected.
General rules can sustain full conviction despite local reductions in felt force and can resist assent despite local increases in imaginative vivacity.
Belief, causal inference, motivation, passion, aesthetic reception, persuasion, and madness operate within a common economy of distributed mental force.
Cognition and affect form a feedback system: belief excites passion, passion vivifies its object, and the vivified object strengthens belief.
Belief is not psychologically binary; inert fiction, poetic counterfeit belief, probable conviction, and impression-like certainty occupy differentiated positions within one mechanism.
The distinction between genuine and counterfeit conviction must be relocated from apparent intensity to causal provenance, felt character, and correction by general rules.
The mechanism that enables action toward absent realities also exposes judgment to capture by temperament, eloquence, repetition, and pathological vivification.
Belief cannot be a sui generis rational act independent of the manner in which an idea is conceived.
Representational content alone cannot determine motivational or affective efficacy.
Judgment, passion, and imagination cannot be causally sealed faculties.
Truth cannot possess an intrinsic psychological mark that automatically guarantees assent or imaginative pleasure.
First-order vividness cannot authenticate its own epistemic legitimacy.
Fiction and factual conviction cannot be separated by an impermeable boundary at the level of conception alone.
The foreclosed possibility is an infallible immediate criterion by which consciousness always distinguishes genuine belief from its counterfeit.
The system excludes a pure rational agency insulated from custom, bodily disposition, passion, and rhetoric.
No origin-independent warrant is supplied for the general rules that correct vivid appearances; their authority remains the terminal unformalized condition of epistemic discrimination.
Impressions alone → no motivation by foreseen objects; every idea efficacious → perpetual disturbance; selectively vivified ideas → viable motivational medium.
Present impression → customary relation → transferred force and vivacity → intensified idea → belief → action and passion.
Affecting object → incipient passion → diffusion into imagination → intensified object-idea → assent → reinforced passion.
Believed or familiar anchor → relational transmission → vivified fictional network → easy reception → imaginative and affective entertainment.
Temperament, eloquence, or bodily ferment → non-customary vivification → counterfeit belief; extreme vivification → collapse of truth-falsehood discrimination.
Reflection on source and reality-connection → application of general rules → correction of apparent intensity → restoration of graded conviction.

Educational resistance → scale objection → motivational extremes → belief as selective medium → definition by vivacity → passion-belief reciprocity → truth reduced to easy reception → poetic substitution → imaginative production of assent → madness as limit case → correction by reflection and general rules.
Belief is reclassified from a distinct judgmental content into a mode of conceiving an idea.
Motivation is extended from present sensation to absent and future objects through selective vivification.
Truth in imaginative works is reclassified as one mechanism of easy reception rather than an inviolable aesthetic requirement.
Judgment, passion, and imagination become reciprocally permeable rather than hierarchically independent.
Causal conviction, poetry, eloquence, and madness are placed on one field of vivification while remaining differentiated by source and regulation.
Epistemic correction shifts from measuring apparent agitation to applying second-order rules about causal origin and connection with reality.
Surface: belief modifies the effects of ideas on action, passion, and imaginative enjoyment.
Structural: mental force is transmitted through custom, affect, familiarity, and relations among ideas.
Metastrategic: phenomena of passion, fiction, eloquence, and madness are converted into tests of the general theory of belief.
Ontological/Temporal: absent and future objects acquire present efficacy through graded modes of perception rather than through direct presence.
The extracted axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the chapter’s principal definition, reciprocal mechanisms, limiting cases, and corrective closure.
The magnitude and qualitative dimensions of force and vivacity remain underdetermined.
The structure is coherent at the functional level because the same mechanism explains action, passion, imaginative reception, and counterfeit belief.
The strongest inference is the reciprocal confirmation obtained by showing belief vivifying passion and passion vivifying belief.
The inference from similarity of effects to similarity in force and vivacity depends on the compressed premise that force and vivacity exhaust the relevant differences among perceptions.
The claim that nature selected a motivational medium supplies a functional rationale rather than an independent causal demonstration.
The scalar reduction is strained by the claim that poetical imagery may appear more vivid than experience while remaining weaker and qualitatively different in feeling.
General rules repair this strain, but the chapter does not fully specify their origin, authority, or mode of operation.
Reconstruction preserves the real movement only if poetry and madness are retained as mechanism-testing cases rather than discarded as illustrations.

identity.title: Sect. X. Of The Influence Of Belief

units.title: Sect. XIII. Of Unphilosophical Probability

items.text: Problem: philosophically disallowed variations of belief arise from the same principles as sanctioned probability.
Thesis: every judgment short of knowledge consists in a degree of force and vivacity communicated to a perception.
Mechanism: present impression → customary transition → related idea; diminution of either source force or transitional facility weakens belief.
Diagnostic movement: temporal fading → inferential attenuation → homogeneous-chain qualification → prejudicial generalization.
Corrective movement: first-order custom mistakes accidental resemblance for efficacy; second-order general rules condemn that operation.
Structural contradiction: custom and rule-following generate unphilosophical probability and provide its only correction.
Argument type: reconstructive psychology joined to skeptical diagnosis and a unified causal account of probability.
Belief in existence is the force and vivacity of a perception in every judgment that does not amount to knowledge.
Memory possesses the greatest force and vivacity available to nondemonstrative belief.
Causal inference borrows vivacity from a present impression and transfers it to a related idea through habit.
Evidential force varies with the strength of the originating impression and the facility of the associative transition.
Repeated conjunction produces a customary transition of the imagination that precedes reflection and cannot be prevented by it.
Custom extends from identical cases to resembling cases, losing force by degrees as resemblance diminishes.
Temporal remoteness and heterogeneous inferential mediation dissipate vivacity independently of logical validity.
Resemblance among successive inferential links permits cognitive compression and limits the attenuation caused by numerical length.
In contrary experience, each remembered possibility separately affects the imagination, while net belief follows numerical superiority with a deduction for opposition.
Frequent conjunction enables salient accidental circumstances to evoke the effect associated with efficacious circumstances.
Reflective general rules derived from experience of the understanding distinguish efficacious circumstances from accidental conjunctions.
The more extensive and constant inference is attributed to judgment, while the irregular and uncertain exception is attributed to imagination.
Common, universal, direct, and unitary signs communicate vivacity more effectively than rare, oblique, or dispersed signs.
A lively idea and its corresponding passion can reciprocally amplify one another.
Philosophical and unphilosophical probabilities differ in normative authorization, not in the psychological principles generating them.
Actual conviction is not fixed by philosophy’s recognition of an argument as legitimate.
The unchanged content of an argument does not preserve invariant authority as its originating impression recedes.
The infallibility of individual links does not guarantee conviction across a heterogeneous inferential chain.
The numerical length of historical transmission does not by itself extinguish evidence.
Homogeneous copying is not correctly modeled as an indefinite series of independent probabilistic diminutions.
Resemblance to a familiar cause does not establish the presence of its efficacious circumstances.
Present observation does not automatically defeat a customary association.
General rules are not uniformly philosophical; rash generalization is itself a source of prejudice.
Reflection does not prevent the imagination’s initial customary transition.
Equal assent to the same conclusion does not entail equal imaginative or affective influence.
The common origin of judgment and imagination in custom does not prevent them from issuing opposed inferences.
From CH_THN_SXUP:A1 + CH_THN_SXUP:A3 + CH_THN_SXUP:A4 + CH_THN_SXUP:A7, the same remembered fact loses authority as its impression fades despite retaining the same propositional content.

From CH_THN_SXUP:A3 + CH_THN_SXUP:A4 + CH_THN_SXUP:A5 + CH_THN_SXUP:A7 + CH_THN_SXUP:A14, recent observations receive disproportionate weight because both their impressions and their customary transitions remain intact.
From CH_THN_SXUP:A3 + CH_THN_SXUP:A4 + CH_THN_SXUP:A7, demonstratively connected reasoning can psychologically degenerate into probability when it requires many distinct transitions.
From CH_THN_SXUP:A4 + CH_THN_SXUP:A8, historical evidence survives long transmission when repeated links are sufficiently homogeneous to be traversed as a compressed general sequence.
From CH_THN_SXUP:A7 + CH_THN_SXUP:A8, a chain composed of genuinely distinct probabilistic links would undergo repeated diminution, whereas homogeneous proof-preserving links need not.
From CH_THN_SXUP:A5 + CH_THN_SXUP:A6 + CH_THN_SXUP:A10, prejudice is ordinary causal habit extended from conspicuous resemblance while material differences are neglected.
From CH_THN_SXUP:A10 + CH_THN_SXUP:A11 + CH_THN_SXUP:A12, philosophical correction occurs when a more general rule reclassifies a first-order customary inference as accidental.

From CH_THN_SXUP:A1 + CH_THN_SXUP:A4 + CH_THN_SXUP:A12 + CH_THN_SXUP:A13 + CH_THN_SXUP:A14, convergence between judgment and a common sign produces stronger affect than an equally certain conclusion assembled from oblique signs.
From CH_THN_SXUP:A11 + CH_THN_SXUP:A13 + CH_THN_SXUP:A14, social rules can make an originally stronger offense indirectly less painful by supplying a vivid adverse inference about the offender.
From CH_THN_SXUP:A1 + CH_THN_SXUP:A2 + CH_THN_SXUP:A3 + CH_THN_SXUP:A4 + CH_THN_SXUP:A9, memory, proof, and probability form a descending continuum of vivacity rather than distinct species of belief.

From CH_THN_SXUP:A5 + CH_THN_SXUP:A10 + CH_THN_SXUP:A11 + CH_THN_SXUP:A12, philosophical correction redirects custom from first-order resemblance toward more extensive regularity rather than opposing custom with an independent faculty.
From CH_THN_SXUP:A1 + CH_THN_SXUP:A4 + CH_THN_SXUP:A7 + CH_THN_SXUP:A13, logical warrant and experienced conviction can vary independently because only the latter tracks the transmission of vivacity.
From CH_THN_SXUP:A7 + CH_THN_SXUP:A8 + CH_THN_SXUP:A13, effective inferential distance is determined by cognitive heterogeneity and labor rather than by the number of links alone.
From CH_THN_SXUP:A13 + CH_THN_SXUP:A14, modes of presentation can reorganize passion without altering the conclusion accepted by judgment.

From CH_THN_SXUP:A1 + CH_THN_SXUP:A2 + CH_THN_SXUP:A3 + CH_THN_SXUP:A9, proof and probability differ by the organization and intensity of one mechanism, not by possessing different psychological foundations.
From CH_THN_SXUP:A12 + CH_THN_SXUP:A15, philosophy remains disposition-sensitive because either the prejudicial rule or its corrective metarule may prevail in a particular mind.
No independent rational faculty produces belief outside the operations of custom, imagination, and vivacity.
No proposition carries an intrinsic belief-force invariant under memory, mediation, and presentation.
No causal discontinuity separates sanctioned probability from prejudice.
No simple accumulation of inferential links determines evidential loss without regard to their resemblance and cognitive organization.
No reflective correction permanently abolishes the first customary propensity it regulates.
No affective response remains insulated from the imaginative mode by which its object is conceived.
An extra-customary tribunal of reason is unavailable; philosophical authority can appear only as a more extensive and constant ordering of custom.
An invariant correspondence between logical validity and felt conviction is structurally foreclosed.
A final reconciliation between judgment and imagination is absent; corrective judgment competes with rather than extinguishes irregular transition.
A temporally and affectively invariant believing subject is unavailable within the system.
Repeated conjunction → custom.
Present impression + custom → imaginative transition → vivified related idea → belief.
Source faintness, temporal remoteness, diminished resemblance, contrary instances, or heterogeneous mediation → reduced vivacity → weakened evidence.
Homogeneous inferential links → compressed traversal → limited attenuation despite numerical length → preservation of historical belief.
Resemblance + salient accidental conjunction → first-order general rule → expected effect without efficacious condition → prejudice.
Reflection on prior operations + counterinstances → more general rule → accidental–efficacious distinction → corrective judgment.
First-order rule ↔ second-order rule → disposition-sensitive conflict between imagination and judgment.
Sign generality and unity → facilitated transition; sign rarity and dispersion → cognitive labor → diminished vivacity and passion.
Opposed remembered possibilities → separate imaginative forces → aggregation and cancellation → graded probability.
All outputs → single custom–imagination–vivacity architecture → normative division between philosophical and unphilosophical probability.

Sanctioned/unphilosophical disparity → common belief mechanism → recency effects → inferential attenuation → ancient-history objection → homogeneous-chain resolution → prejudice as extended custom → corrective metarules → conflict of general rules → presentational and affective consequences → unified theory of probability.
Philosophical probability and prejudice become differently regulated outputs of one psychological mechanism.
Evidential validity and actual conviction become separable dimensions.
Inferential distance is redrawn as cognitive heterogeneity rather than numerical length.
Prejudice is reclassified from an alien defect of reason into an excessive operation of ordinary causal habit.
The opposition between judgment and imagination becomes a conflict between first-order and second-order general rules.
Memory, proof, and probability become positions on a continuum of force rather than psychologically independent kinds.
Social and affective responses become functions of sign structure and transitional facility, not merely of what the judgment accepts.
Surface: belief varies with recency, inferential distance, generalization, and mode of presentation.
Structural: custom transfers vivacity through imagination, while resemblance, mediation, opposition, and sign form regulate that transfer.
Metastrategic: philosophy corrects natural bias only by redirecting the same generalizing mechanism that produced it.
Ontological/Temporal: belief is a temporally variable event of force-transmission rather than an invariant possession attached to propositional content.
The axioms are sufficient to reconstruct the four unphilosophical probabilities, the historical-evidence objection, the conflict of general rules, and the final unification of belief.
The quantitative relation between impression-strength, transitional facility, and resulting conviction remains unspecified.
The authority of the “more general and authentic” corrective rule remains underdetermined, and the complete regulative rules are deferred beyond the chapter.
The system is internally coherent as a psychological explanation of variations in conviction.
Its strongest operation is the derivation of multiple evidential distortions from a single model of vivacity transmission.
The historical repair depends on treating initial testimony as proof and subsequent transmission as cognitively homogeneous.
The central fault line is that custom supplies prejudice, philosophical correction, and the standard by which correction is preferred.
The argument depends on inherited premises that belief is vivacity and causal reasoning is customary transition rather than establishing them anew.
Reconstruction preserves the real movement only if historical homogeneity is treated as a qualification of attenuation and the social cases as tests of the same mechanism.

identity.title: Sect. XIII. Of Unphilosophical Probability

units.title: Sect. XV. Rules By Which To Judge Of Causes And Effects

items.text: Problem: a priori inspection cannot distinguish actual causal relations from unrestricted causal possibilities.
Core thesis: actual causation is judged through constant conjunction constrained by contiguity, temporal priority, and causal uniformity.
Argument type: reconstructive and methodological, terminating in an anti-scholastic restriction on formal rules.
Movement: a priori causal indeterminacy → empirical criteria → comparative rules → controlled experimentation.
Comparative regularities isolate common causes, differentiating causes, compound effects, and incomplete causes.
Formal rule-production yields to recursive experimental application requiring judgment, perseverance, and widened experience.
Neither causal capacity nor causal incapacity can be determined by mere inspection independent of experience.
No objects are properly contrary except existence and non-existence.
Causation depends wholly on constant conjunction.
Cause and effect are contiguous in space and time.
A cause is temporally prior to its effect.
The same cause always produces the same effect.
The same effect never arises except from the same cause.
Every natural phenomenon is compounded and modified by multiple circumstances.
Decisive causal inquiry requires experimentally separating superfluous circumstances from essential ones.
Every new experiment remains subject to renewed circumstance-analysis.
The operative circumstances of moral phenomena are more numerous, implicit, and obscure than those of natural phenomena.
Increased security requires enlargement of the experimental sphere.
No object is identifiable as a cause or non-cause through mere conception.
No intrinsic classification of objects restricts in advance what may cause what.
Mere occurrence without constant conjunction does not constitute causation.
A non-contiguous or effect-prior relation cannot qualify as causal.
A few experiments cannot establish proportional causal decomposition.
Covariation within an observed range does not license indefinite extrapolation beyond that range.
An object fully present before the effect cannot be the sole complete cause of that effect.
Formal logical precepts neither eliminate experimental judgment nor establish the superiority of scholastic reasoning.
Before experience, anything imaginable remains a possible cause or effect of anything else.
A clear causal experiment licenses projection to phenomena of the same kind without awaiting renewed constant repetition.
When different objects produce the same effect, causation must be assigned to a quality common to them.
When resembling objects produce different effects, the causal difference must be assigned to the circumstance in which they differ.
Adequately repeated proportional covariation indicates a compound effect composed of effects corresponding to parts of the cause.
If a putative cause is fully present while its effect is absent, an auxiliary causal principle is required.
Causal investigation proceeds recursively by varying circumstances, testing essentiality, and submitting each result to renewed variation.
Complex experimental application requires perseverance in inquiry and sagacity in selecting discriminating tests.
Moral inquiry requires broader experimentation because its operative variables are less directly identifiable.
Causal rules regulate inference among experienced regularities rather than disclose intrinsic productive powers.
Within an adequately specified class, apparent irregularity is reassigned to an unisolated difference, compound contribution, or missing co-cause rather than admitted as brute exception.
Experimental correction is structurally open-ended because every control becomes a new object of control.
Causal method cannot be reduced to a self-applying algorithm because no rule independently selects the decisive experimental variation.
Moral inquiry employs the same causal architecture as natural inquiry under conditions of greater variable opacity.
Causal identity shifts from whole objects to experimentally isolated qualities or circumstances.
Objects must not possess causally legible powers available independently of observed conjunction.
Kinds, qualities, and relevant similarities must not be wholly unstable, or comparative causal projection becomes impossible.
Essential circumstances must not be experimentally inseparable in principle.
Causal irregularity must not be brute; it must remain attributable to an undiscovered difference, scope condition, or auxiliary cause.
The obscurity of moral circumstances must not amount to absolute inaccessibility, or enlarged experimentation could provide no increased security.
No observable necessary connection beyond regular conjunction is available to ground causal judgment.
No a priori ontology assigns fixed causal or receptive roles to kinds of objects.
No self-executing logical system can replace experimental discrimination and human judgment.
No terminal experiment closes causal inquiry against further circumstance-analysis.
Non-contrariety + absence of a priori causal discrimination → unrestricted candidate causal relations.
Candidate relation + spatial-temporal contiguity + cause-priority + constant conjunction → causal attribution.
Clear causal instance + cause-effect uniformity → projection to phenomena of the same kind.
Same effect across differing objects → isolate common circumstance; differing effects across resembling objects → isolate differing circumstance.
Repeated proportional part-covariation → compound-effect decomposition; full cause without effect → incomplete-cause diagnosis.
Compound phenomenon → remove or vary circumstance → test essentiality → reanalyze resulting experiment → repeat.
Increasing circumstantial complexity → increasing dependence on perseverance, sagacity, and expanded experimental range.

A priori causal indeterminacy → constant conjunction as empirical ground → spatiotemporal and uniformity rules → comparative isolation → decomposition and completion tests → recursive experimental difficulty → enlargement of experience.
Causal possibility is detached from the conceptual content of objects and left open pending experience.
Actual causes are distinguished from merely possible causes by observed relational structure rather than intrinsic intelligibility.
Resemblance and difference become experimental operators for locating causal circumstances.
Disappointed expectation becomes evidence of an omitted distinction or condition rather than an immediate defeat of causal uniformity.
Proportional covariation reclassifies effects as compounds while restricting inference to adequately tested ranges.
